s: Temperature entered computation through the Metropolis et al. 1953 Monte Carlo method, which weights configurations by exp(-E/kT); simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi 1983) turned the analogy to annealing in solids into a general optimisation method. (The further claim that Smolensky did not invent temperature in neural nets is model knowledge, not checked here.)

s: In Smolensky's harmony theory, processors choose values that increase harmony, with randomness set by a computational temperature T that is lowered to zero; he states that the machine will eventually 'freeze' into a completion that maximizes harmony. He describes harmonium as a special case of the Boltzmann machine whose connections run only between two layers (the architecture later called the restricted Boltzmann machine).

They attribute this mainly to InstructGPT contributing less diverse text; user-written text was unaffected.

src.l: Vishakh Padmakumar, He He, 2024, Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?

s: Huh et al. hypothesize that representations in large neural networks are converging, across architectures and data modalities, toward a shared statistical model of reality, which they call the platonic representation. They also discuss limitations and counterexamples.

src.l: Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Tongzhou Wang, Phillip Isola, 2024, The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Tongzhou Wang, Phillip Isola, 2024, The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
J. Derek Lomas, 2026, Research Review: Math, Harmony & the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (SEMF talk prep, 7 March 2026)

s: Baek, Liu, Tyagi & Tegmark define harmonic loss: logits are Euclidean distances d_i from the representation to class-center weights, and probability is HarMax, p_i = (1/d_i^n) / sum_j (1/d_j^n), with n a 'harmonic exponent'. The paper is scale-invariant with a finite convergence point (the class center). The authors report better interpretability, less data needed to generalise and reduced grokking than cross-entropy.

src.l: David D. Baek, Ziming Liu, Riya Tyagi, Max Tegmark, 2025, Harmonic Loss Trains Interpretable AI Models

s: Soudry et al. prove that gradient descent on unregularised logistic (and similar exponential-tail) losses over linearly separable data diverges in norm, w(t) = w_hat log t + rho(t), while converging in direction to the max-margin (hard-margin SVM) solution; convergence in direction is only logarithmically slow.

src.l: Daniel Soudry, Elad Hoffer, Mor Shpigel Nacson, Suriya Gunasekar, Nathan Srebro, 2018, The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data

s: Gröger, Wen & Brbić (Feb 2026) report that common representational-similarity metrics are inflated by network depth and width; after permutation-based null calibration, the apparent global convergence reported for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis largely disappears, while local neighbourhood similarity (not local distances) keeps significant cross-modal agreement. They propose the 'Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis': networks converge to shared local neighbourhood relationships.

src.l: Fabian Gröger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbić, 2026, Revisiting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: An Aristotelian View

s: The strongest published objection to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis as evidence of convergence: similarity metrics are confounded by model scale, and after calibration global convergence mostly disappears. Only shared local neighbourhood structure survives. Any use of PRH as support for 'AI converges on a shared whole' must say which of the two is meant.

src.l: Fabian Gröger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbić, 2026, Revisiting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: An Aristotelian View
src.loc: Abstract; Sec. on model-size trend; 'Relationship to the Platonic hypothesis'

s: Quanta (Jan 2026) reports the Platonic Representation Hypothesis debate: Isola argues that commonalities have more explanatory power than differences; Efros (UC Berkeley) argues the differences between models reveal more than the similarities, and notes that the Wikipedia image-text dataset used by Huh contains very similar information in both by design; Christopher Wolfram (U Chicago) cautions that results from one dataset may not generalise to others.

s: Hopfield (1982) gave a model in which a system of simple, asynchronously updating neuron-like units has collective properties that include content-addressable memory, recovering a whole memory from a sufficiently large subpart.

src.l: John J. Hopfield, 1982, Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities

s: Hopfield's asynchronous threshold dynamics, for symmetric T_ij, decrease the energy E = -1/2 sum_{i!=j} T_ij V_i V_j monotonically, so stable memory states are local minima. The energy has the same form as the negative of Smolensky's harmony, which makes it a precursor of the Boltzmann-machine energy (the lineage is our interpretation, not Hopfield's claim).

src.l: John J. Hopfield, 1982, Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities

s: Bostrom (2012) states the orthogonality thesis as: intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary, so that more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal. He notes caveats, including memory and processing demands of holding a goal set, and that a mind with an urgent desire to be stupid might not stay intelligent.

src.l: Nick Bostrom, 2012, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents

s: Grietzer's 'A Theory of Vibe' (Glass Bead, Site 1, 2017) models a vibe on the autoencoder: a network that learns to reconstruct a set of objects, whose 'canon' (inputs reconstructed with zero error) is individually complex but collectively simple; a style or vibe is such a set aligned to one generative logic, tied to Heidegger's Stimmung, grasped as 'sensible cognition' and shareable only by building idealised sets, not by paraphrase.

src.l: Peli Grietzer, 2017, A Theory of Vibe

s: Philolaus holds that like things need no harmony; harmony is required precisely to lock together things that are unlike, unrelated and unequal in rank.

src.l: Philolaus, F. W. A. Mullach (ed.), 5th c. BCE (ed. 1881), Fragmenta philosophorum graecorum, vol. 2 (Philolai fragmenta)
src.loc: p. 1 [scan 110], fr. on nature and harmony (Stobaeus Ecl. I.21.7d; DK 44 B6)
src.q: Now, things that were similar and of the same kind had no need of harmony; but things that were dissimilar and neither of the same kind nor of equal rank, had to be locked together by such a harmony if they were to be held together in a world.
src.qo: Τὰ μὲν ὦν ὁμοῖα καὶ ὁμόφυλα ἁρμονίας οὐθὲν ἐπεδέοντο· τὰ δὲ ἀνομοῖα μηδὲ ὁμόφυλα μηδὲ ἰσοτελῆ, ἀνάγκα τᾷ τοιαύτᾳ ἁρμονίᾳ συγκεκλεῖσθαι, εἰ μέλλοντι ἐν κόσμῳ κατέχεσθαι.

s: Philolaus defines harmonia concretely as the octave (fourth + fifth) and states it contains five 9:8 tones and two dieses — the octave does not divide evenly into whole tones.

src.l: Philolaus, F. W. A. Mullach (ed.), 5th c. BCE (ed. 1881), Fragmenta philosophorum graecorum, vol. 2 (Philolai fragmenta)
src.q: Thus harmony contains five epogdoa and two dieses

s: Philolaus claims everything that is known has number, since nothing can be thought or known without it.

src.l: Philolaus, F. W. A. Mullach (ed.), 5th c. BCE (ed. 1881), Fragmenta philosophorum graecorum, vol. 2 (Philolai fragmenta)
src.q: And indeed all things that are known have a number. For it is not possible for anything to be either thought of or known without this.
src.qo: Καὶ πάντα γα μὰν τὰ γιγνωσκόμενα ἀριθμὸν ἔχοντι. Οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε οὐθὲν οὔτε νοηθῆμεν οὔτε γνωσθῆμεν ἄνευ τούτω.

s: Aristotle reports that the Pythagoreans, seeing musical harmonies depend on number, took the elements of number to be the elements of all things and the whole heaven to be a harmony and a number.

src.l: Aristotle, 4th c. BCE (Aldine 1552), Metaphysics (in Aristotelis Problemata ... et Metaphysices, tomus 4)
src.q: Furthermore, they saw that the properties and ratios of musical harmonies depend on numbers. Since all other things seemed to be modeled in their whole nature after numbers, and numbers are the first things in all of nature, they supposed the elements of numbers to be the elements of all existing things. They even thought that the whole heaven was a harmony and a number.
src.qo: ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ἁρμονικῶν ἐν ἀριθμοῖς ὁρῶντες καὶ τὰ πάθη καὶ τοὺς λόγους. ἐπειδὴ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς ἐ- φαίνετο τὴν φύσιν ἀφωμοιῶσθαι πᾶσιν, οἱ δ' ἀριθμοὶ πάσης τῆς φύσεως πρῶτοι, τὰ τῶν ἀριθμῶν στοιχεῖα, τῶν ὄντων στοιχεῖα πάν- των ὑπέλαβον. καὶ ὅσα εἶχον καὶ τὸν ὅλον οὐρανὸν ἁρμονίαν εἶναι καὶ ἀ- ριθμόν.

s: Aristotle charges that the Pythagoreans fitted the heavens to their numbers, inventing a counter-earth so that the moving heavenly bodies would total the 'perfect' ten.

src.l: Aristotle, 4th c. BCE (Aldine 1552), Metaphysics (in Aristotelis Problemata ... et Metaphysices, tomus 4)
src.q: If there was a gap anywhere, they hurried to fill it so that their entire system would be coherent. I mean, for example, that since the decad is thought to be perfect and to encompass the whole nature of numbers, they say the bodies moving in the heavens are ten. But since only nine are visible, they create a tenth, the counter-earth.

s: Aristotle reports a Pythagorean table of ten paired principles (limit/unlimited, odd/even, one/plurality, right/left, male/female, rest/motion, straight/curved, light/dark, good/bad, square/oblong) and concludes that for them opposites are the principles of things.

src.l: Aristotle, 4th c. BCE (Aldine 1552), Metaphysics (in Aristotelis Problemata ... et Metaphysices, tomus 4)
src.q: they say there are ten principles arranged in coordinate pairs: Limit and Unlimited; Odd and Even; One and Plurality; Right and Left; Male and Female; Resting and Moving; Straight and Curved; Light and Darkness; Good and Bad; Square and Oblong.

s: De Mundo argues nature makes concord from opposites rather than from like things, citing music (high and low, long and short notes mixed into one harmony), painting and grammar, and quoting Heraclitus.

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE (MS 1490), De Mundo (Peri Kosmou), in Bern Burgerbibliothek Cod. 402 (Theophrastus–Aristotle corpus)
src.q: Perhaps nature strives for opposites and desires to create harmony from these, not from like things.
src.qo: ἴσως δὲ τῶν ἐναντίων ἡ φύσις γλίχετ[αι] καὶ ἐκ τούτων ἀποτελεῖν τὸ σύμφωνον οὐκ ἐκ τῶν ὁμοίων.

s: Heraclitus (as quoted in De Mundo): couplings are wholes and not wholes, concordant and discordant; from all things one and from one all things — discord lies inside the whole.

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE (MS 1490), De Mundo (Peri Kosmou), in Bern Burgerbibliothek Cod. 402 (Theophrastus–Aristotle corpus)
src.loc: De Mundo 5, 396b (DK 22 B10); Bern Cod. 402 p. 245
src.q: Couplings are wholes and not wholes, concurring and differing, concordant and discordant, and from all things one, and from one all things.
src.qo: συλλάψιες ὅλα, καὶ οὐχ ὅλα συμφερόμενον καὶ διαφερόμενον, συνᾷδον καὶ διᾷδον, καὶ ἐκ πάντων ἕν, καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντα.

s: De Mundo compares the cosmos to a city that holds together poor and rich, young and old, weak and strong, calling this the most wonderful thing about political harmony.

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE (MS 1490), De Mundo (Peri Kosmou), in Bern Burgerbibliothek Cod. 402 (Theophrastus–Aristotle corpus)
src.q: It is as if some were to wonder about a city, how it remains constituted from opposing peoples: I mean poor and rich, young and old, weak and strong, wicked and good. They are ignorant that this is the most wonderful thing about political harmony
src.qo: ὡς κἂν εἰ πόλιν τινὲς θαυμά- ζοιεν, ὅπως διαμένει συνεστηκυῖα ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων ἐθνῶν, πενήτων λέγω καὶ πλουσίων, νέων καὶ γερόντων, ἀσθενῶν ἰσχυρῶν, πονηρῶν, χρηστῶν.

s: De Mundo names equality — no element more powerful than another — as in some way the savior of concord.

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE (MS 1490), De Mundo (Peri Kosmou), in Bern Burgerbibliothek Cod. 402 (Theophrastus–Aristotle corpus)
src.q: And of this agreement, it is equality and the fact that none of them is more powerful than another. ... with nature teaching in the greater matters that equality is in some way the savior of concord.
src.qo: τῆς δὲ ὁμολογίας, ἡ ἰσομοιρί καὶ τὸ μηδὲν αὐτῶν πλέον δύνασθαι ἑτέρου. τὴν γὰρ ἰσην ἀντί- στασιν ἔχει τὰ βαρέα πρὸς τὰ κοῦφα, καὶ τὰ θερμὰ πρὸς τὰ ψυχρά, τῆς φύσεως ἐπὶ τῶν μειζόνων διδασκούσης, ὅτι τὸ ἴσον σωστικόν πως ἐστὶ ὁμονοίας.

s: Alexander of Aphrodisias distinguishes the harmony from what is produced by things arranged through harmony: a cithara is tuned even when silent, and not every ratio-mixture is a harmony — against the soul-as-harmony view.

src.l: Alexander of Aphrodisias, Hieronymus Donatus (tr.), c. 200 CE (Latin 1495), De anima ex Aristotelis institutione
src.q: For it is not the same thing for a cithara to be tuned by harmony and to emit sounds. For it is already tuned by harmony, even if it emits no sounds.
src.qo: Namque non eadem res est in cythara per harmoniam aptari et sonos edere. Iam enim aptata est per harmoniam potest: tametsi sonos nullos edat.

s: Iamblichus says Pythagoras sought a stable, unerring instrument for hearing, as sight has the compass and ruler and touch the balance — harmony begins as a measurement problem.

src.l: Iamblichus, c. 300 CE (MS c. 1450), Works (Greek MS), incl. On the Pythagorean Life
src.q: Being once in thought and intense calculation, as to whether he might be able to devise some stable and unmistakable instrumental aid for hearing, such as sight has through the compass and the ruler, or through sighting instruments.
src.qo: ἐν φροντίδι ποτὲ καὶ λογισμῷ συντεταμένῳ ὑπάρχων, εἰ ἄρα δύναιτο τῇ ἀκοῇ βοήθειάν τινα ὀργανικὴν ἐπινοῆσαι παγίαν καὶ ἀπαραλόγιστον. οἵαν ἡ μὲν ὄψις διὰ τοῦ διαβήτου καὶ διὰ τοῦ κανόνος, ἢ καὶ διὰ διοπτρῶν ἔχειν

s: Iamblichus narrates Pythagoras hearing consonant hammers in a smithy, attributing pitch to the hammers' weights, then reproducing the octave, fifth and fourth with strings hung with weights 6, 8, 9, 12.

src.l: Iamblichus, c. 300 CE (MS c. 1450), Works (Greek MS), incl. On the Pythagorean Life
src.q: he determined the difference of the sound—not from the force of those striking, nor from the shapes of the hammers, nor from the shifting of the iron being worked—having accurately grasped the weights and equal inclinations of the hammers
src.qo: ῥαιόντων· καὶ τοῖς ἤχοις παραμὶξ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀποδιδομένων, πλὴν μιᾶς συζυγίας· ἐπεγίνωσκε δ' ἐν αὐτοῖς, τήν τε διὰ πασῶν, τήν τε διὰ πέντε, καὶ τὴν διὰ τεσσάρων συμφωνίαν· τὴν δὲ μεταξὺ τῆς τε διὰ τεσσάρων καὶ τῆς διὰ πέντε, ἀ- σύμφωνον μὲν ἑώρα αὐτὴν καθ' ἑαυτήν, συμπλη- ρωτικὴν δὲ τῆς ἐν αὐτοῖς μεγεθότητος. ἀσμε- νίσας δὲ ὡς κατὰ θεὸν συμβάσης αὐτῷ τῆς προθέσεως, εἰσέ- δραμεν εἰς τὸ χαλκεῖον· καὶ ποικίλαις πείραις παρὰ τῶν ἐν ταῖς ῥαιστῆρσι γινομένων ὡρῶν τὴν διαφορὰν τοῦ ἤχου, οὐχὶ παρὰ τὴν τῶν ῥαιόντων βίαν, οὔτε παρὰ τὰ σχήματα τῶν σφυρῶν, οὐδὲ παρὰ τὴν τοῦ ἐλαυνομένου σιδήρου μετάθεσιν, σηκώματα ἀκριβῶς ἐκλαβὼν καὶ ῥοπὰς ἴσας τὰς τῶν ῥαιστήρων,

s: Galileo (in Mersenne's French) explains that a struck string sets unstruck strings vibrating at unison, octave and fifth because their natural periods match the repeated pushes of the air, like timed breaths swinging a pendulum.

src.l: Galileo Galilei, Marin Mersenne (adapt.), 1639, Les nouvelles pensées de Galilée

src.qo: Expliquer pourquoy une chorde de Luth ou d'Espinette touchee fait branler les autres chordes non touchees, qui sont à l'unisson, à l'octave, & à la quinte.

s: Rameau holds that every sounding body carries within itself the harmony it makes resonate and is its generator (fundamental sound).

src.l: Jean-Philippe Rameau, 1750, Démonstration du principe de l'harmonie
src.q: Every sonorous body, taken individually, is always understood to carry with it the same harmony that it makes resonate; it is its generator
src.qo: Tout corps sonore, pris en particulier, est toujours censé porter avec lui la même har- monie qu'il fait résonner, il en est le générateur,

src.l: Gaspar Ens, 1636, Thaumaturgus Mathematicus
src.q: To make the string of a lute tremble perceptibly without being touched by anyone.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1662, Kircherus Jesuita Germanus Germaniae redonatus (German Musurgia abridgement)
src.q: it resonated and sounded by itself at intervals several times
src.qo: frei von sich selbsten per intervalla etlich mal resoniret und gelautet hat/

src.l: Kaspar Schott, 1674, Magiae universalis naturae et artis, pars II, acustica
src.q: It follows furthermore how one might exhibit sympathetic organic music
src.qo: Sequitur præterea, quomodo quis musicam sympathicam organicam exhibere,

src.l: William Holder, 1731, A Treatise of the Natural Grounds and Principles of Harmony
src.q: GALILEO, from this Doctrine of Pendulums, easily and naturally explains the so much admired sympathy of Consonant strings

src.q: in this life every soul is captivated by musical sounds because it carries into the body the memory of the music whose glory it had in heaven
src.qo: quia i cor pus defert memoriam muli ce. cuius in celo fuit glcia.

s: Proclus: all bodies are preserved on account of harmony and good order; the beautiful is the well-rhythmed and well-ordered.

src.l: Proclus, 5th c. CE (MS), In Platonis Rempublicam commentarii
src.q: So that all bodies are preserved on account of harmony and good order, which is in all things that exist.

s: Ficino argues for a communion between the music of the soul and of the body, so that both may be tempered by the same physician-musician.

s: In the Timaeus (in Jowett's rendering) the god divides the soul-stuff in the ratios 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27, fills the double and triple intervals with two kinds of means, and introduces ratios of 3:2, 4:3 and 9:8, leaving a remnant of 256:243.

s: Thomas Taylor's introduction to the Timaeus lists the soul's numbers as 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27 and explains arithmetical, geometrical and harmonic proportion, with 6, 4, 3 as the harmonic example.

src.l: Plato, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1793, The Cratylus, Phaedo, Parmenides, and Timaeus of Plato

s: Kepler dates the discovery of the period-distance rule in Harmonices Mundi V.3: the idea came to him on 8 March 1618 but was rejected after a calculation error, and returned on 15 May 1618, when it agreed with his seventeen years of work on Brahe's observations.

src.loc: Book V, ch. 3, heading VIII; scan 316, printed p. 189
src.q: it was conceived in the mind on the 8th of March of this year, 1618, but brought to calculations unluckily, and therefore rejected as false. Finally, returning on the 15th of May with a new impulse, it overcame the darkness of my mind

s: In Republic IX (577c-578a) Socrates argues that the tyrannical man is like the tyrannized city: the best parts of his soul are enslaved to a small, most wicked and mad part, so the soul as a whole has least power to do what it wishes and is driven by a gadfly, full of confusion and regret.

src.l: Plato, n.d., Platos Republic (Greek text with English)
src.q: Are not those parts of his soul enslaved which were the most virtuous, while a small part—the most wicked and the most mad—acts as the master?
src.qo: καὶ ταῦτα αὐτῆς τὰ μέρη δουλεύειν, ἅπερ ἦν ἐπιεικέστατα, σμικρὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ μοχθηρότατον καὶ μανικώτατον δεσπόζειν ;

src.l: Plato, n.d., Platos Republic (Greek text with English)
src.q: the tyrannized soul, as well, will have the least power to do what it wishes—speaking of the soul as a whole.

s: At the end of Republic IX (591d-592b) the wise man tunes the harmony of his body for the sake of the concord (symphonia) in his soul, and the city described in the dialogue, which may exist nowhere on earth, is a pattern laid up in heaven by which a person can found a city within himself.

src.l: Plato, n.d., Platos Republic (Greek text with English)
src.q: he will always be seen adjusting the harmony of the body for the sake of the symphony in his soul
src.qo: ἀλλ᾽ ἀεὶ τὴν ἐν τῷ σώματι

src.l: Plato, n.d., Platos Republic (Greek text with English)
src.q: a pattern is laid up in heaven for him who desires to see it, and seeing it, to found a city within himself
src.qo: ἀνάκειται τῷ βουλομένῳ ὁρᾶν καὶ ὁρῶντι ἑαυτὸν p. 592. κατοικίζειν.

s: Agrippa (I.10) calls certain virtues of things 'occult' because their causes are hidden from the human intellect, so that philosophers acquired most of them by long experience rather than by the investigation of reason; such virtues act strongly in small quantities, unlike elemental qualities.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera, in duos tomos concinne digesta, vol. 1
src.q: They are called properly occult properties, because their causes are latent, such that the human intellect cannot investigate them throughout; wherefore philosophers have obtained the greatest part of them by long experience more than by the investigation of reason.
src.qo: Vocantur autem proprie proprietates occultæ, quia causæ earum latentes sunt, ita quòd humanus intellectus non potest eas vsquequaque inuestigare: quare philosophi maximam earum partem longa experientia plus quàm rationis indagine adepti sunt.

s: Agrippa (I.15, 'How we ought to investigate and experience the virtues of things through the path taken from similarity') says occult properties are hidden from the senses and scarcely known to reason, investigable only 'through experience and conjectures', and that the method is likeness: every thing moves and converts to its like.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.q: every thing moves and converts to its like, and inclines toward itself according to its whole power

s: In the first edition of the Opticks (1704) Newton asks whether rays of different colours make vibrations of different sizes that excite colour sensations as air vibrations excite sounds (Qu. 13), and whether 'the harmony and discord of Colours' might arise 'from the proportions of the vibrations propagated through the fibres of the optick Nerves into the Brain', as harmony and discord of sounds arise from the proportions of air vibrations (Qu. 14).

src.l: Isaac Newton, 1704, Opticks (first edition)
src.q: May not the harmony and discord of Colours arise from the proportions of the vibrations propagated through the fibres of the optick Nerves into the Brain, as the harmony and discord of sounds arises from the proportions of the vibrations of the Air?

s: Goethe's historical volume of the Farbenlehre (1810) quotes an account of Malebranche's theory in which colours, like tones, arise from faster or slower 'vibrations of pressure' with diverse numerical ratios, followed by the caution: 'In music, one has determined the ratios of numbers that produce the various tones; but it is not to be hoped that this will also succeed with colors.'

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Zweyter Band (Historischer Teil)
src.q: In music, one has determined the ratios of numbers that produce the various tones; but it is not to be hoped that this will also succeed with colors.
src.qo: Man hat in der Musik die Verhältnisse der Zahlen bestimmt, welche die verschiedenen Töne hervorbringen; aber es läßt sich nicht hoffen, daß dieses auch bey den Farben gelinge.

s: Plotinus (Enn. IV.5.1-3) argues that seeing does not happen because the air between eye and object is affected, as wax takes an impression: a fire or a beacon is seen across darkness that it does not light. Perception at a distance works because the cosmos is one living being in sympathy with itself (sympathes to zoon); without that sympathy no part could share in the power of a distant part.

src.l: Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1580, Plotini operum philosophicorum omnium libri LIV (Greek-Latin, with Ficino's commentary)
src.q: For perhaps sense exists in this way because the entire living being is sympathetic to itself. If this were not so, how could one part share in the power of another, especially one far away?

src.l: Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1580, Plotini operum philosophicorum omnium libri LIV (Greek-Latin, with Ficino's commentary)
src.q: vision does not occur because the medium is physically affected

s: In his commentary on Enn. IV.5 (first printed 1492) Ficino sums up Plotinus: sight and its object act on each other by a conformity of sympathy even when the medium suffers nothing, as when one string sounds and another trembles, one man yawns and another yawns, and when one friend imagines something, sometimes his closest friend imagines the same. He adds that the common life of the world tunes sense to the sensible as one moved lyre string moves another.

src.l: Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1580, Plotini operum philosophicorum omnium libri LIV (Greek-Latin, with Ficino's commentary)
src.loc: Ficino, comm. on Enn. IV.5.2; p. 449 [scan 480]
src.q: just as when one string vibrates, another string nearby also trembles; or when one person yawns, another follows; or when a friend imagines something very dear, sometimes his closest friend imagines the same thing

src.l: Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1580, Plotini operum philosophicorum omnium libri LIV (Greek-Latin, with Ficino's commentary)
src.loc: Ficino, comm. on Enn. IV.5.2; p. 444 [scan 479]
src.q: just as when one string is moved on a lyre, another immediately moves in harmony

s: Problemata Book VII is titled 'Things arising from sympathy' (hosa ek sympatheias) and collects bodily contagion between people: why we yawn when others yawn, urinate when others do, set our teeth on edge watching someone eat sour things, faint at seeing a hanging, and 'suffer with' someone being cut or burned. Its explanations are memory and imagination ('the memory produces the movement') and kinship: 'our nature is common to all'; the eye 'most becomes like what it sees' and is disturbed by looking at a disturbed eye.

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: Then, the memory produces the movement, just as it does with sexual desire or hunger.

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: Is it because our nature is common to all? Thus, when one sees such a thing, one suffers with the sufferer because of kinship.

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: of all the parts it most becomes like what it sees, so that it is moved by what is moving

s: Problemata XIX.40 asks why we enjoy hearing songs we already know, and offers that the listener is 'in sympathy' (sympathes) with the singer of what is familiar: 'he sings along with him', and everyone sings when glad.

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: Or is it because the listener feels sympathy with the one singing what is familiar? For he sings along with him.

s: Problemata XIX.42 is an early written report of sympathetic resonance: when the nete is struck and stopped, the hypate an octave below 'alone seems to sound in response'. The explanations offered are cautious: the dying nete becomes like the hypate's sound, so by similarity it seems to move it; or the struck string moves the bridge, which moves all the strings, and the hypate's share is loudest because the nete's ending coincides with its own sound. The author notes it is a case where 'we cannot know the exact truth either by reasoning or by perception'.

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: Why, if one strikes the nete and stops it, does the hypate alone seem to sound in response?

src.l: Aristotle, pseudo-Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera, ed. Bekker, Vol. 2 (incl. Problemata)
src.q: reasonably then, because of the similarity, the nete seems to move the hypate

s: Cicero (De divinatione II.33-34, 44 BCE) reports the evidence the Stoics collected for a natural kinship (cognatio) among distant things: mouse livers grow in winter, pennyroyal blooms at the solstice, 'when certain strings of the lyre are struck others sound', shellfish wax and wane with the moon, tides follow the moon. He grants the kinship but rejects divination built on it, mocking any 'sympathy, as the Greeks term it' between a cleft liver and his purse.

src.l: Cicero, W. A. Falconer (tr.), 1923, De senectute, De amicitia, De divinatione (Loeb 154)
src.q: that at times when certain strings of the lyre are struck others sound

src.l: Cicero, W. A. Falconer (tr.), 1923, De senectute, De amicitia, De divinatione (Loeb 154)
src.q: What natural tie, or what 'symphony,' so to speak, or association, or what 'sympathy,' as the Greeks term it, can there be between a cleft in a liver and a petty addition to my purse?

s: Diogenes Laertius (VII.138-140) reports Chrysippus and Posidonius: mind pervades every part of the cosmos as soul pervades us, more in some parts and less in others, so the whole cosmos is one ensouled, rational animal; there is no void inside it, and this unity 'forces' the breathing-together and co-tension (sympnoia kai syntonia) of heavenly things with earthly ones.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, 1533, De vitis, dogmatibus et apophthegmatibus philosophorum (Greek editio princeps)
src.q: And in the world there is no void, but it is unified. For this forces the sympathy and coherence of heavenly things toward earthly things.

s: Marcus Aurelius (VI.38, IV.40) tells himself to meditate on the interdependence of all things: they are mutually intertwined and 'have a liking for one another', consequent on one another 'by reason of their contracting and expanding motion' (tonike kinesis), the sympathy (sympnoia) that breathes through them, and the unity of substance; the universe is one living being with a single sentience, 'how intertwined in the fabric is the thread'.

src.l: Marcus Aurelius, C. R. Haines (tr.), 1916, Communings with Himself (Loeb)
src.q: For these things are consequent one on another by reason of their contracting and expanding motion, the sympathy that breathes through them, and the unity of all substance.

src.l: Marcus Aurelius, C. R. Haines (tr.), 1916, Communings with Himself (Loeb)
src.q: Cease not to think of the Universe as one living Being, possessed of a single Substance and a single Soul

s: Diogenes Laertius (VII.158) reports that the Stoics hold sleep comes when the sensory tension (tonos) around the ruling faculty slackens, and that they make 'the turnings (tropai) in the pneuma' the causes of the passions.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, 1533, De vitis, dogmatibus et apophthegmatibus philosophorum (Greek editio princeps)
src.q: Sleep occurs when the sensory tension around the commanding faculty is released. They leave the disturbances in the breath as the causes of the passions.

s: Sextus Empiricus (Adv. Math. IX.78-80) reports the Stoic argument that the cosmos is a unified body (henomenon), proved by its sympathies: moon and tides, star-risings and weather; in a unified body the parts suffer together, as when a finger is cut the whole body is affected, whereas the survivor of a destroyed army feels nothing.

src.l: Sextus Empiricus, 1718, Opera Graece et Latine (ed. J. A. Fabricius)
src.q: In unified bodies, however, there is a certain shared affection; if a finger is cut, the whole body is affected along with it. Therefore, the world is also a unified body.
src.qo: In iis autem quæ ſunt unita, eſt quædam affectio per conſenſum, ſiquidem ſciſſo digito totum corpus ſimul afficitur. Unitum eſt ergo corpus etiam mundus.

s: Seneca (NQ II.6-9) argues that air is one continuous body whose tension (intentio) holds bodies together, moves the soul and transmits sense: there is no tension without unity, and the voice and light cross whole cities and the world at once because air is never divided.

src.l: Seneca, John Clarke (trans.), 1910, Physical Science in the Time of Nero: being a translation of the Quaestiones Naturales of Seneca
src.q: What constitutes that motion if it be not tension? What tension can there be except from unity?

src.l: Seneca, John Clarke (trans.), 1910, Physical Science in the Time of Nero: being a translation of the Quaestiones Naturales of Seneca
src.q: For there is nothing that does not become more active through tension

s: Cleomedes (Caelestia I.1) argues there is no void inside the cosmos: without a continuous substance there would be no sympathy of its parts, and if the pneuma were not continuous throughout, we could not see or hear, because gaps would block the senses.

src.l: Cleomedes, 1605, Cleomedis Meteora Graece et Latine (ed. R. Balfour)
src.q: it would not be possible for us to see or hear. For as there would be vacuities in between, our senses would be hindered by them.
src.qo: μεταξὺ γὰρ ὄντων κενωμάτων, ἐνεποδίζοντο ἂν ὑπ' αὐτῶν αἱ αἰσθήσεις.

s: Diogenes Laertius (VII.157) reports Chrysippus's theory that we see because the air between eye and object is stretched into a cone, so the object is 'announced as if through a staff of stretched air', and that we hear because air struck by the speaker undulates in spheres like water in a cistern.

src.l: Diogenes Laertius, 1533, De vitis, dogmatibus et apophthegmatibus philosophorum (Greek editio princeps)
src.q: Thus, the thing seen is announced as if through a staff of stretched air. Hearing occurs when the air between the speaker and the hearer is struck spherically, then undulates, and falls upon the ears

s: Philo (De migratione Abrahami 178-180) describes the Chaldeans as fitting earthly things to heavenly ones and showing, 'as if through music', the most harmonious symphony of the whole through the fellowship and sympathy of its parts; Moses, he says, agrees about the sympathy of the parts but not that the cosmos is the first God.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), Paul Wendland (ed.), 1896, Philonis Alexandrini Opera Quae Supersunt, vols. 1-3
src.q: as if through the music of words, demonstrating the most harmonious symphony of the whole through the fellowship and sympathy of the parts towards one another, though separated by places, they were not separated in kinship.

s: Alexander of Aphrodisias (De mixtione 216.14 Bruns, SVF II.473) reports Chrysippus's view that the whole of substance is unified by a pneuma extending through all of it, by which the whole is held together and is sympathetic with itself; true blending (krasis) is the total interpenetration of bodies that keep their own qualities.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippi fragmenta logica et physica (Teubner reprint of 1903)
src.loc: SVF II.473 (Alex. De mixt. 216.14 Bruns); p. 154 [scan 164]
src.q: by which the whole is held together, persists, and is sympathetic to itself.
src.qo: ὑφ' οὗ συνέχεται τε καὶ συμμένει καὶ συμπαθές ἐστιν αὑτῷ τὸ πᾶν·

s: Alexander of Aphrodisias (De mixtione 223-224 Bruns, SVF II.441-442; De anima mantissa 130-131, SVF II.448, 864) presses the Peripatetic critique of Stoic tonos: a fluid, easily divided pneuma cannot give bodies cohesion, 'tonic motion' is incoherent, and if sight were tension of air perception should break off wherever the tension fails.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippi fragmenta logica et physica (Teubner reprint of 1903)
src.loc: SVF II.441 (Alex. De mixt. 223.25 Bruns); p. 145 [scan 155]

s: Cicero's Stoic spokesman Balbus (De natura deorum II.19) argues from cosmic sympathy to a single divine pneuma: the 'consenting, conspiring, continuous kinship of things' (consentiens, conspirans, continuata cognatio rerum) - seasons, solstices, tides moved by the moon, the stars' courses - could not occur with all parts of the world 'singing together' (concinentibus) unless held together by one divine and continuous spirit. The Academic Cotta (III.28) grants the coherence but naturalises it: it holds by the forces of nature, not of the gods - 'that consensus which the Greeks call sympathia'.

src.l: Cicero, 1504, De natura deorum (early printed edition, BSB copy bsb11054324)
src.q: These such great things could not happen with all parts of the world singing in harmony with one another, unless they were held together by one divine and continuous spirit.

src.l: Cicero, 1504, De natura deorum (early printed edition, BSB copy bsb11054324)
src.q: That truly coheres and remains by the forces of nature, not of the gods;

s: Epictetus (Discourses I.14) argues that all things are 'mutually connected and united' and that earthly things feel the influence of heavenly ones - plants bloom and drop leaves in season, things wax and wane with the moon - so if leaves and bodies have 'this connection and sympathy with the whole', souls, as portions of God, have it much more, and God perceives every movement of them.

src.l: Epictetus, Thomas Wentworth Higginson (tr.), 1866, The Works of Epictetus (Discourses, Enchiridion, Fragments)
src.q: Do not you think, said Epictetus, that all things are mutually connected and united?

s: Immediately after meditating on how all things are woven together through sympnoia (VI.38), Marcus Aurelius turns the physics into an ethic (VI.39): 'fit yourself together with' (synarmoze seauton, from harmozo, to tune/join) the circumstances your lot has cast you among, and love the people you live with, truly. Gataker's Latin renders it 'eis te accommoda'; the musical root is lost in both Latin and English.

src.l: Marcus Aurelius, Thomas Gataker (ed.), 1652, Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν (Meditationes), Greek-Latin with Gataker's commentary

s: Posidonius, quoted by Galen (PHP V.6) against Chrysippus's purely cognitive theory of the passions, holds that the passionate part of the soul is irrational and is 'aroused and calmed through irrational motions' - which is why the right rhythms and harmonies are a regimen for the soul, and why Damon could stop drunken, rioting youths at once by telling the piper to change from the Phrygian to the Dorian mode. They did not change their opinions; the music moved them below reason.

src.l: Galen, Iwan Müller (ed.), 1874, De placitis Hippocratis et Platonis libri novem, vol. I
src.q: the irrational, passionate part of the soul is aroused and calmed through irrational motions.

s: Nemesius of Emesa (De natura hominis 2), arguing that the soul cannot be a body, records the Stoic answer to 'what holds a body together?': a tonic motion (tonike kinesis) in bodies that moves at once inward and outward, the outward motion producing magnitudes and qualities, the inward producing unity and substance - a standing oscillation as the principle of a thing's identity.

src.l: Nemesius of Emesa, Nicasius Ellebodius (ed., tr.), 1565, De natura hominis (first Greek-Latin edition)
src.q: moving at once inward and outward, and that the outward motion is the producer of magnitudes and qualities

s: Della Porta (Magia naturalis I.6-7, 1589) grounds natural magic in a continuous chain from God through mind and soul to the lowest things, 'as if a cord were stretched from the heavens down to these lowest things', so that if one end is touched the whole trembles - Homer's golden chain and Plato's rings. The magus 'marries' lower things to higher virtues. The next chapter names the working principle: a 'compassion' in all things, 'which the Greeks call sympatheia and antipatheia, and we more commonly call consent and dissent'.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1589, Magiae naturalis libri viginti

The same chapter has a deaf person hearing a lute by biting its neck.

s: Kircher (Magnes, 1641/1643, III 'Magnetismus plantarum') reduces every sympathy and antipathy to one mechanism: something subtle is diffused from a body through the medium within its 'sphere of activity' and alters only bodies 'conformable, proportionate, and homogeneous' to it, as in two equally strung polychords only the congruent strings move; because the medium shows no sensible effect, sympathy looks like action at a distance, but 'an agent never acts on the extremity without acting through a medium'.

s: In the Platonic Theology (XIII, 1482) Ficino argues that the soul's imagination shapes not only its own body but, 'through fascinations and evil spells', another's: 'the imagination of fever vibrates (vibrat) the feverish spirits', which rouse feverish vapours that rush out with the spirit 'like arrows' to where the malicious imagination aimed, above all through the eyes, and infect a child's spirits and humours. The soul 'does not lack a continuation of means' to carry its action into a foreign body. Elsewhere in the same work (IX) dark vapours 'vibrating' the spirit of the brain stir up horrible images in the imagination.

s: In De amore VI.10 Ficino defines magic as love: 'the entire power of magic consists in love', and 'the work of magic is the attraction of one thing by another from a certain kinship of nature'. The parts of the world, like the limbs of one animal, suffer together when one suffers; 'from a common kinship, a common love is born, and from love, a common attraction. This is true magic.' Art only supplies, through vapours, numbers, figures and qualities, what natural kinship lacks, restoring 'the concord of things' where it is missing.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: from a common kinship, a common love is born, and from love, a common attraction. This is true magic.

s: In De amore VII.4 ('Vulgar love is a certain fascination') Ficino gives a physical mechanism for falling in love: the heart makes a subtle vapour of blood, the spirit, which shines out through the eyes as rays; a gaze fixed on someone shoots that spirit into their eyes, it travels to their heart and turns back into blood, so that the lover carries the beloved's blood. Bleary eyes infect an onlooker the same way. Of Phaedrus and Lysias: 'The ray of Phaedrus is easily coupled to the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit.'

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)

s: In his summary of Enneads IV.4.40-41 Ficino says magic's marvellous power rests on four things - hidden qualities, figures, harmonies (concentus) and prayers - since lower figures and harmonies 'reflect' heavenly ones, and prayer is 'a certain vehement movement of our soul'. Because our life is joined to the life of the world, 'the powerful movements of our soul, poured out through the common life that flourishes everywhere, reach even to the mundane divinities'. Distance is no obstacle where the lower thing is kindred to the higher, 'just as the movement of a nerve in a lyre reaches another nerve, even if they are far apart, provided they are tuned to the same pitch'.

s: Wittkower (1949) proposed that musical harmonic ratios were a principle underlying Palladio's ground plans in Book II of the Quattro libri; the theory was widely accepted although based on detailed analysis of only 8 of the 44 plans.

src.l: Deborah Howard, Malcolm Longair, 1982, Harmonic Proportion and Palladio's "Quattro Libri"

s: Howard and Longair's quantitative survey of all 44 Book II plans finds that Palladio preferred dimensions relatable by musical ratios, but only about two-thirds of dimensions can be so related, and he often did not adjust published measurements to make them harmonic, so his dependence on musical proportion was far less than Wittkower implied.

src.l: Deborah Howard, Malcolm Longair, 1982, Harmonic Proportion and Palladio's "Quattro Libri"

s: Palmer and Schloss's ecological valence theory holds that average colour preference is explained by how much people like the objects strongly associated with each colour (blues with clear sky and water liked; browns with faeces and rotten food disliked).

src.l: Stephen E. Palmer, Karen B. Schloss, 2010, An ecological valence theory of human color preference

s: In Palmer and Schloss's test on 32 colours, the weighted affective valence estimate (WAVE) correlated r = +0.893 with average colour preference (80% of variance, no free parameters), beating the cone-opponent model, which explained 37% of variance on their data.

src.l: Stephen E. Palmer, Karen B. Schloss, 2010, An ecological valence theory of human color preference

s: Schloss and Palmer (2011) found that pair preference and pair harmony for colour combinations both increase as hue similarity increases, while highly contrastive hue pairs are generally judged neither preferable nor harmonious; harmony is explained mainly by preference, hue similarity and low saturation.

src.l: Karen B. Schloss, Stephen E. Palmer, 2011, Aesthetic response to color combinations: preference, harmony, and similarity

s: Empirical colour harmony as rated by observers tracks similarity (low hue contrast, low saturation), whereas the KB's working definition and Philolaus put harmony in the fitting together of unlike things; these are different senses of 'harmony' and should not be merged.

src.l: Karen B. Schloss, Stephen E. Palmer, 2011, Aesthetic response to color combinations: preference, harmony, and similarity

s: No test of whether viewers perceive or prefer musical ratios in architecture was found in this pass; the evidence located is a survey of dimensions in Palladio's plans (not of viewers) and observer studies of colour, not of proportion.

src.l: Deborah Howard, Malcolm Longair, 1982, Harmonic Proportion and Palladio's "Quattro Libri"

s: Critique: Wittkower's thesis that Palladio built his plans on musical harmonic ratios was generalised from 8 of 44 plans; a systematic check finds ratios present in about two-thirds of dimensions, often not corrected where it was easy, and the best 'harmonic' examples cluster after Palladio's work with Barbaro.

src.l: Deborah Howard, Malcolm Longair, 1982, Harmonic Proportion and Palladio's "Quattro Libri"

s: Against Plato's Republic, Aristotle argues that a city pressed toward too much unity stops being a city or becomes a worse one, 'just as if someone were to make a harmony into a unison, or a rhythm into a single beat'; a city is by nature a multitude, and the less unified is more self-sufficient.

src.q: For the household and the city must be one in a way, but not in every way. For there is a sense in which, as it proceeds, it will not be a city; and there is a sense in which it will be, but being close to not being a city, it will be a worse city. Just as if someone were to make a harmony into a unison, or a rhythm into a single beat.

s: In Politics VIII.5 Aristotle holds that melodies and rhythms contain likenesses of character, so the musical modes dispose listeners differently (Mixolydian mournful, the relaxed modes softening, Dorian 'middle and most settled', Phrygian enthusiastic), and therefore music must be part of the education of the young.

src.q: music is able to produce a certain quality of character in the soul. If it is able to do this, it is clear that the young must be led into it and educated in it.

s: In De anima I.4 Aristotle rejects the view that the soul is a harmony: harmony is a ratio or composition of mixed parts, and neither sense fits the soul (which parts would reason combine? and differently mixed flesh and bone would give many souls); yet in Politics VIII.5 he reports without rebuttal that, because modes and rhythms seem akin to the soul, some wise men say the soul is a harmony and others that it has harmony.

src.q: Harmony, say its advocates, is a mixture and combination of opposites. The body, too, is composed of opposites. Although it is true that harmony is a sort of relation in mixed parts or a combination of parts, we maintain that it is impossible for the soul to be either of these.

src.l: Aristotle, William Alexander Hammond (tr.), 1902, Aristotle's Psychology: De Anima and Parva Naturalia
src.loc: De anima I.4, 408a5-18; scan 119, printed p. 27
src.q: If all the parts of the body are composed of mixed elements, and the ratio of this mixture constitutes harmony and soul, we have the absurd result that we possess many souls distributed through the entire body.

src.l: Aristotle, 4th c. BCE (Aldine 1495-98), Aristotelis Opera, Vol. 6 (Aldine): Ethica, Politica, Oeconomica
src.q: There seems to be a certain kinship between the harmoniai and rhythms; therefore, many wise men say: some, that the soul is a harmony; others, that it possesses harmony.

s: The Aristotelian Problems (XIX.38) explains why we delight in consonance: it is a mixture of opposites that stand in a ratio to one another, and ratio is order, which is naturally pleasant; everything mixed is pleasanter than the unmixed.

s: Problems XIX.39 holds that every consonance is pleasanter than a single note and the octave the most pleasant; singing in octaves (boys with men) pleases because the sounds have a ratio of movement like metrical feet, and 'the most pleasant thing from different sources becomes one and common through the octave'.

s: Plotinus (Enn. s: In Harmonics III.8 Ptolemy compares the complete two-octave system to the zodiac: both are circular, with no beginning by nature but only by convention, and if the zodiac is cut at an equinox and unrolled it can be fitted to the double octave, the uncut equinox falling on the mese.

s: Nicomachus reports that some call the harmonic proportion 'harmonic' after Philolaus because the cube, the 'geometric harmony', displays it: 12 edges, 8 corners, 6 faces, with 8 the harmonic mean of 6 and 12.

src.l: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Richard Hoche (ed.), 1866, Introductionis Arithmeticae libri II
src.loc: Introduction to Arithmetic II.26; Hoche 1866, scan 153, printed p. 135
src.q: Some believe that this proportion is called "harmonic" in accordance with the views of Philolaus, because it accompanies every geometric harmony. They say that "geometric harmony" is the cube because it is harmonized across three dimensions

s: Nicomachus ends the Introduction to Arithmetic with the 'most perfect' proportion, a four-term, three-dimensional one in which a harmonic and an arithmetic mean stand between two extremes so that the geometric proportion appears interwoven (e.g. 6, 8, 9, 12); he says this alone can properly be called harmonia.

src.l: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Richard Hoche (ed.), 1866, Introductionis Arithmeticae libri II
src.loc: Introduction to Arithmetic II.29; Hoche 1866, scan 162, printed p. 144
src.q: Finally, I shall briefly articulate the most perfect mean, which is three-dimensionally extended and encompasses all the others. This mean is highly useful for all progress in music and natural science; for this alone could properly and truly be called harmony in a way that the others cannot.

src.l: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Richard Hoche (ed.), 1866, Introductionis Arithmeticae libri II
src.loc: Introduction to Arithmetic II.29; Hoche 1866, scan 163, printed p. 145
src.q: whichever of them maintains the harmonic proportion, the remaining one completes the arithmetic proportion. For when the four terms are thus arranged, it is necessary that the geometric proportion appears interwoven

s: Augustine (City of God XI.18) says God adorns the order of the ages 'like a most beautiful poem' with antitheses: as opposites set against opposites make speech beautiful, so the beauty of the world is composed by an eloquence of things through the opposition of contraries, evil men included.

s: Against those offended by fire, cold or wild beasts, Augustine (City of God XI.22) says such things flourish in their own places and natures and contribute their portions to the beauty of the universe 'as if to a common commonwealth', and that even poisons, used fittingly, become medicines.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, Bernhard Dombart (ed.), 1877, De Civitate Dei libri XXII, vol. I

s: In Confessions X.33 Augustine wavers over church singing: he recalls weeping at the Church's songs and grants their use to stir weaker minds, yet counts it a sin when he is moved more by the singing than by what is sung.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, n.d. (SL record: 1900), Confessions (English translation)
src.loc: Confessions X.33.50; English tr., scan 248, printed p. 220
src.q: Thus vacillate I between dangerous pleasure and tried soundness

src.q: Yet when it happens to me to be more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess myself to have sinned criminally, and then I would rather not have heard the singing.

s: Boethius holds that sounds that do not differ at all make no consonance: consonance is 'the concord of dissimilar sounds reduced into one'.

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.3; Friedlein 1867, scan 210, printed p. 191
src.q: But in those sounds which do not differ by any inequality, there is no consonance at all. For consonance is the concord of dissimilar sounds reduced into one.
src.qo: Sed in his vocibus, quae nulla inaequalitate discordant, nulla omnino consonantia est. Est enim consonantia dissimilium inter se vocum in unum redacta concordia.

s: Boethius defines consonance as a mixture of high and low sound reaching the ears sweetly and uniformly, and dissonance as a harsh striking of two sounds that refuse to mix, each striving to arrive whole and obstructing the other.

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.8; Friedlein 1867, scan 214, printed p. 195
src.q: Consonance is the mixture of a high and a low sound reaching the ears sweetly and uniformly. Dissonance, on the other hand, is a harsh and unpleasant striking of two sounds mixed together as they reach the ear.
src.qo: Con- sonantia est acuti soni gravisque mixtura suaviter unifor- miterque auribus accidens. Dissonantia vero est duorum sonorum sibimet permixtorum ad aurem veniens aspera atque iniucunda percussio.

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.8; scan 214, printed p. 195
src.q: For since they refuse to be mixed with one another and each strives, in a sense, to arrive as a complete whole, and as one obstructs the other, both are transmitted to the senses in an unpleasant way.
src.qo: Nam dum sibimet misceri no- lunt et quodammodo integer uterque nititur pervenire, cumque alter alteri officit, ad sensum insuaviter uterque transmittitur.

s: Boethius (I.9) says not all judgment should be given to the senses: hearing supplies the beginning and a reminder, but perfection and recognition lie in reason, because perception differs between people and within one person.

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.9; Friedlein 1867, scan 214, printed p. 195
src.q: hearing holds the beginning in a certain way and serves as a kind of reminder; however, the final perfection and the power of recognition consist in reason, which, holding itself to fixed rules, never falls into any error
src.qo: postrema vero perfectio agnitionisque vis in ratione consistit, quae certis regulis sese tenens nun- quam ullo errore prolabitur.

s: Boethius (I.1) argues music is joined to character: we delight in harmonious sounds because we are built on the same proportions, 'likeness is friendly, unlikeness hateful', so each people delights in modes like its character, and changing music corrupts morals (after Plato).

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.1; Friedlein 1867, scan 199, printed p. 180
src.q: For when we receive that which is aptly and harmoniously joined in sounds through that which is joined and harmoniously fitted within ourselves, and we are delighted by it, we recognize that we ourselves are also constructed according to that same likeness. For likeness is friendly, while unlikeness is hateful and contrary.
src.qo: Cum enim eo, quod in nobis est iunctum convenienterque coaptatum, illud excipimus, quod in senis apte convenienterque coniunctum est, eoque delectamur, nos quoque ipsos eadem similitudine compactos esse cognoscimus. Amica 10 est enim similitudo, dissimilitudo odiosa atque contraria.

s: Boethius (I.34) ranks knowing over doing: performers are named from their instruments and serve like slaves, while the true musician is the one who judges modes, rhythms and songs by reason and speculation.

src.l: Boethius, c. 500 CE, De Institutione Arithmetica & De Institutione Musica
src.loc: De institutione musica I.34; Friedlein 1867, scan 243, printed p. 224
src.q: But he truly is a musician who, having weighed it with reason, has taken up the science of singing not by the servitude of work but by the command of speculation.

s: In the Latin De radiis, al-Kindī holds that every star pours its rays into every place, that each place receives a different blend of rays derived from the 'total harmony of the stars', and that this celestial harmony, diversifying itself continuously, is what makes places and individuals differ.

src.l: al-Kindī (Alkindus), c. 1601 (MS copy, per SL record), Traités et notes d'alchimie (Paris, Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève MS 2240), containing Alkindus, De radiis
src.loc: Alkindus, De radiis (Latin), ch. on the rays of the stars; §§27, 29; scan 174
src.q: For in every place, every star pours out its rays, because of which the diversity of rays, combined into one place, varies all things contained in those places, since in every place there is a different tenor of rays which is derived from the total harmony of the stars.
src.qo: cum in omni loco diversa diversa sit tenor radiorum qui a totali stellarum harmonia derivatur

src.l: al-Kindī (Alkindus), c. 1601 (MS copy, per SL record), Traités et notes d'alchimie (Paris, Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève MS 2240), containing Alkindus, De radiis

src.qo: cum in omni loco diversa diversa sit tenor radiorum qui a totali stellarum harmonia derivatur

s: De radiis claims that everything acting in the elemental world, however small, is a state of the whole celestial harmony, so that one individual fully known would show the whole condition of that harmony 'as if through a mirror'.

src.l: al-Kindī (Alkindus), c. 1601 (MS copy, per SL record), Traités et notes d'alchimie (Paris, Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève MS 2240), containing Alkindus, De radiis
src.loc: Alkindus, De radiis (Latin), ch. on the rays of the stars; §§53, 56; scan 179, MS p. 88
src.q: For everything that acts, however small, in the World of the Elements is a state of the entire celestial harmony.

src.l: al-Kindī (Alkindus), c. 1601 (MS copy, per SL record), Traités et notes d'alchimie (Paris, Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève MS 2240), containing Alkindus, De radiis
src.loc: Alkindus, De radiis (Latin), ch. on the rays of the stars; §56; scan 179
src.q: the condition of a single individual of this World having been fully known, one would foresee the entire condition of celestial harmony as if through a mirror; since every thing of this World is thus an example of the one harmony.
src.qo: tanquam per speculum coelestia harmonia conditionem totam praesentiret; cum omnia res huius Mundi sic exemplum unius salia harmonia.

s: De radiis generalises from the stars to all things: everything in the elemental world emits rays in every direction, so every place holds the rays of all existing things; the examples include fire's heat, earth's cold, medicines, colour, and sound, which spreads 'through rays of its own mode'.

src.l: al-Kindī (Alkindus), c. 1601 (MS copy, per SL record), Traités et notes d'alchimie (Paris, Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève MS 2240), containing Alkindus, De radiis

s: De radiis says that rays of different things falling on the same thing temper one another: they increase the effect where they agree and diminish it where they disagree.

s: In the Great Book of Music al-Fārābī makes pleasure the test of what is natural for hearing: perception that is perfected is followed by pleasure, so the pleasures felt by all or most people are to be used as the measures of what is natural to man.

src.l: al-Fārābī, modern Arabic edition (SL record gives 950), Kitāb al-mūsīqī al-kabīr (Great Book of Music)
src.loc: Kitāb al-mūsīqī al-kabīr, Introduction, Second Article (natural melodies); scan 102, printed p. 107
src.q: The faculties that possess perceptions, when they are perfected, are followed by pleasure.
src.qo: والقوى التي هي ذوات إدراكات(٤) إذا استكملت تبع كمالها الأخير لذةٌ ،

src.l: al-Fārābī, modern Arabic edition (SL record gives 950), Kitāb al-mūsīqī al-kabīr (Great Book of Music)
src.q: Therefore, it is necessary that the pleasures resulting from them be used as measures for what are perfections for the sense, and those among them that are for people always or for most of them be used as measures for what is natural to man.

s: Al-Fārābī holds that one person's ear cannot settle what is consonant: some hear the incompatible as compatible, as a sick man tastes sweet as bitter, so the measure needs 'the testimonies of the rest of humanity', as in astronomy.

src.q: a human is not sufficient with what he alone measures, without also having the measures of the perception of others. Therefore, nothing of these is complete without the testimonies of the rest of humanity, just as it is in the science of astronomy.

s: Al-Fārābī grades the consonances ('agreements') by perfection: the octave and its multiples first, then the fifth and its compounds, then the fourth, with the octave-plus-fourth least perfect; practising musicians drop that last interval because melodies do not use it, while the Pythagorean theorists drop it on their own principles.

src.q: It has been made clear that these agreements vary in their perfection. The best and most perfect is the agreement of the "all," and the agreement of its double and its multiples up to where it reaches.

s: In the Virtuous City al-Fārābī likens the excellent city to a completely healthy body whose diverse limbs, competing for precedence, all assist one another under the heart as chief, in ranks down to limbs 'that only serve, but do not rule anything at all'.

s: The Latin De ortu scientiarum, ascribed to al-Fārābī, says music arose as the science of high, low and middle sounds and their comparison, and that its use is to temper the characters of living beings that exceed balance, perfect those not yet perfect, preserve the balanced, and heal the body by healing the soul.

src.l: al-Fārābī (attrib.), Clemens Baeumker (ed.), 1916, Alfarabi, Über den Ursprung der Wissenschaften (De ortu scientiarum)
src.loc: De ortu scientiarum, ch. 4 (Baeumker ed.); scan 27, printed p. 19
src.q: Its utility is for tempering the characters of living beings that exceed balance, and for perfecting the beauties of those which are not yet perfect, and for preserving those who appear balanced and have not yet reached any extreme.
src.qo: Cuius utilitas est ad temperandos mores animalium qui excedunt aequalitatem

src.l: al-Fārābī (attrib.), Clemens Baeumker (ed.), 1916, Alfarabi, Über den Ursprung der Wissenschaften (De ortu scientiarum)

s: In the Canon (I, fen 2) Avicenna says 'musical nature is found in the pulse': as music is built from sounds in proportion of high and low and in cycles of time between beats, so the pulse has proportions of time and of strength.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.loc: Canon I, fen 2, doctr. 3 (Latin, Venice 1595); scan 208, printed p. 141
src.q: You must know that musical nature is found in the pulse, for just as the art of music is completed by the addition of sounds according to the proportion accompanying them between the high and the low, through cycles of cases between their beats, so is the disposition of the pulse
src.qo: in pulfu reperitur natura mufica

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.q: in pulfu reperitur natura mufica

s: Avicenna reports Galen's view that the felt proportions of the pulse follow the musical ratios, and answers that discerning such proportions by touch is easy only for someone trained in touching who has also acquired knowledge of music by art.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.loc: Canon I, fen 2, doctr. 3 (Latin, Venice 1595); scan 208, printed p. 141
src.q: I say, however, that it is easy for him who is accustomed to the grade of touching, and who knows the nature of sounds by art, after he will have the power of knowing music acquired
src.qo: dico tamen, quòd ei eft facile qui in gradu tangendi confuefcit

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.q: dico tamen, quòd ei eft facile qui in gradu tangendi confuefcit

s: Avicenna's Canon makes temperate complexion relative, not absolute: each people (his examples are Indians and Slavs) has its own healthy complexion, temperate for it and not for the other, and every individual ought to have a complexion proper to himself alone.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.loc: Canon I, fen 1, doctr. 3, ch. 1 (on complexions; Latin, Venice 1595); scan 79, printed p. 12
src.q: And each one of them, by comparison to its own species, is temperate: which, by comparison to another, is not temperate. For the body of an Indian, when it becomes like the complexion of a Slav, will either fall ill or die.
src.qo: & vnaquæque earum per comparationem ad suã speciem [suę speciei comparatione] est temperata: quę comparatione alterius non est temperata. corpus nãque Indi, quũ secundum complexionem Sclaui, quale fiet; aut infirmabitur, aut morietur.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.q: You must know, however, that every individual ought to have a complexion solely proper to him
src.qo: Debes autem scire, quod oẽ indiuiduum debet habere cõplexionem sibi solummodo propriam, in qua alium ei associare

s: Avicenna defines complexion as the quality arising from the mutual action of contrary elemental qualities, and holds that a human approaches true equality only by weighing unequal members against each other (hot heart, cold brain, moist liver, dry bones), each member's own 'equality' being an excess of one quality.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.loc: Canon I, fen 1, doctr. 3, ch. 1; scan 78, printed p. 11
src.q: Complexion is a quality which arises from the reciprocal action and passion of contrary qualities found in the elements
src.qo: COmplexio est qualitas, quæ ex actione ad inuicem & passione contrariarum qualitatum in elementis inuentarum: quorum partes

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.q: of the hot, such as the heart: and of the cold, such as the brain: and of the moist, such as the liver: and of the dry, such as the bones. When, therefore, they are weighed and equalized, he will be close to certain equality.
src.qo: calidorum, sicut cor: & frigidorum, sicut cerebrum: & humidorum, velut hepar: & siccorum, sicut ossa. Quum ergo ponderabuntur, & æquabuntur; erit vicinus æqualitati 20certæ.

src.l: Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), 1595, Avicennae Canon Medicinae, Vol. I (Latin, Venice 1595)
src.q: for the equality of the bone is that dryness should abound in it more; and of the brain, that moisture should abound in it the most; and of the heart, that there should be more heat in it
src.qo: æqualitas nanque ossis est, vt siccitas in eo plus abundet: & cerebri, vt humiditas in eo plurimũ abundet: & cordis, vt in eo sit plus caliditatis; &

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ tie the oud's four strings to the four elements and humours: each string's tone strengthens one humour and opposes another, and melodies played at times of day contrary to a disease's nature soothe it, which they give as the reason musicians used them in hospitals.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); on the four strings; scan 108
src.q: The tone of the zir strengthens the bile humor, increases its power and effect, and opposes the phlegm humor, refining it.
src.qo: وذلك ان نغمة الزير تقوي خلط الصفراء وتزيد في قوتها وتاثيرها وتضاد خلط البلغم وتلطفه

src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); scan 108
src.q: When these tones are arranged in melodies suitable for them, and those melodies are used during times of the night and day whose nature is contrary to the nature of prevailing diseases and occurring ailments, they soothe them, break their intensity, and alleviate the pain of the sick.

s: The Ikhwān's music epistle holds that the best-made things are built on the best proportions, and that every limb of the human body is proportional to the whole by one ratio and to another limb by another; a well-formed newborn is eight of its own spans tall and eight spans across the outstretched arms.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); on proportion in the human frame; scan 115
src.q: if you contemplate it and consider every limb of the human body, it is proportional to the whole body by one ratio, and proportional to some other limb of the body by another ratio.

s: Among the philosophers' sayings in the Ikhwān's music epistle is the view that souls delight in measured, proportional melody because the soul's substance is like the compositional numbers, so the pleasure comes from 'similarity, proportionality, and homogeneity'; the same rule is applied to beautiful faces.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); sayings of the philosophers on music; scan 124
src.q: Since the substance of the soul was homogeneous and similar to the compositional numbers, … the natures found delight in them, the spirits rejoiced in them, and the souls were happy with them because of the similarity, proportionality, and homogeneity between them.
src.qo: استلذتها الطباع وفرحت بها الارواح وسرت بها النفوس لما بينهما من المشاكلة والتناسب والمجانسة

s: The Ikhwān say the sages used music in temples, especially sad melodies, to soften hard hearts and turn souls toward their spiritual world, and that some religious laws forbid music only because people use it for amusement and worldly desire.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); on the sages’ use of music; scan 105
src.q: especially the sad melodies that soften hard hearts and remind heedless souls and playful spirits who are neglectful of the joy of their spiritual world
src.qo: وبخاصة الالحان الحزينة المرققة للقلوب القاسية المذكرة للنفوس الساهية والارواح اللاهية الغافلة عن سرور عالمها الروحانى ومحلها النورانى ودارها الحيوانية

src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition); scan 106
src.q: As for the reason for its prohibition in some religious laws, it is because of people's use of it in a way other than that which the sages used—rather, on the path of amusement and play

s: Natyashastra ch. 6 explains the name rasa by tasting: rasa is so called 'because it is to be tasted' (āsvādyatvāt); refined spectators taste the durable states (sthāyibhāva), as made manifest by the various bhāvas and kinds of acting, the way refined diners taste the flavours of food prepared with many condiments. The text adds that rasas arise from bhāvas and not bhāvas from rasas, and rejects the view that each arises from the other.

src.l: Bharata (attrib.), 1929, Natya Shastra of Bharata (Sanskrit text)
src.loc: ch. 6, prose after v. 31; scan 137, printed p. 71
src.q: रस इति कः पदार्थः ? अत्रोच्यते । आस्वाद्यत्वात् ।

src.l: Bharata (attrib.), 1929, Natya Shastra of Bharata (Sanskrit text)
src.loc: ch. 6, prose after v. 31; scan 137, printed p. 71 (SL translation)
src.q: Just as people of refined mind, eating food prepared with various condiments, taste the flavors and obtain joy and other [emotions], in the same way, refined spectators taste the sthāyibhāvas
src.qo: रस इति कः पदार्थः ? अत्रोच्यते । आस्वाद्यत्वात् ।

s: Natyashastra ch. 28 classes the seven notes, by their shruti relations, as vādī, samvādī, anuvādī and vivādī; the vādī is the note that is the aṃśa (focal note), and two notes separated by nine or thirteen shrutis are samvādī (consonant) to each other: in the shadja-grama Sa–Ma, Sa–Pa, Ri–Dha and Ga–Ni; in the madhyama-grama the same except Sa–Pa, with Pa–Ri consonant instead.

src.l: Bharata (attrib.), 1929, Natya Shastra of Bharata (Sanskrit text)
src.loc: ch. 28, v. 20 and prose after it; scan 383, printed p. 327

src.l: Bharata (attrib.), 1929, Natya Shastra of Bharata (Sanskrit text)
src.loc: ch. 28, vv. 20-21; scan 383, printed p. 327 (SL translation)
src.q: There, the note that is the focal point is the vadi; and those that are separated by nine or thirteen microtones are consonant to each other.

s: Natyashastra ch. 28 names dissonant (vivādī) pairs Ri–Ga and Dha–Ni, and calls all remaining notes anuvādī ('following'); it glosses the four names: vādī because it speaks, samvādī from consonance, vivādī from dissonance, anuvādī because it follows. In the Kashi edition the vivādī interval is printed as 'twenty' shrutis (viṃśati), although Ri–Ga and Dha–Ni are neighbouring notes only two shrutis apart in the text's own allocation.

src.l: Bharata (attrib.), 1929, Natya Shastra of Bharata (Sanskrit text)

src.q: The dissonant notes are those that have an interval of twenty microtones. For example: rishabha and gandhara, dhaivata and nishada. Thus, when the vadi, samvadi, and vivadi are established, the remaining ones are called anuvadi.

s: Śārṅgadeva opens the second section of the Saṅgītaratnākara by making song, instrumental music and dance dependent on nāda (sound), and then the world: letters are manifested through sound, words from letters, speech from words, and all worldly interaction runs through speech, so 'the world is dependent upon sound'. Kallinātha's commentary cites Mataṅga's Bṛhaddeśī for the stronger statement that the world is composed of sound.

src.l: Śārṅgadeva, 13th c. (edition n.d. in SL record), Saṅgītaratnākara, Vol. 1: Svaragatādhyāya, with the commentaries of Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla
src.q: नादेन व्यज्यते वर्णः पदं वर्णात्पदाद्वचः । वचसो व्यवहारोऽयं नादाधीनमतो जगत् ॥

src.l: Śārṅgadeva, 13th c. (edition n.d. in SL record), Saṅgītaratnākara, Vol. 1: Svaragatādhyāya, with the commentaries of Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla
src.q: Through sound, letters are manifested; from letters, words; from words, speech; Through speech, all worldly interaction is carried out; therefore, the world is dependent upon sound.
src.qo: नादेन व्यज्यते वर्णः पदं वर्णात्पदाद्वचः । वचसो व्यवहारोऽयं नादाधीनमतो जगत् ॥

src.q: There is no song without Sound, nor are there musical notes without Sound. There is no dance without Sound; therefore, the world is composed of Sound.

s: Saṅgītaratnākara 1.3.3-6 describes the production of sound: the self, wishing to speak, impels the mind; the mind strikes the fire in the body, which impels the breath; the breath rising from the brahmagranthi manifests sound at navel, heart, throat, head and mouth; and nāda is so named because na is breath and da is fire, 'born from the union of breath and fire'.

src.l: Śārṅgadeva, 13th c. (edition n.d. in SL record), Saṅgītaratnākara, Vol. 1: Svaragatādhyāya, with the commentaries of Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla

src.q: the mind strikes the fire residing in the body, which in turn impels the breath. … The syllable na is known as the name of breath, and the syllable da is known as fire. Because it is born from the union of breath and fire, it is called Nada.

s: Saṅgītaratnākara 1.3.47-49 defines the vādī as the note most used in performance and makes two notes mutually samvādī when twelve or eight shrutis lie between them, with Ni and Ga vivādī to the others; the commentary printed under the verses explains samvādī as sustaining the melodic character the vādī creates and vivādī as 'destroying the aesthetic delight' (rakti), and itself objects that natural Ma and Ni are in fact consonant.
