s: The Yueji (Record of Music, Book XVII of the Liji, tr. Legge) opens by deriving music from the mind moved by external things: the affections so produced appear in sounds, the sounds' responses to one another make modulations, and the pleasing combination of modulations, with the dances, is music.

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: All the modulations of the voice arise from the mind, and the various affections of the mind are produced by things (external to it).

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: Music is (thus) the production of the modulations of the voice, and its source is in the affections of the mind as it is influenced by (external) things.

s: The Yueji says the ancient kings instituted ceremonies, music, laws and punishments as one set of instruments by which 'the minds of the people are assimilated' and good order is made to appear, and that the airs of a well-ordered age show composure and enjoyment while those of a disordered age show dissatisfaction and anger.

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: they are the instruments by which the minds of the people are assimilated, and good order in government is made to appear.

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: Hence, the airs of an age of good order indicate composure and enjoyment. The airs of an age of disorder indicate dissatisfaction and anger

s: The Yueji pairs music and ceremony as complementary: similarity and union are the aim of music, difference and distinction that of ceremony; union yields mutual affection and difference mutual respect; and each alone has its failure mode — where music prevails there is 'a weak coalescence', where ceremony prevails 'a tendency to separation'.

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: Similarity and union are the aim of music; difference and distinction, that of ceremony. From union comes mutual affection; from difference, mutual respect. Where music prevails, we find a weak coalescence; where ceremony prevails, a tendency to separation.

s: The Yueji calls music (an echo of) the harmony between heaven and earth and ceremonies the reflection of their orderly distinctions: from that harmony all things receive their being, and to the distinctions they owe their differences; music has its origin from heaven, ceremonies take form from earth.

src.l: James Legge (tr.), 1885, The Sacred Books of China: The Texts of Confucianism, Part IV: The Li Ki, XI-XLVI (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 28)
src.q: Music is (an echo of) the harmony between heaven and earth; ceremonies reflect the orderly distinctions (in the operations of) heaven and earth. From that harmony all things receive their being; to those orderly distinctions they owe the differences between them.

s: The Huainanzi's first chapter (Yuandao) says the ancient sovereigns, tranquil and without pride, attained harmony (和); that though there are ten thousand differences, each finds ease in its own nature; and that the Way's virtue harmonizes yin and yang, regulates the four seasons and tunes the Five Phases.

src.l: Liu An (ed.), Gao You (comm.), 1782, 淮南鴻烈解 卷一~卷三 (Huainan honglie jie, juan 1-3: Yuandao, Chuzhen, Tianwen), Siku quanshu
src.q: 恬愉無矜而得于和 … 有萬不同而便于性 … 其德優天地而和隂陽 … 節四時而調五行

src.l: Liu An (ed.), Gao You (comm.), 1782, 淮南鴻烈解 卷一~卷三 (Huainan honglie jie, juan 1-3: Yuandao, Chuzhen, Tianwen), Siku quanshu
src.q: Being tranquil and pleasant without pride, they attained harmony. … Though there are ten thousand differences, all find convenience in their own nature. … Its Virtue is more abundant than Heaven and Earth and it harmonizes Yin and Yang.
src.qo: 恬愉無矜而得于和 … 有萬不同而便于性 … 其德優天地而和隂陽 … 節四時而調五行

s: The Huainanzi Tianwen chapter generates the twelve pitch-pipes from Huangzhong as gong (number 81, the eleventh month) by alternate 'descending' and 'ascending' generation: Linzhong 54, Taicu 72, Nanlü 48, Guxian 64, Yingzhong 42, Ruibin 57, then Dalü 76 by a second ascent, and so on, each pipe assigned to a month.

src.l: Liu An (ed.), Gao You (comm.), 1782, 淮南鴻烈解 卷一~卷三 (Huainan honglie jie, juan 1-3: Yuandao, Chuzhen, Tianwen), Siku quanshu
src.loc: juan 3 (天文訓 Tianwen); scan 138 (untranslated; search snippet)
src.q: 黃鍾為宮宮者音之君也故黃鍾位子其數八十一主十一月下生林鍾林鍾之數五十四主六月上生太蔟太蔟之數七十二主正月下生南呂南呂之數四十八

s: In the section 'Do not use three-part loss and gain' (不用三分損益第三) Zhu Zaiyu puts the traditional pitch-pipe method alongside the calendar's quarter-day and the ratios 'square 5, diagonal 7' and 'circumference 3, diameter 1' as rough approximations, 'not the refined principles' (非精義), and announces a new method for music and for square and circle alike based on right-triangle (gougu) computation.

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.loc: Lülü jingyi, 'Bu yong sanfen sunyi, no. 3'; scan 114, leaf 1
src.q: 律家三分損其一三分益其一歷家四分度之一四分日之一與夫方則直五斜七圓則周三徑一等率皆舉大略而言之耳非精義也新法算律與方圓皆用勾股術

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: These, along with such ratios as … "if the circle is round, the circumference is three and the diameter is one," are all just rough approximations. They are not the refined principles. My new method for calculating music and the dimensions of square and round objects both utilize the gougu theorem.
src.qo: 律家三分損其一三分益其一歷家四分度之一四分日之一與夫方則直五斜七圓則周三徑一等率皆舉大略而言之耳非精義也新法算律與方圓皆用勾股術

s: Zhu Zaiyu computes equal-tempered pipe ratios by successive root extraction on a one-chi square: its diagonal, 1.414213562373095048801689, is the ratio of the doubled Ruibin pipe; a further square root gives 1.189207115002721 (doubled Nanlü); and a cube root gives 1.059463094359295264561825, the ratio of the doubled Yingzhong pipe — i.e. 2^(1/12).

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.loc: Lülü jingyi, 'Bu yong sanfen sunyi'; scan 115, leaf 6 (SL translation)
src.q: You obtain a hypotenuse of 1.414213562373095048801689 feet. This is the diagonal of the square, which is the diameter of the circle. It is also the ratio for doubling the pitch in the "rotating the mode" system.

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: 開立方法除之得一尺〇五分九釐四毫六絲三忽〇九纖四三五九二九五二六四五六一八二五即應鐘倍律之率

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: Applying the cubic root method to divide it, one obtains 1.059463094359295264561825 feet. This is the ratio of the Yingzhong double-octave scale.
src.qo: 開立方法除之得一尺〇五分九釐四毫六絲三忽〇九纖四三五九二九五二六四五六一八二五即應鐘倍律之率

s: Zhu Zaiyu presents closure as the point of the new method: the twelve pitches begin at Huangzhong and end at Yingzhong, 'returning to the beginning in an endless cycle', which he calls a natural truth; and computing back from Zhonglü (ratio 0.749153538) by the new method yields Huangzhong at exactly ten cun, 'returning to the origin' (還元).

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: Since the twelve pitches begin with Huangzhong and end with Yingzhong, returning to the beginning in an endless cycle, this is a natural truth.

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: 新法置仲呂之率七億四千九百一十五萬三千五百三十八為實十億乘之七億四千九百一十五萬三千五百三十八除之所得億約為寸得黃鍾長十寸還元

s: A leaf headed 'Corrective Regulations' (修正條例), bound into SL's copy of the Yuelü quanshu and citing the Qing Shuli jingyun, says Zhu's milü ('precise ratio') is simply the root-extraction method of the Shuli jingyun 'disguised under the name of gougu', so the right-triangle framing is unnecessary.

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: 密率即數理精蘊內開諸乘方之法也而飾為勾股之名

src.l: Zhu Zaiyu, 1596 (SL record; Siku quanshu text), 樂律全書 Yuelü quanshu, vol. 1 (incl. Lülü jingyi, inner chapters)
src.q: The milü is in fact the method of roots and powers found within the Shuli Jingyun. It was disguised under the name of gougu.
src.qo: 密率即數理精蘊內開諸乘方之法也而飾為勾股之名

s: In the money treatise Oresme, following a Plutarch-to-Trajan image, compares the kingdom to a human body that cannot live long except by due and equal proportion, and calls a prince who draws excessive riches to himself a monster, like a head too large for its body.

src.l: Nicole Oresme, Louis Wolowski (ed.), 1864, Traictie de la première invention des monnoies de Nicole Oresme ... et Traité de la monnoie de Copernic
src.loc: p. lxxviii [scan 158], French text, chapter on tyranny (ed. Wolowski)
src.q: for such a body cannot live for long except by due and equal proportion
src.qo: car tel corps ne peult, sinon par deue et esgalle proportion, longuement vivre.

src.l: Nicole Oresme, Louis Wolowski (ed.), 1864, Traictie de la première invention des monnoies de Nicole Oresme ... et Traité de la monnoie de Copernic
src.q: he is like a monster in nature, like a body whose head is so large that the remainder of it is so weak that it cannot sustain it
src.qo: il est comme ung monstre à nature, si comme ung corps duquel la teste est si grosse que le residu d'icelui est si foible qu'il ne la peut soustenir.

s: Oresme holds that the ratio of gold to silver coin (e.g. 20:1) must follow the natural relative preciousness of the two metals and may not be changed at the prince's will, since a prince who could set it could draw his subjects' wealth to himself.

src.l: Nicole Oresme, Louis Wolowski (ed.), 1864, Traictie de la première invention des monnoies de Nicole Oresme ... et Traité de la monnoie de Copernic
src.loc: p. xxx [scan 110], ch. 10, On the mutation in the proportion of money
src.q: Nevertheless, this proportion must follow the natural custom or value of gold to silver in preciousness.
src.qo: mais toutesfois ceste proportion doit ensuivir le naturel habitude ou valeur de l'or à l'argent, en préciosité;

src.l: Nicole Oresme, Louis Wolowski (ed.), 1864, Traictie de la première invention des monnoies de Nicole Oresme ... et Traité de la monnoie de Copernic
src.q: For if he changed, at his will, the proportion of said gold, he could, by his will, unduly attract to himself the wealth and substances of his subjects
src.qo: car s'il muoit, à sa voulenté, la proporcion d'iceluy or, il, par sa voulenté, pourroit attraire à soy indeuement les pecunes et substances de ses subjectz,

s: A comment printed in Pierre d'Ailly's 1483 Imago mundi volume credits 'Master Nicolaus Oresme' with showing that whether the heaven's motions are commensurable or incommensurable is unproven, only rhetorically probable; d'Ailly's De legibus et sectis (1480 print) argues the same question, judges irrational ratios between unknown motions more likely than rational ones, and concludes it is a 'neutral problem'.

src.l: Pierre d'Ailly, 1483, Imago mundi and other treatises
src.q: That the heaven has commensurable or incommensurable motions of the signs, and furthermore that certain planets dominate this or that nation, is entirely unproven.
src.qo: Oelum habere commensurabiles vel incommensurabiles motus signorum insuper et certos planetas huic vel illi genti dominari prorsus est inuctum.

src.l: Pierre d'Ailly, 1483, Imago mundi and other treatises
src.q: They have erred, as experience has taught, wishing to bring certainty where only rhetorical probability can be had, as Master Nicolaus Oresme deduces, and after him the Lord Cardinal Petrus de Alliaco

src.l: Pierre d'Ailly, 1480, De legibus et sectis contra superstitiosos astronomos
src.q: it is more likely that it is irrational than rational, if no other reason stands in the way
src.qo: verisimilius est ipsam irrationalem esse et rationalem

src.l: Pierre d'Ailly, 1480, De legibus et sectis contra superstitiosos astronomos
src.q: it is probably inferred that the proposed question concerning the commensurability of celestial motions is a neutral problem, about which evident certainty cannot naturally be had
src.qo: probabiliter infertur quod proposita questio de commensurabilitate motuum celestium est problema neutrum de quo naturaliter haberi non potest euidens certitudo.

s: In De vita III Ficino argues that song acts on the human spirit because its matter is warm, living air, purer and closer to the heavens than medicine, so that a song 'can be called a kind of aerial and rational animal' and a musical spirit acts directly on the spirit that mediates between body and soul.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.loc: p. 159, Book III (De vita coelitus comparanda)
src.q: the very matter of musical harmony is much purer and more similar to the heavens than the matter of medicine
src.qo: Iam uero materia ipſa concētus purior eſt admodū/cęloq; ſimilior q̄ materia medi- cinę.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: thus, it can be called a kind of aerial and rational animal
src.qo: ut animal quoddā aeriū/& ratio- nale quodāmodo dici poſſit.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: such a musical spirit properly touches and acts upon the human spirit—the mediator between the body and the soul—affecting both with its own disposition
src.qo: Præsertim quoniā spūs eiusmodi musicus pprie tangit, agitqz in spūm: inter corpus aiāmqz mediū: & utrūqz affectione sua prorsus afficiente.

s: Ficino holds that because the heavens are composed and move by harmonic ratio, harmony is what makes lower things receptive to celestial influence, and he lays out seven levels through which it is applied (images, tempered medicines, odours, songs, imagination, reason, contemplative mind).

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: Since, indeed, the heavens are composed according to a harmonic ratio / and move harmonically
src.qo: Quoniam uero celum est harmonica ratione cōpositum

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: We distribute this harmony, which makes one capable of receiving higher things, through seven levels of things in the higher realms.
src.qo: Harmonīa uero capacem supiorū p̅ septē rerū gradus i̅ supioribus distribuimus.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: harmonies, through their numbers and proportions, have a wonderful power to steady, move, and affect the spirit

s: Ficino restricts musical harmony to four planets (Sun/Apollo, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury); Saturn, Mars and the Moon 'have voices indeed, but not songs'.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: Likewise, musical harmonies pertain only to these four planets.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: The remaining three planets, however, have voices indeed, but not songs.
src.qo: Tres uero reliquos uoces quidem habere non cantus.

s: In the Platonic Theology Ficino argues that the soul is not a harmony of the humours: harmony arises when strings are moved by something else, and every composite body has some concord of parts, so if harmony were the soul every composite body would be alive; the living body's specific consonance is regulated by a power above it.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1482, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum
src.loc: p. 215, chs. 10-12 of the arguments against the soul as harmony
src.q: For harmony does not move the strings itself; rather, harmony is born when the strings are moved from elsewhere.
src.qo: Quippe non mouet ipsa cordas: sed iis aliunde motis nascitur harmonia.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1482, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum
src.q: In every body composed of many parts, there is some harmony of those parts through which they harmonize in mutual concord. Thus, if harmony itself were the soul, any composite body would be alive and grow together.
src.qo: In omni corpore ex multis cõposito ẽ aliqua suarũ ptiũ harmo nia: p̃ quã cõspiratione mutua cõcinnũt. Itaq; si harmonia ipsa sit aĩa: corpora quelibet cõposita uiuent & coalescẽt.

s: Following Augustine's De musica, Ficino holds that delight in a sung verse is itself a judgement by 'judicial numbers' in the soul: unless the sense of delight were imbued with numbers it could not assent to equal intervals and reject disordered ones, and reason judges that delight by still higher numbers.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1482, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum
src.q: we hear the numbers of the verse itself through the numbers of sensing, and we take delight through the judicial numbers
src.qo: numeros ipsius uersus p numeros sentiendi audimus, & per iudiciales numeros delectamur.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1482, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum
src.q: unless the sense of delight were itself imbued with certain numbers, it could in no way assent to equal intervals and reject disordered ones

s: In the De amore Ficino calls love 'the perpetual knot and connection of the world' and argues that no member of the world hates another: apparent contraries (fire and water, wolf and lamb) act from self-love and self-preservation, not from hatred.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1469, Platonis Dialogi Marsilio Ficino interprete (with De amore)
src.loc: p. 551, De amore, Oration III, end of ch. 3 and ch. 4
src.q: love is the perpetual knot and connection of the world, and the immovable support and firm foundation of the whole machine of its parts
src.qo: vt merito dici possit amor nodus perpetuus et copula mundi par tiumq; eius immobile substentaculum ac firmum totius machine fundamentum.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1469, Platonis Dialogi Marsilio Ficino interprete (with De amore)
src.q: For fire does not flee water out of hatred for the water, but out of love for itself
src.qo: Non enim ignis aquam aque odio fugit sed sui ipsius amore ne ab aque frigore extinguatur.

s: Gaffurius retells the Pythagoras-in-the-smithy story as fact (Pythagoras 'having abandoned the judgment of the ears' turns to weights), disputing Boethius only on a detail: Pythagoras did not discard the fifth hammer but added a sixth, giving weights 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16 pounds.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: And since there were five hammers, he cast out the fifth according to Boethius, because it was dissonant with all the others.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: it must be considered and maintained that Pythagoras did not reject the fifth hammer, but rather took up a sixth.
src.qo: extimandū tū eſt atq; tenēdum pithagoraz quintū non reieciſſe maleuz ſed potius z ſextū reſupſiſſe

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: the first hammer was of four pounds weight, the second six, the third eight, the fourth nine, the fifth twelve, and the sixth contained sixteen pounds of weight
src.qo: At cū primus maleus esset quattuor librarʒ pōderis. secūdus sex tertiuſ octo. quartus nouem q̄ntuſ duodeci. sextus sexdecī libras pōderis cōtinebāt

s: Gaffurius repeats the Boethian scheme: the seven planets sound 'so concordant that they sing together a most sweet melody' inaudible to us, and human music is the tempering of incorporeal reason with the body 'as if of high and low voices', producing a single consonance.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: yet are so concordant that they sing together a most sweet melody, although it is inaudible to us because of the sheer magnitude of the sound

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: a certain fitting-together and a tempering—as if of high and low voices—producing, as it were, a single consonance

s: Gaffurius says the seven sounds 'that nourish all of music' are each distinct, each one 'rejects similarity to the others' and they are entirely different from one another, in the image of the seven planets.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1480, Theoricum opus musice discipline
src.q: because there are only seven sounds that nourish all of music—each of which is separated from the others by its distinctness, for each one rejects similarity to the others and they are entirely different from one another
src.qo: quorum alter ab altero diſſimilitudine diſgregatur eorū naqʒ alter alterius ſimilitudinem negat Sūt eniʒ ſibiiplis penitus diſſimiles.

s: In the Practica musicae Gaffurius ranks concords by how much room they leave for consonant middle notes: the more the interval between the extremes can be filled variably, the more the mixture partakes of harmony, while the third, with a single middle step, is 'far removed from the harmonic nature of sweetness'.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.q: But the more the intermediate interval between the extremities is increased and variable, the more this kind of mixture will perceive the nature of harmony.
src.qo: At quanto auctius & uariabile fuerit mediu ipsas extremitatu interuallu: tanto huiusmodi commixtio naturam percipiet harmoniae.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.q: because of its simplicity, it is far removed from the harmonic nature of sweetness
src.qo: ob sui simplicitatem ab harmonica suauitatis natura longe disiuncta est:

s: Gaffurius reports that organists let the fifth be diminished by 'a small, hidden, and in some way uncertain quantity' which they call 'participated', and that in sixths the middle note must be slightly relaxed, as the experience of instruments teaches: exact ratios are bent in practice.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.loc: fol. 50v [scan 106], Book III, ch. 3, second rule
src.q: the fifth itself (as organists claim) tolerates the diminution of a small, hidden, and in some way uncertain quantity, which is indeed called "participated" by them.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.loc: fol. 48v [scan 102], Book III, ch. 2, on the sixth
src.q: it requires the middle chord to be relaxed slightly (as we are taught by the experiment of instruments)
src.qo: mediam ipsam chordam aliquantulo postulat relaxari (quod instrumentorum edocemur experimento)

s: Gaffurius forbids two successive perfect consonances of the same kind, requires at least one imperfect concord (third or sixth) as mediator between two perfect ones, and admits seconds, fourths and sevenths only in the fastest passing notes, where they 'achieve no stable place in songs'.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.loc: fol. 50v [scan 106], Book III, ch. 3, third rule
src.q: at least one imperfect concordance, such as a third or sixth and suchlike, must be established as a mediator
src.qo: una saltem imperfecta concordantia: puta tertia uel sexta & eiusmodi: debet media constitui.

src.l: Franchinus Gaffurius, 1502, Practica musicae utriusque cantus
src.q: they achieve no stable place in songs (unless in the fastest passage of temporal measurement)
src.qo: quippe quæ in cantilenis (nisi uelocissimo mensuræ temporalis transitu) nullum consequuntur stabilem locum.

s: Salinas (1577) praises Gaffurius's reading but says he recited Ptolemy, Aristides and Bryennius 'so confusedly that it seems he read them rather than understood them', wavered between Boethius and Ptolemy, rebuked Ramis for 5:4 and 6:5 thirds, and yet conceded that the 81:80 ratio is greatest for tempering all harmonies.

src.l: Francisco de Salinas, 1577, De musica libri septem
src.q: though so confusedly that it seems he read them rather than understood them
src.qo: Ac verum est, quod hos libros legit, vt in ſuis oſtendit operibus, in eo præſertim, quod de Harmonia inſtrumentali cōſcripſit, vbi omnes fermè eorum poſitiones recitat, ita tamen confuſè, vt potiùs eos legiſſe, quàm intellexiſſe videatur.

src.l: Francisco de Salinas, 1577, De musica libri septem
src.q: he confesses that the power of the sesquioctuagesima ratio is greatest for tempering all musical harmonies

s: Zarlino holds that the 'sonorous number' is contained in the senary (1-6), the first perfect number, and that within it lie all the forms of the simple consonances: 2:1, 3:2, 4:3, and also the major third 5:4 and minor third 6:5.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.loc: p. 23 [scan 41], end of Part I, ch. 13
src.q: Within this number are contained all the forms of the simple consonances possible to be found, which are fit to produce harmonies and melodies.
src.qo: Nel quale numero ſono contenute tutte le forme delle ſemplici conſonanze poſſibili da ritrouarſi, atte a produr le harmonie & le melodie:

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: The Ditone is then contained between 5 and 4 in the Sesquiquarta ratio; and the Semiditone in the Sesquiquinta ratio between 6 and 5.
src.qo: Il Ditono poi è contenuto tra 5. & 4. nella Seſquiquarta proportione; & il Semiditono nella Seſquiquinta tra 6. & 5.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: It is truly marvelous how Nature has ordered one consonance after another in such a way.
src.qo: Questo è veramente marauiglioso, che la Natura habbia ordinato in tal maniera l'una Consonanza dopo l'altra,

s: Zarlino says Moses chose the number six for creation because of the harmony enclosed in it, a harmony that preserves the world's being, without which the world 'would not endure at all' and the confusion of Chaos would return.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.loc: p. 23 [scan 41], end of Part I, ch. 13
src.q: Without this harmony, the world would not endure at all; it would either be utterly annulled or, with things returning to their first state (if one may say so), the confusion of ancient Chaos would be seen once more.
src.qo: non hauendo Iddio nelle ſue operationi mai hauuto biſogno di tempo: percioche, come colui, che d'ogni ſcienza era perfetto maeſtro, conoſcendo per opera del Spirito diuino l'harmonia, che in tal numero era rinchiuſa; & che dalle coſe viſibili & apparenti conoſciamo le inuiſibili d'Iddio, la ſua onnipotenza, & la diuinità ſua; volſe col mezo di tal numero in vn tratto eſprimere & inſieme moſtrare la perfettione dell'opera, & in eſſa la rinchiuſa harmonia, conſeruatrice dell'eſſer ſuo, ſenza la quale a patto alcuno non durarebbe:

s: Zarlino defines counterpoint as a harmony arising from a body with various parts, 'a certain artful union of diverse sounds, reduced to concordance', and says harmony 'arises from nothing other than the diversity of things that are put together and are opposite to one another', hence parts should move by contrary motion.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: Or rather that it is a certain artful union of diverse sounds, reduced to concordance.
src.qo: Oueramente che'l sia una certa vnione arteficiosa de suoni diuersi, ridutta alla concordanza.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: for Harmony arises from nothing other than the diversity of things that are put together and are opposite to one another
src.qo: conciofiache l'Harmonia non nasce da altro, che dalla diuersità delle cose, che si pongono insieme, & sono tra loro opposite.

s: Zarlino holds that dissonances, placed by rule, make the following consonance more delightful (like light after darkness) and that compositions of consonances alone would be 'almost imperfect'; a cadence has no grace without its dissonance. Yet dissonance remains incidental: placed at random it yields confusion.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.loc: p. 173 [scan 191], end of the chapter before ch. 28
src.q: Dissonance makes the Consonance that immediately follows it seem more delightful

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: such compositions (not having the Consonances mixed with Dissonances) would be almost imperfect
src.qo: Concioſiache ſe fuſſero compoſte di conſonanze ſolamente, con tutto che faceſſero bello vdire, & da loro ne uſciſſero buoni effetti, hauerebbero tuttauia tali compoſitioni (non eſſendo meſcolate le Conſonanze con le Diſſonanze) quaſi dello imperfetto, ſi dalla parte del cantare, come anco per l'aiuto della compoſitione:

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: one primarily uses Consonances in compositions, and then Dissonances as an incidental feature

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: -all, or any elegance in itself, if it is without the Dissonance

s: In the Dimostrationi Zarlino concedes that dissonances also have rational ratios but denies them the 'reason of numbers', which he reserves for ratios between the parts of the senary; and he defines 'harmony simply so-called' as at least two parts joined by harmonic proportionality that reaches the hearing pleasantly.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1571, Dimostrationi harmoniche
src.q: But Dissonances cannot be said to be so, nor to have such reasons, because their ratios are contained among numbers other than those placed between the aforementioned parts.
src.qo: Ma le Dissonanze non possono esser dette, ne hauere cotali ragioni: percioche hanno le proportioni loro contenute tra altri numeri, che quelli posti tra le parti nominate.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1571, Dimostrationi harmoniche
src.q: Harmony Simply so-called is the ensemble that arises from at least two parts joined together, according to the steps of Harmonic proportionality: which reaches the Hearing pleasantly.
src.qo: Harmonia Semplicemente detta è il concento, che nasce da due parti almeno insieme unite, secondo i gradi dell'Harmonica proportionalità: la quale soauemente peruiene all'Vdito.

s: Vincenzo Galilei's Dialogo (1581) attacks the tuning Zarlino said is sung today (Ptolemy's syntonic diatonic): in it the minor third D-F is not 6:5 but the ancient dissonant semiditone 32:27, a comma smaller, which 'the senses ... accept without resistance', and he treats the senario's power as an artefact of arranging superparticular numbers.

src.l: Vincenzo Galilei, 1581, Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna
src.q: Such is the Genus in which one composes, sings, and plays today, according to the pleasure of the Reverend Master Gioseffo Zarlino. In refuting his opinion
src.qo: e tale è secondo che piace al Reuerendo M. Gioseffo Zarlino, il Genere nel quale si compone, si canta, & si suona hoggi.

src.l: Vincenzo Galilei, 1581, Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna
src.q: And although the senses (as has been said) accept it without resistance, we will nonetheless prove it to the intellect in this manner
src.qo: & con tutto che il senso (per quello che si è detto) lo concede senza repugnanza, lo proueremo nondimeno all'intelletto in questa maniera.

s: Kepler argues in Harmonices Mundi IV.1 that harmony is a relation, and that a relation is nothing without a mind that compares; so a sensible harmony needs, besides its two sounding terms, a comparing soul, without which the two sounds remain two things and not one harmony.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.loc: Book IV, ch. I; scan 228, printed p. 109
src.q: there must also be a comparing Soul. For if this Soul is removed, the terms will indeed be two sensible things, but they will not be one Harmony, which is a being of reason.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.q: so that this proportion may be called harmonic, the soul makes it so by the comparison with its own Archetype. It could not be called harmonic, nor would it obtain any power to move souls, if this Archetype were not present.
src.qo: ut ut hæc proportio sit harmonica, ipsa sui Archetypi collatione facit; quæ harmonica dici non posset, nec vim ullam sortiretur in movendis animis, si hic Archetypus non esset.

s: Kepler derived the consonances not from numbers but from the division of the circle by constructible (demonstrable) regular plane figures, after first finding the seven harmonic sections of the string by ear; in HM III.2 he calls his 1596 attempt to derive them from the five regular solids a delusion.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.loc: Book III, ch. II; scan 133, printed p. 27
src.q: wrongly striving to deduce their number and ratios from the number of the five Regular solid bodies. The truth is rather this: both the five solid figures and the Musical harmonies and string sections share a common origin in the plane Regular figures.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1621, Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum), 2nd edition with notes
src.loc: Mysterium cosmographicum ch. XII (1596 text); scan 70, printed p. 42
src.q: And so, properly speaking, we have only five concordances in Music, corresponding to the number of the five bodies.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia (Defense of The Harmony of the World)
src.loc: Apologia, answer to the Analysis section preceding Analysis X; scan 20, printed p. 11
src.q: in place of the ancients' Numbers (a discrete quantity ), I have substituted the circle and Geometric figures (a continuous quantity ).

s: Kepler insists that the ear, not reason, fixes which intervals are consonant, and that his geometric definition only explains what the ears of all men already approve; he faults the Pythagoreans for abandoning the ear for reason alone.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.loc: Book III, ch. II; scan 134, printed p. 28
src.q: they proceeded for a short while by the judgment of the ears, but soon, having despised their guides, they completed the rest of the journey following Reason alone
src.qo: qui aurium judicio progreffi aliquatenus, mox contemptis ducibus, reliquum itineris, Rationem fecuti, perfecerunt; auribus vi quafi pertractis, & planè obfurdefcere juffis.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia (Defense of The Harmony of the World)
src.loc: Apologia, appendix on Harmonics; scan 25, printed p. 16
src.q: it is not that one thing pleases the ears of this man and another the ears of that man; but the same number of consonances is approved by the ears of all men, which is evidence that this is the work of nature.

s: Kepler concludes HM V.7 that the heavenly motions are a perennial, rational (not audible) concert of six voices that moves through dissonant tensions, like syncopations or cadences, toward prescribed closes; human polyphony, unknown to the ancients, imitates it.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.loc: Book V, ch. VII; scan 341, printed p. 213
src.q: the motions of the heavens are nothing other than a certain perennial concert (rational, not vocal ) tending toward certain and prescribed musical endings [clausulae] through dissonant tensions, like certain Syncopations or Cadences

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices Mundi
src.loc: Book V, end of ch. IV; scan 329, printed p. 202
src.q: individual planets will be compared with the Choral Music of the ancients, and its properties will be shown in the motions of the planets; but in the following chapters, the planets joined together will be shown to match with modern figurated music.
src.qo: ejusque proprietates in planetarum motibus ostendentur: at capitibus sequentibus, juncti planetæ, cum figuratâ modernâ Musicâ paria facere demonstrabuntur.

s: Answering Fludd in the 1622 Apologia, Kepler says he would agree that the same harmony is in man, the world and the archetype, if only Fludd took mathematics into the kernel of harmony instead of calling it a husk or shadow; he also distinguishes three senses of 'harmony' and charges Fludd with stretching the word further.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia (Defense of The Harmony of the World)
src.loc: Apologia, answer to the Analysis section preceding Analysis X; scan 20, printed p. 11
src.q: if you did not relegate Mathematics to the mere husk or outer skin, or even label it a vain and frivolous shadow, but rather received it into the very Kernel itself: then truly no one among the truly philosophizing would fail to applaud you

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia (Defense of The Harmony of the World)
src.loc: Apologia, answer to the Analysis section preceding Analysis X; scan 20, printed p. 11
src.q: one person, following common usage, accepts Harmony only as that of Concord, which involves sound; another, following the original root of the word, accepts it for every kind of congruence of geometric things

s: In De musica mundana (UCH I, tract. I, bk. III, ch. 3) Fludd imagines a monochord stretched from the summit of the Empyrean to the base of the earth, divided like an instrument's string so that the regions of the cosmos stand in musical intervals; pressing it at the half gives the octave.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi historia, Tomus primus (De macrocosmo)
src.loc: Tract. I, Book III (De musica mundana), ch. III; scan 87, printed p. 85
src.q: if a monochord were imaginatively extended from the summit of the Empyrean heaven to the base of the earth itself, constituting the radius of either pyramid, we will perceive that it is divided into parts constituting consonances; of which if the half part were pressed, it would produce the Diapason consonance

s: Fludd holds that world harmony arises only from the mixture of two opposed pyramids, a formal pyramid of light descending and a material pyramid of dark matter ascending, as a lute needs a musician; neither nature is worth anything without the other.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi historia, Tomus primus (De macrocosmo)
src.loc: Tract. I, Book III, ch. III; scan 87, printed p. 85
src.q: neither is a lute without a musician, nor a musician without a lute sufficient to make musical consonances

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi historia, Tomus primus (De macrocosmo)
src.loc: Tract. I, Book III, ch. III; scan 87, printed p. 85
src.q: one nature, whether material or formal, is worth nothing without the other, and hence World Music arises from both pyramids mixed in the smallest degree.

s: Fludd divides his world monochord into a material octave (earth to the Sun's 'sphere of equality', founded on the imperfect fourth) and a spiritual or formal octave (Sun to the Empyrean, founded on the perfect fifth), and ranks the formal octave and its consonances far above the material.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi historia, Tomus primus (De macrocosmo)
src.loc: Tract. I, Book III, ch. III; scan 88, printed p. 86
src.q: just as an Octave was produced from the center to the sphere of the Sun, which was material, so also another Octave is raised upward from the head of the material pyramid to the supreme peak of the Empyrean heaven, which exists as a spiritual Octave.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi historia, Tomus primus (De macrocosmo)
src.loc: Tract. I, Book III, ch. III; scan 89, printed p. 87
src.q: just as the Earth is far more ignoble than the solar body, so also the material Octave and the consonances included within it are to be placed far behind those spiritual ones.

s: In the Philosophia sacra (1626) Fludd reads the old pair of strife and friendship, Dionysus scattering and Apollo uniting 'with the bonds of harmony', as the two-fold operation of a single divine essence, acting kindly or destructively as one fire warms at a distance and scorches up close.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1626, Philosophia sacra et vere christiana seu meteorologia cosmica
src.loc: Sect. I, Portion IV, Part II, Book IV, Member II, ch. VII; scan 257, printed p. 260
src.q: just as it was the role of Apollo, according to the intention of the Poets, to compose and unite with the bonds of harmony, so it was the property of Dionysus to destroy what was composed through the antipathy of discord and to scatter what was united. And yet, both Apollo and Dionysus represented only a single essence of divinity
src.qo: ita quidem Dionysii proprietas erat, cōposita discordiae antipathia destruere, atque vnita dissipare, & tamen tā Apollo, quā Dionysius non nisi vnica diuinitatis essentiam fecerunt,

s: Replying to Kepler's Apologia in the Monochordum mundi symphoniacum (1622), Fludd grants that Kepler's harmony is praiseworthy as external, common mathematics but says it stands to formal mathematics as the letter to the spirit and the body to the soul, a shadow of the truth and not the truth.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1622, Monochordum mundi symphoniacum (The Symphonic Monochord of the World)
src.loc: On Analysis XXV; scan 82, printed p. 81
src.q: the external doctrine of Johannes concerning the Harmony of the world stands in such a relation as the letter to the spirit, and the body to the soul.
src.qo: Sic etiam externam Ioannis doctrinam de mundi Harmonia dixi ita se habere, vt litera ad spiritum & anima ad corpus.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1622, Monochordum mundi symphoniacum (The Symphonic Monochord of the World)
src.loc: On Analysis XXV; scan 83, printed p. 82
src.q: as a shadow is to the reality of the thing—a shadow, I say, of the truth but not the truth itself.
src.qo: vt rei vmbra ad eius realitatem, vmbra (inquam) est veritatis sed non ipsa veritas.

s: In Harmonie universelle (Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV) Mersenne counts the unison a consonance and the 'exemplary cause and end' of all consonances, and argues it is sweeter than the octave because its sounds unite more often and more easily.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 533, printed p. 10
src.q: the unison is the exemplary cause and the end of all consonances, since they all tend toward said unison from which they draw their origin—just as all mathematical ratios of inequality derive from the ratio of equality.
src.qo: puis qu'elles tendent toutes audit vnisson, d'où elles tirent leur origine, comme les raisons d'inegalité tirent la leur de la raison d'egalité,

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 534, printed p. 11
src.q: I say first that there is no doubt it is sweeter, since it unites its sounds more often and more easily.
src.qo: ie dis premierement qu'il n'y a nul doute qu'il ne ſoit plus doux, puis qu'il vnit ſes ſons plus ſouuent & plus aiſément,

s: Mersenne measures the sweetness of consonances and their divisions by how quickly and often the strings' returns coincide, so a division that unites twice as fast is twice as excellent (octave 2:3:4 beats 3:4:6 as 13 to 9); in the Harmonicorum libri he uses the same coincidences to rank how strongly a sounding string shakes an untouched one.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Prop. XXXVII; scan 622, printed p. 99
src.q: since the excellence of divisions is measured by the ease and speed of their meeting and their union, each division is that much more excellent as its sounds unite more often: and consequently if they unite twice as fast, it is twice as excellent.
src.qo: ce des diuiſions eſt meſuree par la facilité & la viſteſſe de leur rencontre & de leur vnion; chaque diuiſion eſt dautant plus excellente, que ſes ſons ſ'vniſſent plus ſouuent: & conſequemment s'ils ſ'vniſſent deux fois plus viſte, elle eſt deux fois plus excellente.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonicorum libri XII
src.loc: On consonances, end of the proposition before Prop. XXIX; scan 83, printed p. 67
src.q: the ratio of the power of each Consonance is the same as that which was previously placed in the excellence and sweetness of each.
src.qo: adeovt eadem sit ratio virtutis vniuscuiusque Consonantiæ, quæ priùs in vniuscuiusque excellentiâ, atque dulcedine posita est:

s: Mersenne reports the view that the octave and other consonances please more than the unison because 'nature delights in diversity' (citing Zarlino's comparison of unison and octave to white and black), and then rejects it: he judges the unison more pleasant and calls the pleasure in diversity a sign of our neediness and imperfection.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 536, printed p. 13
src.q: many believe that the Octave and other Consonances are more pleasant than the Unison, since they possess variety within their union, and nature delights in diversity

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 536, printed p. 13
src.q: the Unison would please all kinds of men more if they were in a state of perfection; a state which seems to reject diversity, the pleasure of which testifies to our neediness and our imperfection.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 537, printed p. 14
src.q: I estimate, therefore, that the Unison is more pleasant than Consonances, and that we must feel compassion for the fragility and inconstancy of men who do not share this sentiment
src.qo: I'estime donc que l'Vnisson est plus agreable que les Consonances, & qu'il faut porter compassion à la fragilité & inconstance des hommes qui n'ont pas ce sentiment,

s: Mersenne rejects Aristotle's objection (Politics II) that counting the unison a consonance is like introducing community of all things into a republic: he calls that community most desirable and diversity 'the source of corruption', and says resemblance is the source of love and preservation.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 534, printed p. 11
src.q: And as for the communal sharing in Republics, which Aristotle opposed in order to contradict his Master, it is most desirable; but it must not be hoped for as long as people prefer diversity to equality.
src.qo: Et quant à la communauté des Re- publiques, à laquelle Ariſtote s'eſt oppoſé pour contredire à ſon Maiſtre, elle eſt tres-ſouhaitable; mais il ne la faut pas eſperer tandis que l'on prefere la diuerſité à l'égalité;

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1636, Harmonie universelle (vol. I as held: includes Traité des consonances)
src.loc: Traité des consonances, Bk. I, Prop. IV; scan 535, printed p. 12
src.q: for resemblance is the source of love, and the preservation of the being and nature of each thing, which is better preserved by uniformity than by deformity.
src.qo: car la reſſemblance eſt la ſource de l'amour, & la conſeruation de l'eſtre & de la nature de chaque choſe, qui ſe conſerue mieux par l'vniformité que par la difformité.

s: In the Quaestiones in Genesim (1623) Mersenne summarises Fludd's world monochord, two pyramids and material and spiritual octaves among modern cosmogonies, then gives a 'judgment on Fludd' that his Kabbalistic exegesis either repeats what every Catholic knows or proposes falsehoods.

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1623, Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim
src.q: Indeed, they compare the whole world to a harmonic monochord. In this, the spirit or soul of the world, or rather God himself, being placed outside the monochord, produces all the consonances.
src.qo: in quo mundi spiritus, vel anima, vel potiùs ipse Deus extra monochordum positus omnes consonãtias edat,

src.l: Marin Mersenne, 1623, Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim
src.q: What he has concerning the Kabbalah in this prelude and throughout the book either contains only what theologians and philosophers commonly teach and every Catholic knows, or it proposes falsehoods.
src.qo: Quæ de Cabala habet in hoc præludio, & toto libro, vel tantùm continent, quod vulgò Theologi, & Philosophi docent, & singuli Catholici nouerunt, vel falsa proponit:

s: Descartes's Compendium opens by making musical pleasure relational: every sense can be pleased, but only by an object standing in a certain proportion to the sense, and the parts of an object are 'less different' (hence easier to perceive) the greater the proportion between them.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: This pleasure requires a certain proportion between the object and the sense itself.
src.qo: 2°. Ad hanc delectationem requiritur proportio quædam objecti cum ipso sensu,

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: We say that the parts of the whole object are less different among themselves, between which there is a greater proportion.

s: Descartes requires that the perceived proportion be arithmetic rather than geometric, and holds that incommensurable parts can never be perceived together by the sense, which is 'perpetually deceived' into approximating them by a simple arithmetic ratio.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: That proportion must be Arithmetic, not Geometric, the reason for which is that there are not so many things to be noted in it, since the differences are everywhere equal.
src.qo: cujus ratio est, quia non tam multa in ea sunt advertenda, cum æ- quales sint ubique differentiæ.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: which are incommensurable. And therefore, as I judge, they can by no means be perfectly known by the sense simultaneously
src.qo: Ideoque, ut arbitror, nullo pacto simul possunt à sensu perfectè cognosci,

s: Descartes holds that what pleases the mind most is neither the most easily nor the most laboriously perceived object, but one easy enough not to fatigue the sense yet not so easy that the sense's natural desire is left unfilled; and he adds that variety is most pleasing in all things.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: that is not most pleasing to the mind which is perceived most easily by the sense, nor even that which is perceived with most difficulty
src.qo: 7º. Inter objecta sensus, illud non animo gratissimum est quod facillime sensu percipitur, neque etiam quod difficillime ;

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: Finally, it should be noted that variety is most pleasing in all things
src.qo: 8º. Denique notandum est varietatem omnibus in rebus esse gratissimam,

s: Descartes calls the fifth the most pleasing consonance because it sits between the sharp ditone and the 'languid' octave; the octave can be used alone only because its two voices are heard 'as if they were one', whereas the fifth used alone without variety would soon cause disgust.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: This is the most pleasing of all consonances and the most acceptable to the ears
src.qo: Hæc est consonantiarum omnium gratissima atque auribus acceptissima,

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: it contains the unison within itself, and then the two voices are heard as if they were one

s: In the Compendium Descartes justifies syncopated dissonances: they are tolerated because the memory of the preceding consonance remains, their variety makes the surrounding consonances heard better, and by suspending judgment they increase expectation so that the awaited consonance pleases more.

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: Indeed, the variety of these causes the consonances among which they are situated to be heard better, and they also excite attention.
src.qo: immo etiam harum varietas efficit, ut consonantiæ, inter quas sunt sitæ, melius audiantur, atque etiam attentionem excitant;

src.l: René Descartes, 1656, Compendium musicae (Amsterdam: Jansson, 1656)
src.q: that which has been awaited for longer is more pleasing when it finally arrives
src.qo: quia magis placet, quod diutius expectatum, tandem accedit,

s: In a letter to Mersenne (18 March 1630) Descartes says the beautiful and the pleasant signify only a relation between our judgment and the object, and since human judgments differ so much they have no fixed measure; the same tune can make some want to dance and others weep, through associations stored in memory (a dog whipped to a violin would howl at it).

src.l: René Descartes, 1897, Œuvres de Descartes, ed. Adam & Tannery, vol. I: Correspondance (1622–1638)
src.loc: Letter XX to Mersenne, 18 March 1630, AT I p. 133 [scan 247]
src.q: neither the beautiful nor the pleasant signifies anything other than a relationship between our judgment and the object; and because human judgments are so different, one cannot say that the beautiful or the pleasant have any fixed measure.

src.l: René Descartes, 1897, Œuvres de Descartes, ed. Adam & Tannery, vol. I: Correspondance (1622–1638)
src.q: the same thing that makes some want to dance can give others the urge to cry.

s: Rameau holds that harmony moves different passions in proportion to the chords used, and that even in songs of cheerfulness, which should use consonant chords as much as possible, dissonant chords cannot be dispensed with and should be born naturally and prepared.

src.l: Jean-Philippe Rameau, 1722, Traite de l'harmonie reduite a ses principes naturels
src.loc: Traité, Book II, ch. 20 'On the property of chords', p. 141 [scan 179]

src.qo: IL est certain que l'Harmonie peut émouvoir en nous, differentes passions, à proportion des Accords qu'on y employe.

src.l: Jean-Philippe Rameau, 1722, Traite de l'harmonie reduite a ses principes naturels
src.q: as one cannot dispense with intermingling dissonant chords in them, one must ensure that the dissonances are born in them naturally

s: Helmholtz claims to have solved Pythagoras' enigma of why consonance is determined by small whole-number ratios: the ear resolves sounds into partials (Fourier), consonance requires that two lower partials coincide exactly, otherwise beats disturb; and he calls the ancient, medieval and oriental number speculation on consonance 'extravagant and fanciful'.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part II, ch. XII Retrospect, p. 229 [scan 251]
src.q: the condition of consonance is that two of the lower partial tones of the notes combined shall be of exactly the same pitch; when they are not, disturbance arises from beats.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part II, ch. XII Retrospect, p. 229 [scan 251]
src.q: The relation of whole numbers to consonance became in ancient times, in the middle ages, and especially among Oriental nations, the foundation of extravagant and fanciful speculation.

s: Helmholtz separates sensuous pleasure from aesthetic beauty: whether one combination is rougher than another depends only on the anatomy of the ear, but how much roughness a hearer will endure as a means of expression depends on taste and habit, so the boundary between consonance and dissonance has frequently changed.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XIII, p. 234 [scan 256]
src.q: Whether one combination is rougher or smoother than another, depends solely on the anatomical structure of the ear, and has nothing to do with psychological motives. But what degree of roughness a hearer is inclined to endure as a means of musical expression depends on taste and habit

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XIII, p. 234 [scan 256]
src.q: hence the boundary between consonances and dissonances has been frequently changed.

s: Helmholtz states that the system of scales, modes and harmonic tissue is (in the 1865 German edition) not founded on unalterable natural laws but the consequence of aesthetic principles that have changed and will change with human development; the English (Ellis, from a later edition) softens this to 'not solely' and 'at least partly', and adds that the choice was nevertheless not arbitrary.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, 1865, Die Lehre von den Tonempfindungen als physiologische Grundlage für die Theorie der Musik (2nd ed.)
src.loc: Lehre von den Tonempfindungen (1865), Dritte Abtheilung, Abschnitt 13, p. 358 [scan 378]
src.q: dass das System der Tonleitern, der Tonarten und deren Harmoniegewebe nicht auf unveränderlichen Naturgesetzen beruht, sondern dass es die Consequenz ästhetischer Principien ist, die mit fortschreitender Entwickelung der Menschheit einem Wechsel unterworfen gewesen sind und ferner noch sein werden.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XIII, p. 235 [scan 257]
src.q: the system of Scales, Modes, and Harmonic Tissues does not rest solely upon inalterable natural laws, but is also, at least partly, the result of esthetical principles, which have already changed, and will still further change, with the progressive development of humanity.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XIII, p. 235 [scan 257]
src.q: But it does not follow from this that the choice of those elements of musical art was perfectly arbitrary

s: Helmholtz concludes from the anatomy of the cochlea that the auditory nerve endings are everywhere connected with an elastic auxiliary apparatus that can be set in sympathetic vibration by external vibration and then 'probably' excites the nerves.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part I, ch. VI, p. 142 [scan 164]
src.q: The essential result of our description of the ear may consequently be said to consist in having found the terminations of the auditory nerves everywhere con- nected with a peculiar auxiliary apparatus, partly elastic, partly firm, which may be put in sympathetic vibration under the influence of external vibration

s: Despite relativising scales to culture, Helmholtz holds that the natural major third depends on 5/4, that any other third is an unsatisfactory substitute, that equal-tempered thirds 'simply sound out of tune and wrong', and that the fault of tempered intonation lies in the thirds, not the fifths.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XVI Tempered Intonation, p. 315 [scan 337]
src.q: The natural relation of the major Third to the tonic, both melodically and harmonically, depends on the ratio 5/4 of the pitch numbers. Any other Third is only a more or less unsatisfactory substitute for the natural major Third.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part III, ch. XVI, p. 314 [scan 336]
src.q: they simply sound out of tune and wrong.

s: Helmholtz objects to Euler's degree-of-agreeableness theory that it cannot explain why a slightly mistuned consonance sounds almost as good as a just one, and that it says nothing of how the mind could perceive numerical ratios; on his account the mind perceives only their physical effect, continuous or intermittent nerve sensation.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part II, ch. XII Retrospect, p. 231 [scan 253]
src.q: Euler's system gives no explanation of the reason why a consonance when slightly out of tune sounds almost as well as one justly tuned, and much better than one greatly out of tune

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.loc: Sensations of Tone, Part II, ch. XII Retrospect, p. 231 [scan 253]
src.q: According to the latter, the human mind perceives commensurable ratios of pitch numbers as such; according to our method, it perceives only the physical effect of these ratios, namely, the continuous or intermittent sensation of the auditory nerves.

s: In Legge's Zuozhuan (Zhao 20), Yanzi lists the paired contrasts of music (clear and thick, small and large, fast and slow, high and low, and so on) 'by which the parts are all blended together', and says the purpose is that the listener's mind be composed.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: Then there are [the distinctions of] clear and thick, small and large, short and long, fast and slow, solemn and joyful, hard and soft, lingering and rapid, high and low, the commencement and close, the close and the diffuse, by which the parts are all blended together.

s: Yanzi's harmonious minister corrects the ruler from both sides so that 'the government is made equal' and the people have no quarrel with it; the ode he cites praises a sacrifice with no contention in it.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: In this way the government is made equal, with no infringement of what is right, and there is no quarrelling with it in the minds of the people.

s: In the Zuozhuan (Zhao 20) Confucius (Zhongni) praises Zichan's advice: mild and severe government must alternate, each correcting the excess of the other, and 'it is in this way that the administration of government is brought to harmony'.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: Mildness serves to temper severity, and severity to regulate mildness; — it is in this way that the administration of government is brought to harmony.

s: In the Zuozhuan (Zhao 21) the music master Ling Zhoujiu warns King Jing against casting the oversized bell Wuyi: notes must be neither too small nor too great, so that music is 'in harmony with things' and the heart can bear it; a bell too large will agitate the king's heart and kill him.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: The smaller notes must not be too small, nor the greater too great. [This being the case], there ensues a harmony with things without, and admirable music is the result.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: This bell will be too large, and the king's heart will not be able to endure it.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: 小者不窕，大者不摐，則和於物。

s: The Han writer Liu Liang's 'Discourse distinguishing he and tong' (辯和同論), anthologised in the Ming Jingji leibian, defines he as using the acceptable to correct the unacceptable and tong as likes and dislikes that do not differ, reusing Yanzi's soup and the single-note zither to praise remonstrance as loyalty.

s: Critique: Yanzi's he is often cited as an ancient 'diversity in wholeness', but in context the diversity is a minister's correction serving the ruler's right judgement, its stated aim is a level government with no contention, and on the same page Confucius uses he for alternating mildness and severity; the parts' own flourishing is not the measure.

src.l: James Legge (trans.), 1960, The Chinese Classics, Vol. 5: The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen
src.q: Then the master eats it, and his mind is made equable.

s: Legge (1861) renders Analects 13.23 君子和而不同 as 'The superior man is affable, but not adulatory', and glosses 同 as 'agreeing with' = flattering: he becomes a manner of social ease and tong becomes flattery.

s: Analects 1.12 (Youzi): in the use of ritual (li), he is what is prized, yet he pursued for its own sake without being regulated by ritual 'is not to be done'; Legge translates he here as 'natural ease' and heads the chapter: ease is to be prized 'and yet to be subordinate to' ritual.

s: In the Zhuzi yulei, Zhu Xi explains that he lies in ritual itself: when the Son of Heaven dances his own dance, the lords theirs and the officers theirs, 'this is he'; when lords usurp the Son of Heaven's dance, ritual is lost, and losing ritual is not he.

s: Critique: in the Analects the he/tong line (13.23) sits beside 1.12, where he is valued only as regulated by ritual, and Zhu Xi reads that he as every rank keeping its own dance; so Confucian he is closer to fitting order within a fixed hierarchy than to parts that flourish in their own right.

s: Xunzi's 'Discourse on Music' (Yuelun) says music 'investigates oneness to establish harmony' (審一以定和), coordinates instruments and blends voices into pattern, and suffices to lead people along one Way and to order ten thousand changes.

s: Xunzi says that when ruler and minister listen to music together in the ancestral temple they are filled with harmony and reverence, father and son at home with harmony and affection, old and young in the village with harmony and compliance: one music, a different bond for each pair in the hierarchy.

s: Xunzi: music is harmony that cannot be changed, ritual is order that cannot be altered; 'music unites the same, ritual distinguishes the different' (樂合同，禮別異).

src.l: Xun Kuang (Xunzi), Yang Liang (comm.), c. 1778, Xunzi 荀子, with Yang Liang's commentary, juan 12–16 (Siku Quanshu Huiyao)
src.q: Furthermore, music embodies harmony that cannot be changed; ritual embodies order that cannot be altered. Music unites and harmonizes; ritual distinguishes and separates.

s: Critique: Xunzi's music-he is fixed from 'the one', is 'the great equaliser of the realm', 'unites the same' and makes 'none fail to obey'; difference belongs to ritual rank. This is a classical Chinese harmony in which unity and compliance are the point, so the tradition does not uniformly support 'diversity in wholeness'.

src.l: Xun Kuang (Xunzi), Yang Liang (comm.), c. 1778, Xunzi 荀子, with Yang Liang's commentary, juan 12–16 (Siku Quanshu Huiyao)
src.q: Going forth to punish, none fail to obey; entering in to yield, none fail to submit.

s: Zhongyong ch. 1: before pleasure, anger, sorrow and joy arise the mind is in zhong (equilibrium); when they arise and all 'hit the measure' (皆中節) that is he (harmony); zhong is the great root of the world and he its universal path.

s: In Zhuangzi Book II (Qiwulun), the 'notes of Heaven' are not a separate sound: the wind blows through myriad hollows of different shapes, each sounds differently and of itself, and no other agency excites them.

src.q: The first notes are slight, and those that follow deeper, but in harmony with them.

s: In the piping passage the word 和 (he) is used in its old musical sense of 'answering' sound: light winds make a small he, gales a great he, and leading sounds are answered by following ones; Legge renders it 'response'.

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East 39): Tao Teh King and the Writings of Kwang-ze, Books I-XVII

s: A 1699 commentary on the Qiwulun reads the ten thousand different sounds of the piping passage as a hidden figure for the unequal opinions of the world (物論不齊), the chapter's theme.

src.l: Zhuangzi, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with side commentary), vol. 1
src.q: the blowing results in ten thousand different sounds. This is to secretly compare the arguments of the world as being unequal.

s: Zhuangzi's sage 'harmonizes' a dispute by holding its 'this' and 'not-this' together and resting in the equal working of Heaven (天鈞), so that both sides stand; the monkeys of 'three in the morning' show that quarrels over equivalents are a matter of viewpoint.

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East 39): Tao Teh King and the Writings of Kwang-ze, Books I-XVII

src.q: Both sides of the question are admissible.

s: In Qiwulun §10, harmonizing conflicting opinions 'in the invisible operation of Heaven' (天倪) does not erase their difference: affirmation stays different from denial; what is given up is the dispute itself.

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East 39): Tao Teh King and the Writings of Kwang-ze, Books I-XVII
src.q: The harmonising of them is to be found in the invisible operation of Heaven

s: Critique: Zhuangzi's harmony keeps diversity but has no whole that the parts build or strengthen; it is reached by forgetting the conflict and appealing to the Infinite, so it fits the 'diversity' half of ideas/01 and not the 'parts and whole strengthen each other' half.

src.l: Zhuangzi, James Legge (trans.), 1891, The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East 39): Tao Teh King and the Writings of Kwang-ze, Books I-XVII
src.q: Let us forget the lapse of time; let us forget the conflict of opinions. Let us make our appeal to the Infinite, and take up our position there.

s: The Lüshi chunqiu chapter 'Great Music' (大樂) says music arises from measure and is rooted in the Great One (太一), which gives out the two poles and yin and yang; they part and rejoin in an endless cycle called 'the constancy of Heaven'.

This is unity over plurality, not diversity in wholeness.

s: Chunqiu fanlu ch. 77 'Following the Way of Heaven' says Heaven has 'two he' (the spring and autumn mid-points, east and west) that complete 'two zhong' (the solstitial centres); zhong is where heaven and earth begin and end, he is how they generate and complete, and 'no virtue is greater than he'. Ruling and nourishing the body by zhong-he gives great virtue and long life.

s: Critique: in Zhu Xi's school he names the ease with which a person fits a fixed order. Huang Gan explains that ritual is strict because 'heaven is high, earth is low, the myriad things are dispersed and distinct, and their portions are fixed and cannot be moved'. Diversity is there as rank; he is consent to it, which is what the guard clause of ideas/01 warns about.

s: Maitri Upanishad 6.22 teaches two brahmans, sound (sabda, the syllable Om) and non-sound; one rises by sound to the soundless, where the many sounds 'disappear' and become 'indistinguishable, like the various juices which have reached the condition of honey'.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: Verily, there are two Brahmas to be meditated upon: sound and non-sound. Now, non-sound is revealed only by sound.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: There they are unqualified, indistinguishable, like the various juices which have reached the condition of honey.

s: Maitri Upanishad 6.22 reports a practice of closing the ears to hear the inner sound of the space in the heart, compared in seven ways (rivers, a bell, a brazen vessel, a wheel, frogs, rain, speech in a sheltered place) - an early description of the varied 'unstruck' inner sound that later nada-yoga develops.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (trans.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: By closing the ears with the thumbs they hear the sound of the space within the heart. Of it there is this sevenfold comparison: like rivers, a bell, a brazen vessel, a wheel, the croaking of frogs, rain, as when one speaks in a sheltered place.

s: The Upanishadic images of the ultimate whole (honey whose juices cannot tell themselves apart; sounds that vanish into the soundless) value unity reached by the disappearance of the parts' distinctness, which is what ideas/01 calls homogenization; the tradition therefore disagrees with, rather than confirms, 'diversity in wholeness' at its highest level.

s: In the Vinaya story of Soṇa Koḷivīsa, the Buddha asks a former lute player whether his lute sounded when its strings were too tight or too loose, and Soṇa agrees it was playable only when they were neither, set 'in even proportion' (Pali samē guṇē patiṭṭhitā).

s: The Buddha applies the lute to effort: over-exerted energy leads to restlessness and slack energy to sloth, so Soṇa should resolve on 'evenness of energy' (vīriyasamatā) and penetrate 'evenness of the faculties' (indriyānaṃ samatā); Rhys Davids and Oldenberg render the second phrase 'harmony of your mental powers'.
