src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: if one makes yang in the qi of yang, or yin in the qi of yin, there will be no harmony, and there will be no realization.
src.qo: 陽の氣に陽とし、陰の氣に陰とせば、和する所あるまじければ、成就もあるまじ

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: 陽の氣に陽とし、陰の氣に陰とせば、和する所あるまじければ、成就もあるまじ

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: It is said in the secret teachings that all things should be known as the realization of the boundary where yin and yang harmonize.
src.qo: 陽の氣に陽とし、陰の氣に陰とせば、和する所あるまじければ、成就もあるまじ

s: Zeami says that when the audience's hearts have gathered and the actor enters at the right moment and lifts his voice, 'the hearts of the ten thousand' and the actor's movements become one (wagō 和合) and the day's performance succeeds.

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: the hearts of the ten thousand, as well as the actor's behavior, will harmonize and become deeply intimate
src.qo: 萬人の心、してのふるまひ、和合してしみじみとなれば

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: 萬人の心、してのふるまひ、和合してしみじみとなれば

s: Zeami applies jo-ha-kyū (introduction, break, rapid finale), the order already used in sectioning musical pieces, to the order of a whole day's programme: the opening piece is plain and auspicious, technique comes later.

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: One should determine this by the mood of the Noh.
src.qo: 能の風情をもてさだむべし。

src.l: Zeami Motokiyo, n.d., Fūshikaden (花傳書 / Kadensho)
src.q: 能に序破急をば、何とか定むべきや

s: The Kangen ongi (管絃音義), a gagaku treatise in the Gunsho ruijū, matches the modes to the Five Phases and the five organs, and pictures bodily harmony as a state: if the heart-king follows the true law, all subordinates follow and 'the five organs are harmonized' (五臟調和); if not, 'the servants rebel'.

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: If the heart practices the true law, all subordinates follow, and the rule is just and peaceful. Thus the five organs are harmonized, the six galleries are in accord, and the Four Elements are at peace.
src.qo: 故「五臟調和」

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: 故「五臟調和」

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: If the heart practices illegal acts, the servants rebel and harm each other.
src.qo: 故「五臟調和」

s: The Kangen ongi explains the name of the hyōjō ('level mode') by the balance of its high and low tones: both are correct ritsu tones and the two are 'evened' (均平); it cites 'the principle of levelness has no bias'.

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: 而二音均平之上

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: 平理未有偏頗

s: Kaibara Ekiken (c. 1710) writes that the sages modelled music on the harmony of Heaven and Earth, that it 'harmonizes those above and below', and that its root is a heart of harmonious joy (waraku 和樂), with sound and dance only ornament.

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, Ekiken zenshū 益軒全集, vol. 2
src.loc: Gakusetsu 樂說, Ekiken zenshū vol. 2, p. 296 (SL translation)
src.q: Therefore, music takes harmonious joy as its foundation, and sound and appearance as its ornamentation.
src.qo: 和二上下一

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, Ekiken zenshū 益軒全集, vol. 2
src.q: It serves the spirits and harmonizes those above and below
src.qo: 和二上下一

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, Ekiken zenshū 益軒全集, vol. 2
src.q: 和二上下一

s: In his preface to an inscription on a wagon (Japanese zither), Ekiken calls birdsong, insects and leaping fish the 'natural music' of things and says the way of making music lies in balancing likes and dislikes without losing harmony and joy.

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, Ekiken zenshū 益軒全集, vol. 2
src.loc: Preface to the Wagon inscription; p. 297 (SL translation)
src.q: Therefore, the way of creating music lies in balancing likes and dislikes and not losing the heart of harmony and joy.

src.l: Kaibara Ekiken, 1910, Ekiken zenshū 益軒全集, vol. 2
src.q: these are all natural impulses that cannot be suppressed
src.qo: 泛觀二霄壤之間一。鳥囀二于春一。蟲鳴二于秋一。鹿之呦呦。魚之𩼈𩼈。皆是天機之不レ能レ自已者。

s: In the Kangen ongi the harmonized body is a polity in which subordinates obey the heart-king and discord means servants rebelling; harmony is right rule, not parts that flourish. Ekiken's music likewise 'harmonizes those above and below'. Japanese music theory here inherits the Chinese ritual-music frame and cuts against ideas/01's guard clause.

src.l: Hanawa Hokiichi (ed.), 1819, Gunsho ruijū 群書類従, vol. 12 (管絃部: Kangen ongi, Gojū jissōki, Ryūmeishō)
src.q: If the heart practices illegal acts, the servants rebel and harm each other.
src.qo: 若「心」行「非法」。則群僕作「亂」。互則侵害。

s: Ibn Khaldun (in de Slane's French) makes kinship, real or adopted through clientage, the essential element of 'asabiyya (group feeling), and says great houses owe their cohesion and fame to it.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, William MacGuckin de Slane (trans.), 1863, Les Prolégomènes d'Ibn Khaldoun, première partie
src.loc: Muqaddima I, tr. de Slane, p. 285 [scan 409]
src.q: ils savent que la parenté est l'élément essentiel de l'esprit de corps, et que les grandes maisons doivent à cet esprit leur consistance et leur illustration

s: Ibn Khaldun compares a tribe's 'asabiyya to the temperament (mizaj) of a body: a mixture of elements that neutralize each other cannot form a temperament, one element must predominate, and likewise one family must be strong enough to absorb the others into a single body under one chief.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, William MacGuckin de Slane (trans.), 1863, Les Prolégomènes d'Ibn Khaldoun, première partie
src.loc: Muqaddima I, tr. de Slane, p. 341 [scan 465]
src.q: l'esprit de corps dans une tribu est comme le tempérament dans les êtres créés. Le tempérament est un mélange des (quatre) éléments, ainsi que nous l'avons exposé ailleurs. Or un mélange d'éléments qui se neutralisent ne saurait former un tempérament : pour que cet effet se produise, il faut absolument que l'un des éléments prédomine sur les autres.

s: Ibn Khaldun holds that 'asabiyya decays: luxury and its enjoyments extinguish the group feeling that leads to sovereignty, and a tribe that has lost it can no longer defend itself.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, William MacGuckin de Slane (trans.), 1863, Les Prolégomènes d'Ibn Khaldoun, première partie
src.loc: Muqaddima I, tr. de Slane, p. 295 [scan 419] (SL translation)
src.q: Indeed, luxury and its enjoyments completely dampen that group feeling which leads to sovereignty; the tribe that has lost it no longer has the strength to attack its neighbors
src.qo: En effet, le luxe et ses jouissances amortissent complétement cet esprit de corps qui conduit à la souveraineté; la tribu qui l'a perdu n'a plus la force d'attaquer ses voisins;

s: Ibn Khaldun assigns 'measure and propriety' (i'tidal, the temperate mean) to the peoples of the central climates and attaches prophecy, royalty, laws, sciences and arts to them, while treating the far south and north as departing from the mean.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, William MacGuckin de Slane (trans.), 1863, Les Prolégomènes d'Ibn Khaldoun, première partie
src.loc: Muqaddima I, third preliminary discourse, tr. de Slane, p. 173 [scan 297] (SL translation)
src.q: As for the inhabitants of the central climates, one finds in them a character of measure and propriety shown in their physical and moral state
src.qo: Quant aux habitants des climats du centre, on trouve chez eux un caractère de mesure et de convenance qui se montre dans leur physique et leur moral,

s: Ibn Khaldun's account of social wholeness cuts against ideas/01: the strongest social whole is a mixture in which one part dominates and absorbs the rest, the chief must be unique, and cohesion is a resource that the whole's own prosperity uses up. It is wholeness without the guard clause.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, William MacGuckin de Slane (trans.), 1863, Les Prolégomènes d'Ibn Khaldoun, première partie
src.loc: Muqaddima I, tr. de Slane, p. 341 [scan 465]
src.q: une de ces familles doit être assez forte pour tenir ensemble les autres, les absorber, les combiner en un seul

s: Farmer (1929) reports that by the time of Safi al-Din al-Urmawi (d. 1294) a new scale had been adopted, probably his, which proceeded by two limmas and a comma and nominally embraced the Pythagorean, Zalzalian and Persian systems; its theorists are called the 'Systematists'.

src.l: Henry George Farmer, 1929, A History of Arabian Music to the XIIIth Century
src.q: This scale, which proceeded by steps of two limmas and a comma, was clearly founded on the old ṭunbūr al-khurāsānī scale, and nominally, at any rate, embraced the Pythagorean, Zalzalian, and Persian systems.

s: Farmer (1929) reports that later theorists, Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi among them, all deferred to Safi al-Din's authority 'even when they have to disagree with him'.

src.l: Henry George Farmer, 1929, A History of Arabian Music to the XIIIth Century
src.q: all prostrate themselves before the authority of Ṣafī al-Dīn 'Abd al-Mu'min, even when they have to disagree with him.

s: Farmer (1929) names Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi (1236-1310) as Safi al-Din's greatest pupil and calls his Durrat al-taj one of the most authoritative works of 'Systematist' music theory.

src.l: Henry George Farmer, 1929, A History of Arabian Music to the XIIIth Century
src.q: His greatest pupil was Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī (1236-1310), the author of the Durrat al-tāj, one of the most authoritative works on the "Systematist" theory of music.

s: The Masnavi opens with the reed-flute (ney) whose music is a lament of separation from the reed-bed: every one far from his source longs for reunion with it.

src.l: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Reynold A. Nicholson (trans.), 1926, The Mathnawí of Jalálu'ddín Rúmí, Books I-II (translation)
src.loc: Masnavi I, Proem, tr. Nicholson, p. 5 [scan 25]
src.q: Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it.

s: Rumi's reed says each hearer befriended it 'from his own opinion' and none sought its secret: listeners hear the music according to their own state.

src.l: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Reynold A. Nicholson (trans.), 1926, The Mathnawí of Jalálu'ddín Rúmí, Books I-II (translation)
src.loc: Masnavi I, Proem, tr. Nicholson, p. 5 [scan 25]
src.q: Every one became my friend from his own opinion; none sought out my secrets from within me.

s: In Rumi's elephant in the dark house, each person's description differs because each touched one part; with a candle in each hand 'the difference would have gone out of their words'. Difference is a product of partial view.

src.l: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Reynold A. Nicholson (trans.), 1930, The Mathnawí of Jalálu'ddín Rúmí, Books III-IV (translation)
src.q:
On account of the (diverse) place (object) of view, their statements differed: one man entitled it "dál," another "alif."
If there had been a candle in each one's hand, the difference would have gone out of their words.

s: In Moses and the Shepherd, God rebukes Moses for silencing a shepherd's uncouth prayer: God looks at the inward state, not the words, and 'the religion of Love is apart from all religions'.

src.l: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Reynold A. Nicholson (trans.), 1926, The Mathnawí of Jalálu'ddín Rúmí, Books I-II (translation)
src.q: I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward (spirit) and the state (of feeling).

s: Rumi's poetry is often cited for harmony-as-diversity, but in the Masnavi plurality is mostly a veil: fixing the gaze on the Light 'delivers' one from dualism and number, and the reed's music is a longing for union with the source. The target state is union, which ideas/01 calls homogenization when it is the whole story.

src.l: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Reynold A. Nicholson (trans.), 1930, The Mathnawí of Jalálu'ddín Rúmí, Books III-IV (translation)
src.q: But if thou keep thy gaze (fixed) upon the Light, thou wilt be delivered from dualism and the numbers (plurality) of the finite body.

s: Al-Ghazali (Ihya, Book of Knowledge) states the principle of his later Book of Listening (sama'): the listener applies everything he hears to whatever dominates his heart, so poetry about created things does not harm an elite gathering absorbed in the love of God.

src.l: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, 1982, Ihya' 'ulum al-din, vol. 1

s: In the Kimiya-yi sa'adat (Homes's 1873 English, from a Turkish version), each faculty's happiness lies in its proper object: 'The enjoyment of the ear is secured in listening to harmonious voices', and the heart's in knowing things as they are.

src.l: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, Henry A. Homes (trans.), 1873, The Alchemy of Happiness
src.loc: Alchemy of Happiness, tr. Homes, p. 34 [scan 46]
src.q: The enjoyment of the ear is secured in listening to harmonious voices.

s: Sefer Yesira (Westcott's English) builds the world from three 'mother' letters that form a balance: one pan guilt, one merit, and Aleph (air) as the tongue of the balance standing between them.

src.l: Anonymous (attr. Abraham / R. Akiba), W. Wynn Westcott (trans.), 1893?, Sepher Yetzirah, the Book of Formation
src.loc: Sefer Yesira III.1, tr. Westcott, p. 19 [scan 19]
src.q: they resemble a Balance, on the one hand the guilty, on the other hand the purified, and Aleph the Air is like the Tongue of a Balance standing between them.

s: The Hebrew of Sefer Yesira III.1 in the Mantua 1562 printing reads 'kaf zekhut ve-kaf hovah ve-lashon hoq makhria' beinatayim': a pan of merit, a pan of guilt, and the tongue of decree deciding between them.

src.l: Anonymous (attr. Abraham), 1562, Sefer Yesira with commentaries
src.q: שלש אמות אמ"ש יסודן כף זכות וכף חובה ולשון חק מכריע בינתים

s: Sefer Yesira applies the same three-term pattern at three levels, the World, the Year and Man: fire and water are opposed and air (the temperate season, the chest) is 'placed as a mediator between the others'.

src.l: Anonymous (attr. Abraham / R. Akiba), W. Wynn Westcott (trans.), 1893?, Sepher Yetzirah, the Book of Formation
src.loc: Sefer Yesira III.3-4, tr. Westcott, p. 19 [scan 19]
src.q: from the air was formed the chest, again placed as a mediator between the others.

s: Sefer Yesira (ch. VI in most editions; 'chapter 5, mishnah 2' in the Mantua running head) says God made every thing one opposite the other, good opposite evil, and that each distinguishes the other.

src.l: Anonymous (attr. Abraham), 1562, Sefer Yesira with commentaries
src.q: God also made every thing, one opposite the other;
src.qo: גם את כל חפץ זה לעומת זה

s: Philo reads the high priest's robe as a model of the world; the bells on its hem are 'the emblem of the concord and harmony' of earth and water, because neither can produce anything without the other.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, C. D. Yonge (trans.), 1854, The Works of Philo Judaeus, vol. 3
src.loc: De vita Mosis II.119-20, tr. Yonge, p. 98 [scan 108]
src.q: the bells are the emblem of the concord and harmony that exist between these things; for neither is the earth without the water, nor the water without the earthly substance, sufficient for the production of anything

s: Philo reads the four-letter divine name as the tetrad, which contains point, line, surface and solid and 'the most excellent symphonies of music': the fourth (4:3), fifth (3:2), octave (2:1) and double octave (4:1).

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, C. D. Yonge (trans.), 1854, The Works of Philo Judaeus, vol. 3
src.loc: De vita Mosis II.115, tr. Yonge, p. 97 [scan 107]
src.q: since all things are comprised in the number four, namely, a point, and a line, and a superficies, and a solid, and the measures of all things, and the most excellent symphonies of music

s: Philo says nearly everything in the world is set opposite something else, that 'one thing consists of the two opposite parts', and claims that Heraclitus's leading principle was an ancient discovery of Moses.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, C. D. Yonge (trans.), 1854, The Works of Philo Judaeus, vol. 2
src.loc: Quis rerum divinarum heres 207-14, tr. Yonge, p. 135 [scan 147]
src.q: it is in reality an ancient discovery of Moses, that out of the same thing opposite things are produced having the ratio of parts to the whole

s: Philo's divine Word stands 'in the midst between' Creator and creature 'like a hostage' to both, so that creation will not choose 'disorder rather than order', and announces peace from God 'who has determined to destroy wars'.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, C. D. Yonge (trans.), 1854, The Works of Philo Judaeus, vol. 2
src.loc: Quis rerum divinarum heres 205-6, tr. Yonge, p. 134 [scan 146]
src.q: being in the midst between these two extremities, like a hostage, as it were, to both parties

s: Matthews glosses the Navajo closing formula biké hozóni as 'his trail of beauty, his happy trail', and says that joined with sána nagaí it means a happy old age; he admits rendering the words by different English equivalents in different places.

src.l: Washington Matthews, 1902, The Night Chant, a Navaho Ceremony
src.q: Biké hozóni signifies, his trail of terrestrial beauty, his happy trail, feet or footprints. But, liberally translated, the two expressions joined mean a happy old age

src.l: Washington Matthews, 1902, The Night Chant, a Navaho Ceremony
src.q: In different connections, it has been found advisable to translate these words with different English equivalents.

s: The Night Chant prayers place beauty on every side of the walker (before, behind, below, above, all around) and end with the refrain 'It is finished in beauty'.

src.l: Washington Matthews, 1902, The Night Chant, a Navaho Ceremony
src.q: With beauty all around me, I walk.

s: In the interlinear prayer of the Night Chant, 'in beauty' (hozógo) is asked for the speaker's female kindred, young men, young women, chiefs, 'us', the corn, and every direction around, before it is asked for goods and old age: the wish extends from the self to the whole kin group.

src.l: Washington Matthews, 1902, The Night Chant, a Navaho Ceremony
src.q: Hozógo <gloss>In beauty</gloss> sezáni <gloss>my female kindred</gloss> kehatíndo. <gloss>may (they) dwell.</gloss>

s: Matthews reports that in the Night Chant's most important song, if a single syllable is omitted or misplaced the ceremony ends at once and nine days of work are void.

src.l: Washington Matthews, 1902, The Night Chant, a Navaho Ceremony
src.q: It is said that, if a single syllable is omitted or misplaced, the ceremony terminates at once; all the preceding work of nine days is considered valueless

s: Brinton, drawing on Mendieta, describes Nahua festival song in which other singers joined until the whole chorus sang, and bystanders by the thousands joined the words, keeping time with concerted movements.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: the other singers united their voices until the whole chorus was in action, and often the bystanders, to the numbers of thousands, would ultimately join in the words of some familiar song, keeping time by concerted movements of the hands and feet.

s: Brinton reports Theodor Baker's judgement that the two-note teponaztli slit drum 'could not have been played in accord with the huehuetl', and reports European travellers finding the chanting harsh: Nahua music is judged here against European accord.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: The teponaztli, he states, could yield but two notes, and could not have been played in accord with the huehuetl. It served as an imperfect contra-bass.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: harsh, strident and disagreeable to the European ear

s: Brinton quotes Sahagún's description of the worthy Nahua singer as one who composes, learns others' songs and is always ready to share them with fellow singers, while the unworthy singer will not communicate what he learns and is envious.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: He composes songs himself and learns those of others, and is always ready to impart either to the fellows of his craft.

s: In the song attributed to Nezahualcoyotl, as given by Brinton from a Spanish version, the singer says that today there is peace and good fellowship so all should join hands in the dance, because worldly life does not begin anew.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: To-day there are peace, and goodfellowship; therefore let all join hands and rejoice in the dances,

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: In the life of this world there is no beginning anew, therefore rejoice, for all good ends.

s: Brinton quotes the Nahuatl opening line 'Xochitl mamani in huehuetitlan' from Torquemada, rendered 'There are fresh and fragrant flowers among the groves', and argues the place word means 'among the cypresses'.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: Xochitl mamani in huehuetitlan

s: In the Popol Vuh the world is made after the Heart of Sky, Tepeu and Gucumatz speak, deliberate and worry together, find each other, and join their words and their thought: creation follows an agreement reached by distinct gods.

src.l: Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed., tr.), K'iche' Maya authors, 1861, Popol Vuh. Le livre sacré et les mythes de l'antiquité américaine
src.q: X-e cha cut, ta x-e naohinic, ta x-e bizonic : x-e riqo quib; x-qui cuch qui tzih, qui naoh.

src.l: Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed., tr.), K'iche' Maya authors, 1861, Popol Vuh. Le livre sacré et les mythes de l'antiquité américaine
src.q: Et ils parlèrent : alors ils se consultèrent et méditèrent : ils se comprirent; ils joignirent leurs paroles et leurs avis.

s: The Popol Vuh's failed mud-man is described (in Brasseur's French) as without cohesion, consistency, movement or force, and is destroyed; the gods' stated aim for humans is beings who will honour and feed them.

src.l: Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed., tr.), K'iche' Maya authors, 1861, Popol Vuh. Le livre sacré et les mythes de l'antiquité américaine
src.q: il était sans cohésion, sans consistance, sans mouvements, sans force, inepte et aqueux

src.l: Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg (ed., tr.), K'iche' Maya authors, 1861, Popol Vuh. Le livre sacré et les mythes de l'antiquité américaine
src.q: essayons de faire des (hommes) obéissants et respectueux qui (soient nos) soutiens et nourriciers.

s: Junod reports that Thonga choruses sing in two or three parts with a system of harmony different from the European one, with successions of fourths and sixths, and that timbila players always play with two hands.

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: The rules of Native harmony are very difficult to detect. They certainly exist . When you hear a chorus of beautiful voices singing in two or three parts, you at once perceive great differences between their system of harmony and ours .

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: One will notice a curious succession of fourths and sixths, quite unusual in our music .

s: Junod notes Thonga songs in which boys answer men and girls answer women 'in the usual antiphonic way', with singers stamping to mark time.

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: In 5 and 6 boys answered to men and girls to women in the usual antiphonic way.

s: The held colonial ethnographies judge non-European music by a European yardstick: Junod assumes the seven-note scale is 'given' to the human ear, expects European instruments to 'raise' Thonga singers, and praises thirty timbila playing the Portuguese anthem in perfect tune; Brinton reports Baker's verdict that Nahua drums could not play 'in accord'. Their reports of 'harmony' therefore cannot be read as native testimony that a tradition shares our concept.

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: The use of European instruments will raise them to that higher level in the course of time.

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: thirty timbila played the National Portuguese Anthem

src.l: Henri A. Junod, 1912, The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2: The Psychic Life
src.q: Their eye has not yet been fully trained.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1887, Ancient Nahuatl Poetry (Library of Aboriginal American Literature, no. 7)
src.q: could not have been played in accord with the huehuetl

s: In Grey's Maori creation account the children of Heaven (Rangi) and Earth (Papa), living in darkness between their clasped parents, debate whether to kill or separate them; Tane-mahuta's proposal to rend them apart wins, so the world begins with a separation, not a union.

src.l: Sir George Grey, 1855, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race
src.loc: 'The Children of Heaven and Earth'; p. 2 [scan 24]

s: Across the held Navajo, Nahua, K'iche', Thonga, Maori and Hawaiian sources read here, no native word is translated 'harmony' by the colonial-era editors; the nearest terms mean beauty and happy long life (hozóni), rightness or wellbeing (pono), or joining words (cuch ... tzih). Where these traditions match 'diversity in wholeness' it is in practice (part-singing, antiphony, divided performing roles, gods who deliberate) rather than in a concept, and 'found in all cultures' cannot be supported from them as a claim about a shared idea.

s: In Periphyseon I Eriugena says that God, who is the opposition of opposites and the contrariety of contraries, gathers all things into one concord by a marvellous harmony: what in the parts of the universe seems opposed, contrary and mutually dissonant is, in the most general harmony of the universe, fitting and consonant.

src.l: John Scottus Eriugena, Thomas Gale (ed.), 1681, De divisione naturae libri quinque (Periphyseon)
src.q: For those things which in the parts of the universe seem opposed and contrary to one another, and dissonant from each other, are, in the most general harmony of the universe itself, considered fitting and consonant.
src.qo: Nam quæ in partibus universitatis opposita sibimet videntur atque contraria, & à se invicem dissona; in generalissima ipsius universitatis harmonia, & considerantur convenientia, consonáque sunt.

src.l: John Scottus Eriugena, Thomas Gale (ed.), 1681, De divisione naturae libri quinque (Periphyseon)

s: In Periphyseon III Eriugena compares the universe to organ music: as an organ melody is made from voices of different qualities and quantities that sound far apart when heard singly but yield sweetness when fitted by the rules of music, so the beauty of the created universe is a wondrous harmony of like and unlike things, compacted into an ineffable unity, in which things dissonant singly are made one.

src.l: John Scottus Eriugena, Thomas Gale (ed.), 1681, De divisione naturae libri quinque (Periphyseon)
src.q: Thus, the beauty of the whole created universe, of similar and dissimilar things, is established by a certain wondrous harmony, compacted into a certain ineffable unity from diverse genera and various forms
src.qo: Ut enim organicum melos ex diversis vocum qualitatibus & quantitatibus conficitur

src.l: John Scottus Eriugena, Thomas Gale (ed.), 1681, De divisione naturae libri quinque (Periphyseon)
src.q: so in the concord of the universe, things that are dissonant when viewed singularly are unified according to the uniform will of the Creator from the diverse subdivisions of the one nature

s: Eriugena argues (Periphyseon III.6) that the Creator made not only things like himself (eternal, simple, immutable) but also unlike and opposite things (temporal, composite, mutable); had he made only the like, he would have fallen short in making the unlike and opposite.

src.qo: VI. Non enim universitatis conditor omnipotens, & in nullo deficiens, & in infinito tendens, similia sibi solummodo, verum etiam dissimilia creare potuit & creavit.

s: In Periphyseon V Eriugena holds that the harmony of the whole creation is composed of what exists and what does not, and is not troubled to hear that 'a most beautiful harmony' will come from the punishments of evil wills and the rewards of good ones, since punishments are good insofar as they are just; he is convinced by seeing low, high and middle sounds make a symphony through their proportions.

s: Answering how punishment and reward can coexist in one restored universe, Eriugena points to a great royal house that holds at once the healthy and the weak, the rich and the needy, a slave being whipped and a master being honoured, a prisoner and an acquitted man, and asks why the whole rational creation should not be gathered in 'one harmony of the universe'; earlier he answers complaints that God makes some masters and others servants by saying temporal goods are not true goods.

In the Ordo Virtutum the Virtues welcome the penitent Soul back and say that therefore 'it befits us to sound in harmony' (in symphonia sonare).

s: In De docta ignorantia II.1 Cusanus argues that precise equality belongs to God alone, so no two voices, pipes or bells can be in exact harmonic proportion; 'the sweetest harmony' cannot be found in sensible things without defect, and the most precise harmony, 'proportion in equality', cannot be heard by a living person.

s: In the Heptaplus Pico holds that the angelic, celestial and elemental worlds are one world, 'tempered by appropriate numbers and gathered by a certain harmonic kinship of nature', because whatever is in all of them is in each. Because 'there is no multitude that is not one', they are bound by a 'discordant concord', and yet each nature keeps its own seat and laws.

s: Paracelsus's microcosm: man is 'constellated' within himself as the heaven is, with his own firmament of bodily planets and stars; and as the heavenly firmament is governed by no creature, so the firmament in man is 'a powerful, free firmament, without any binding'.

s: In De vinculis the same bond binds by contraries (Cupid's one fire drives to joy and sadness, hope and despair), and no single bond binds diverse things, because 'the universe is composed of contraries': goods differ by kind and place, under the waves for some and on dry land for others; what is absolutely good 'flourishes through a diverse kind of bonds'.

s: Maier explains his fifty fugues allegorically: as Atalanta flees, one voice always flees before another and a second follows like Hippomenes, while a third, simple voice 'of a single value' (the golden apple) stabilises them; many fugues are fitted to one simple melody, and the scheme stands for volatile Mercury fixed by sulphur.

src.l: Michael Maier, 1617, Atalanta fugiens, hoc est, emblemata nova de secretis naturae chymica
src.q: As this Atalanta flees, so one musical voice always flees before another, and the other follows, like Hippomenes. Yet in the third, they are stabilized and confirmed, which is simple and of a single value, like a golden apple.
src.qo: Hac Atalanta ut fugit, sic una vox Musicalis semper fugit ante aliam & altera insequitur, ut Hippomenes: In tertia tamen stabiliuntur & firmantur, quae simplex est & unius valoris, tanquam malo aureo

s: In the coniunctio of Sun and Moon (Emblem XXX) each partner gives what the other lacks - the Moon receives splendour and strength, the Sun multiplication - but the marriage is unequal (the Moon is 'exalted' to the Sun) and the work ends when the mixed subjects, 'having passed through various colors', reach 'one color and essence'.

src.l: Michael Maier, 1617, Atalanta fugiens, hoc est, emblemata nova de secretis naturae chymica
src.q: The Sun without the Moon is not of great estimation, and the Moon without the Sun is of abject condition and base origin. But she receives splendor, dignity, and strength—or firmness of mind and body—from the Sun, her spouse, and the Sun receives from the Moon multiplication and the propagation of the species.

s: Comenius makes harmony the foundation of all things and takes musical harmony as the model: it is made 'of voices that are very different, and even contrary', whose contrariety is brought back into consonance; the world likewise 'consists of contraries', without which neither truth nor order could exist - yet the aim of Panharmony is that 'any apparent dissonance vanishes'.

src.l: Jan Amos Comenius, 1644, Pansophiae prodromus (A Forerunner of Universal Wisdom)
src.q: the entire world consists of contraries—for without contraries, neither truth, nor order, nor indeed the very essence of the world could exist.

src.l: Jan Amos Comenius, 1644, Pansophiae prodromus (A Forerunner of Universal Wisdom)
src.q: This Panharmony should win universal agreement for our works, our opinions, and our words—just as it does for divine works—so that any apparent dissonance vanishes.

s: Comenius wants men freed from 'dissensions, so that sects and hatreds may cease', and argues this needs every party satisfied: the opinions of all must be heard, compared calmly, and measured by the laws of truth each side has set for itself.

s: Book III sets out 'common canons of all persuasions': belief in a God who is author of all things, that everyone keep the accepted rites for public peace, and similar rules. Postel limits the list to what all religions share 'in general terms', because whatever belongs to one religion alone makes all of them, 'even the most excellent', mutually ridiculous.

s: On the same page Postel holds both that 'a province is far more happily consistent when it obeys a single persuasion' before different rites and assemblies multiply, and that because every province and sacred place has its own 'tutelary gods' (patron saints), it is right that they be worshipped 'by their own accepted rite'. Local variety of rite is allowed inside one law; variety of persuasion is not wanted.

s: Postel's missionary method in Book IV lets converts keep their rites only for a time. Muslims who will not give up their worship at once 'should be tolerated rather than abolished, until' preaching brings them to 'the sincerity of doctrine and worship'. Christian images of the saints may be removed 'for a time' so as not to offend them. For newly converted Indians, the old ceremonies are 'to be gradually driven out, unless it contains sin', though worship once given to an idol may be ascribed to Christ.

s: In De nativitate Mediatoris (1547) Postel places everyone who lived by conscience 'under whatever absurdity of religion' in the law of nature. Christ does not impute their false persuasion, 'provided that what is worshipped is done for Him … and provided that one stands with one's neighbor'. 'In every nation he who does good is acceptable to him, whether or not the eminence of sacred things be present in the cult.' The end is still that all be 'reintegrated in one under the one God'.

s: In De nativitate Mediatoris Postel uses the body to model how all people will be one in Christ. If each body spread out by itself, we would each be a head and the universe would be 'dissension' (dissidium). In the body, 'one life of the whole becomes a thousand lives of the parts', each member keeps its place, and 'the diminution of one part diminishes the whole'.

s: In the Panthenosia (1551) Postel tells the warring Christian confessions to stop cursing one another: 'Allow among you that each one live according to his own rite, until Christ unites all'. He proposes that all drop 'Papist' and 'Lutheran' and take one common name, 'Jesuan', which Jews and Muslims would share 'in wish and name' and all human nature 'in wish'.

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: Allow among you that each one live according to his own rite, until Christ unites all, with those dissensions removed which are accustomed to dwell in the sacred rite.
src.qo: Permittite inter uos, ut unusquisque pro suo ritu uiuat, donec omnes uniat Christus

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: Permittite inter uos, ut unusquisque pro suo ritu uiuat, donec omnes uniat Christus

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: Let there be no more Papist, no Lutheran, let us all take our name from the desired salvation from JESUS.
src.qo: Permittite inter uos, ut unusquisque pro suo ritu uiuat, donec omnes uniat Christus

s: Answering the charge that he now tries to 'unite again' what his Concordia books had tried to 'dissipate' (by granting some perfection to the Qur'an), Postel says he wrote those books before he knew Christ's indwelling spirit. He calls the reversal the order of nature: nothing is born from a seed 'unless it is first entirely dissipated through putrefaction or art, before it is reduced to a generative union'.

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: although we wrote books on the concord of the world before we truly knew the indwelling spirit of Christ in us by a living faith

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: nothing can be born from any seed at all, unless it is first entirely dissipated through putrefaction or art, before it is reduced to a generative union
src.qo: nisi prius omnino dissipetur per putrefactionem, aut artem, quàm ad unionem ge- nerabilem reducatur.

src.l: Guillaume Postel, 1551, Panthenosia, compositio omnium dissidiorum circa aeternam veritatem aut verisimilitudinem versantium (SL title 'Panthenosia: The Composition of All Dissensions')
src.q: I therefore follow the order of nature, uniting what I have dissipated, so that they may generate fruit from themselves.
src.qo: Sequor itaq; naturæ ordinē, uniendo quæ dissipaui, ut fructum ex se generent.

s: Tartini reports that two loud sustained sounds (two violins, two oboes) produce an audible 'third sound', heard best by a listener midway between two players five or six paces apart; he explains it as the collision of the two volumes of air, and says the unison and the octave give no third sound.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: a third sound is produced by the collision of the two volumes of air moved by the two given sounds
src.qo: Dati due ſuoni di qualunque ſtrumento muſicale, che poſſa protrarre, e rinforzare il ſuono per quanto tempo ſi voglia ( trombe, corni di caccia, ſtrumenti d' arco, oboè ec. ) ſi ha un terzo ſuono prodotto dall' urto de' due volumi di aria moſſi dalli due dati ſuoni.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: A listener placed exactly in the middle between the two players will hear this third sound much more clearly than if they were standing close to either individual player.
src.qo: Dato l' unisono, e data la ragion dupla, o sia praticamente ottava, non risulta terzo suono di sorte alcuna.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: Dato l' unisono, e data la ragion dupla, o sia praticamente ottava, non risulta terzo suono di sorte alcuna.

s: For Tartini the physical marks of harmony (one string sounding three harmonics, organ pipes of different pitch forming one sound, pendulum strings whose oscillations coincide) show that the harmonic system 'reduces the diverse to the same, multiplicity to unity', and that unity is inseparable from it.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: Therefore, the harmonic system reduces the diverse to the same; multiplicity to unity
src.qo: Dunque il ſiſtema armonico riduce il diverſo allo ſteſſo; la moltiplicità alla unità

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: Dunque il ſiſtema armonico riduce il diverſo allo ſteſſo; la moltiplicità alla unità

s: Tartini denies that dissonance is 'unpleasant to the ear': a well-disposed chord of the ninth, eleventh, thirteenth or fourteenth 'in its own way is a unity, and it is within the circle', pleasant in itself, and it shows its diversity only when compared with the harmony of the minor or major third.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: It is physically impossible, because in its own way it is a unity, and it is within the circle. It possesses its own pleasantness by itself
src.qo: nel suo modo è unità, ed è nel circolo. Ha benissimo il suo gradevole per se

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: nel suo modo è unità, ed è nel circolo. Ha benissimo il suo gradevole per se

s: Tartini distinguishes two unities: the principle of harmonic nature (the major-third system) is unity as the whole, the principle of arithmetic nature (the minor-third system) is unity as the least part, and the geometric nature of the dissonances, compounded of both, has its principle in duality.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: The principle of the harmonic nature is unity as the whole; the principle of the arithmetic nature is unity as the minimal part.
src.qo: Principio della natura armonica è la unità, come il tutto; della natura aritmetica la unità, come la minima parte.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: Principio della natura armonica è la unità, come il tutto; della natura aritmetica la unità, come la minima parte.

s: Tartini praises Vallotti's unequal temperament, which keeps the commonly used keys pure and puts the imperfection on rarely used ones, because the contrast of more and less perfect chords across modulations gives a 'chiaro oscuro' that an equal temperament would remove; he also calls the search for one temperament on which discordant nations could agree 'desperate'.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: If the temperament were equal, or a little more or a little less, there would certainly not be this chiaro oscuro
src.qo: Se il temperamento fosse eguale, o poco più poco meno, non vi farebbe certamente questo chiaro oscuro, quale in pratica produce ottimo effetto.

src.l: Giuseppe Tartini, 1754, Trattato di musica secondo la vera scienza dell'armonia
src.q: finding that reasonable temperament in which the nations (discordant among themselves in this) might agree and harmonize

s: In the 1787 Entdeckungen Chladni gives the method in his own words: hold the plate with two fingers at a point that is to stay at rest, scatter sand on it, and bow the edge; the sand gathers on the 'fixed lines' (nodal lines), and he labels each sound by the number of nodal circles over the number of nodal diameters.

src.l: Chladni, E. F. F., 1787, Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges
src.q: After scattering some sand on the surface, one strokes with the
src.qo: streicht. Mehrentheils wird es auch um diese und mehrere solche Klänge zu erhalten, hinlänglich seyn, die Scheibe nur an einer Stelle, nahe am Rande mit zween Fingern zu halten, und an verschiedenen Stellen mit dem Violinbogen zu streichen, da sich denn die mancherley radförmigen Figuren leicht durch verschiedene Töne verrathen, und bey Aufstreuung des Sandes sichtbar seyn werden. Bey den nunmehr zu erwähnenden Arten des Klanges, wo sich mehr als ein Kreis zeiget, ist dieses merkwürdig, daß die Kreise bey jedem Klange eine bestimmte Anzahl von Biegungen haben, ausgenommen der innerste Kreis, welcher bisweilen ganz zirkelförmig, mehrentheils aber oval ist. Die Anzahl der Biegungen ist bey jedem Kreise die nämliche, ihre Lage ist allerzeit so beschaffen, daß die Bogen zweener benachbarten Kreise sich gegenseitig einander abwechselnd nähern und von einander entfernen, und mithin der erste Kreis mit dem dritten, der zweyte mit dem vierten u. s. w. parallel geht, doch mit dem Unterschiede, daß die Bogen der Kreise immer flacher werden, je näher die Kreise der Mitte der Scheibe sind. Um jede Art des Klanges, bey welcher zween und mehrere Kreise sich entweder allein, oder auch von Linien durchschnitten zeigen, einzeln zum Vorschein zu bringen, wird nichts weiter erfordert, als daß man mit dem Daumen an einer Stelle, und mit einem andern Finger derselben Hand an einer andern Stelle des Randes, wo Hervorragungen des äußern Kreises, oder allenfalls wo Enden von Linien sind, die Scheibe berühre, und sie vermittelst dieser beyden Finger an einer gegenüber befindlichen Stelle, wo eine auswärtsgehende Biegung des äußern Kreises oder allenfalls ein Ende einer Linie ist, an irgend einen nicht allzuharten Gegenstand anstemme, und, nachdem man etwas Sand auf die Oberfläche gestreuet hat,

src.l: Chladni, E. F. F., 1787, Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges
src.q: so that the number of circles is placed above the line, and the number of lines is placed below it.
src.qo: so daß die Anzahl der Kreise über den Strich, und die Anzahl der Linien unter denselben gesetzt wird,

s: Chladni argues that because plates, rods and bells have higher tones mostly in 'unharmonic and irrational ratios', no one who knew this would have taken the string's co-sounding harmonic series as essential to every musical sound, still less derived all the principles of harmony from it; what makes a sound musical is only that its vibrations are simultaneous (regular).

src.l: Chladni, E. F. F., 1787, Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges
src.q: for the most part in unharmonic and irrational ratios
src.qo: und größtentheils in unharmonischen und irrationalen Verhältnissen stehen,

src.l: Chladni, E. F. F., 1787, Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges
src.q: or even of deriving all principles of harmony from it
src.qo: oder wohl gar alle Grundsätze der Harmonie daraus herzuleiten.

s: In Die Akustik Chladni holds that we feel ourselves moved by proportions which nature 'calculates for us', that the simplest (consonant) ratios please in themselves but used alone 'would weary us with their uniformity', and that dissonant ratios please when they relate to something simpler and pass into it.

src.l: Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, 1802, Die Akustik
src.q: we do not calculate this ourselves (in the sense that we worry about the numbers by which the time or space ratios can be expressed), but nature calculates for us in a sense
src.qo: wir rechnen dabey nicht selbst (nähmlich so, daß wir uns etwa um die Zahlen, durch welche sich die Zeit- oder Raumverhältnisse ausdrücken lassen, bekümmerten), sondern die Natur rechnet gewissermaßen für uns,

src.l: Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, 1802, Die Akustik
src.q: uniformity; thus, one also finds pleasure in less simple, or dissonant ratios, if they have a relationship to something simpler
src.qo: Einförmigkeit ermüden, man findet also auch an weniger einfachen, oder an dissonirenden Verhältnissen Gefallen,

s: Chladni says the consonances of the numbers 1–6 please the ear as a general fact, but pleasure in less simple ratios and in polyphony where 'each voice has its own path' depends on a receptivity given by nature or acquired by study: a connoisseur is enchanted by a fugued chorus whose voices agree into a harmonious whole, while others find it pointless or unpleasant.

src.l: Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, 1802, Die Akustik
src.q: for many others who are not capable of grasping the path of the various voices and their agreement into a harmonious whole, will have either no effect at all or, rather, an unpleasant one

s: Chladni judges that the degrees of pleasantness Euler assigned to intervals in the Tentamen 'are mostly not confirmed by experience', and endorses instead Descartes' rule that what pleases is perceived neither too easily nor with too much difficulty.

src.l: Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, 1802, Die Akustik
src.q: The degrees of pleasantness of tone ratios indicated by L. Euler in his tentam. nov. theor. Mus.

src.l: Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, 1802, Die Akustik
src.q: that is most pleasing to the mind which is perceived neither with too much ease, nor with too much difficulty
src.qo: inter objecta sensus illud non animo gratissimum est, quod facile sensu percipitur, neque etiam, quod difficillime, sed quod non tam facile, ut naturale desiderium, quo sensus feruntur in objecta, plane non impleat, neque etiam tam difficulter, ut sensus fatiget.

s: Young explains the colours of thin plates and diffraction fringes by the interference of two portions of light from the same origin arriving by different paths, 'in a manner nearly similar' to the beat heard when two strings in imperfect unison sound together: two equal series of waves destroy each other at some points and redouble at others.

src.l: Thomas Young, 1807, A Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy and the Mechanical Arts, Vol. 1
src.q: in a manner nearly similar to that which constitutes in sound the sensation of a beat, when two strings, forming an imperfect unison, are heard to vibrate together

src.l: Thomas Young, 1807, A Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy and the Mechanical Arts, Vol. 1
src.q: We are now to apply the same principles to the alternate union and extinction of colours.

s: Young holds that the constitution of mind that fits it to perceive harmony also causes the love of rhythm and even attachment to familiar persons, places and habits; rhythm is sometimes interrupted only for contrast, 'nearly in the same manner' as discords are mixed with concords 'to obtain an agreeable variety of expression'.

src.l: Thomas Young, 1807, A Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy and the Mechanical Arts, Vol. 1
src.q: The same constitution of the human mind, which fits it for the perception of harmony, appears also to be the cause of the love of rhythm

src.l: Thomas Young, 1807, A Course of Lectures on Natural Philosophy and the Mechanical Arts, Vol. 1
src.q: discords are occasionally mixed with concords, in order to obtain an agreeable variety of expression

s: Fourier writes that Daniel Bernoulli's solution of the vibrating string assumes that any function can be developed in a series of sines or cosines of multiple arcs, and that the most complete proof is actually to resolve a given function into such a series by determining its coefficients, as definite integrals that have values whatever the form of the curve.

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: The solution given by this geometer assumes that any function can always be developed into series of sines or cosines of multiple arcs.
src.qo: La solution donnée par ce géomètre suppose qu'une fonction quelconque peut toujours être développée en séries de sinus ou de cosinus d'arcs multiples.

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: Whatever the function φx may be, or the form of the curve representing it, the integral has a determined value
src.qo: Quelle que puisse être la fonction φx, ou la forme de la courbe qui la représente, l'intégrale a une valeur déterminée

s: In the Discours préliminaire Fourier says mathematical analysis 'brings together the most diverse phenomena, and discovers the secret analogies that unite them', and that the order established in heat phenomena, if our senses could grasp it, would make 'an impression comparable to those of harmonic resonances'.

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: Elle rapproche les phénomènes les plus divers, et découvre les analogies secrètes qui les unissent.

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: ils nous causeraient une impression comparable à celles des résonances harmoniques

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: as if to attest to the unity and simplicity of the plan of the universe
src.qo: ils nous causeraient une impression comparable à celles des résonances harmoniques

s: Fourier says that however infinitely varied the bodies and however arbitrary the first distribution of heat, 'all the inequalities erase themselves rapidly', and the process ends under one law, the same in all cases, which 'no longer bears any perceptible imprint of the initial arrangement'.

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: mais toutes les inégalités s'effacent rapidement et disparaissent à mesure que le temps s'écoule

src.l: Joseph Fourier, 1822, Théorie analytique de la chaleur
src.q: which no longer bears any perceptible imprint of the initial arrangement

s: Rayleigh states Ohm's law of acoustics as found by experiment: whenever theory says a simple (pendular) vibration is present the corresponding tone can be heard, and when it is absent it cannot, so 'simple tones and vibrations of a circular type are indissolubly connected'.

src.l: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), 1894, The Theory of Sound, Vol. I (2nd ed.)
src.q: We are therefore justified in asserting that simple tones and vibrations of a circular type are indissolubly connected. This law was discovered by Ohm.

s: Rayleigh says Ohm's law 'stated in this extreme form' must have exceptions: components of nearly the same frequency are not heard separately but beat, with their relative phase mattering, and a weak component may go unheard in the presence of others.

src.l: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), 1896, The Theory of Sound, Vol. II (2nd ed.)
src.q: It is impossible to suppose that the ear would hear as separate tones simple components of extremely nearly the same frequency.

src.l: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), 1896, The Theory of Sound, Vol. II (2nd ed.)
src.q: It will be advisable to consider these necessary exceptions to the universality of Ohm's law a little more in detail.

s: Rayleigh, after quoting Helmholtz's view that the beats of mistuned consonances between pure tones are due to combination tones, calls consonance among pure tones 'the more difficult subject', on which there are considerable differences of opinion not only about theory but 'as to matters of observation'.

src.l: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), 1896, The Theory of Sound, Vol. II (2nd ed.)
src.q: We have now to consider the more difficult subject of consonance among pure tones; and we shall have to encounter considerable differences of opinion, not only as to theoretical explanations, but as to matters of observation.

s: Goethe holds that the eye, faced with one colour, spontaneously demands its opposite on the colour circle (yellow demands red-blue, purple demands green), because 'the need for totality, which is innate to our organ' frees it from the one-sided colour and 'produces a satisfying wholeness'; these diametric pairs are the 'actually harmonic opposites'.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: then the need for totality, which is innate to our organ, leads us out of this limitation; it sets itself in freedom by producing the opposite of the individual forced upon it, and thus produces a satisfying wholeness.
src.qo: das Bedürfniß nach Totalität, welches unserm Organ eingeboren ist

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: das Bedürfniß nach Totalität, welches unserm Organ eingeboren ist

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: So einfach also diese eigentlich harmonischen Gegensätze sind

s: Goethe calls combinations of neighbouring colours on the circle 'characterless', because 'they lie too close to one another for their impression to become significant', though in some proportions they 'cannot produce a bad effect'; combinations that skip one colour he calls 'characteristic': expressive but unsatisfying, since the characteristic arises only as a part that stands out from a whole without dissolving into it.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: One may well call these combinations characterless, as they lie too close to one another for their impression to become significant.
src.qo: Man kann diese Zusammenstellungen wohl die charakterlosen nennen, indem sie zu nahe an einander liegen, als daß ihr Eindruck bedeutsam werden könnte.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: indem jedes Charakteristi- sche nur dadurch entsteht, daß es als ein Theil aus einem Ganzen heraustritt, mit welchem es ein Ver- hältniß hat, ohne sich darin aufzulösen

s: Goethe says a fully harmonious colouring, with all colours in equilibrium, can be brilliant or pleasant but always has 'something general' and so 'characterless' about it, and that this is why most modern painters' colouring is characterless: following instinct they reach the totality but miss the character the picture might have had.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: both, however, will always have something general and, in this sense, something characterless about them
src.qo: welche beyde jedoch immer etwas Allgemeines und in diesem Sinne etwas Charakterloses haben werden.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1810, Zur Farbenlehre, Erster Band (Didaktischer Teil)
src.q: the last place to which it can lead them remains the totality, which they achieve more or less, but thereby at the same time miss the character that the picture might otherwise have had
src.qo: so bleibt das Letzte, wohin er sie führen kann, die Totalität, die sie mehr oder weniger erreichen, dadurch aber zugleich den Charakter versäumen, den das Bild allenfalls haben könnte.

s: In a student's notes of Schelling's lectures on the philosophy of art, harmony is 'multiplicity in unity' related to the whole, so that 'internal, different contrasts are brought into unity within the whole': the unity of different tones, the reflection of all particular unities into an absolute unity of the whole; the moderns, lacking the ancients' rhythm, replaced it with harmony.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, anonymous student (notes), 1806, Philosophie der Kunst (student's lecture notes)
src.q: diese Vielheit in der Einheit wird auf das Ganze bezogen, so daß innere differente Kontraste zur Einheit im Ganzen gebracht werden; Harmonie ist also Einheit verschiedener Töne

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, anonymous student (notes), 1806, Philosophie der Kunst (student's lecture notes)
src.q: Among the moderns, one replaced the lack of rhythm with harmony
src.qo: Man ersetzte bei den Neueren den Mangel des Rhythmus durch Harmonie

s: The same notes record Schelling's claim that architecture 'adheres to music' and that a beautiful building is 'a simultaneous concert of harmony and harmonic connections frozen in space', harmony being the ideal and dominant part of architecture.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, anonymous student (notes), 1806, Philosophie der Kunst (student's lecture notes)
src.q: Architecture adheres to music, and a beautiful building is a simultaneous concert of harmony and harmonic connections frozen in space.

s: In the Logic's account of measure Hegel uses the musical scale as a case of the 'nodal line': as tones move step by step away from the fundamental, a harmonic relation suddenly appears, 'a return, a surprising correspondence', not prepared by the step before but like an 'actio in distans'; a merely quantitative progression is broken by a qualitative leap.

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1812, Wissenschaft der Logik, Erster Band: Die objective Logik, Erstes Buch (Die Lehre vom Seyn)
src.loc: Book I, sect. 3 (Das Maaß), Remark on the nodal line, p. 311 [scan 357]
src.q: thut sich vielmehr auf einmal eine Rückkehr, eine überraschende Uebereinstimmung hervor, die nicht durch das unmittelbar vorhergehende qualitativ vorbereitet war, sondern als eine actio in distans

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1812, Wissenschaft der Logik, Erster Band: Die objective Logik, Erstes Buch (Die Lehre vom Seyn)
src.q: While following tones seem to move further and further away from the tonic, or numbers seem to become only more different through arithmetic progression, a return, a surprising correspondence, suddenly reveals itself.
src.qo: thut sich vielmehr auf einmal eine Rückkehr, eine überraschende Uebereinstimmung hervor, die nicht durch das unmittelbar vorhergehende qualitativ vorbereitet war, sondern als eine actio in distans

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1812, Wissenschaft der Logik, Erster Band: Die objective Logik, Erstes Buch (Die Lehre vom Seyn)
src.q: thus [entering] into a specific ratio by means of a leap.
src.qo: somit durch einen Sprung ein specifisches Verhältniß ein.

s: Schopenhauer maps harmony onto nature: the ground bass is inorganic nature, the ripieno voices between bass and melody are the scale of Ideas in which the Will objectifies itself (plants, animals), the melody is human will; tempered deviations from arithmetical correctness are like the individual's deviation from the species type, and 'impure dissonances' like monstrous crossbreeds.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (2nd ed.), vol. 1
src.q: Therefore, in harmony, the ground bass is to us what inorganic nature—the crudest mass upon which everything rests and from which everything rises and develops—is to the world.
src.qo: — Der Grundbaß ist uns also in der Harmonie, was in der Welt die unorganische Natur, die roheste Masse, auf der Alles ruht und aus der sich Alles erhebt und entwickelt. —

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (2nd ed.), vol. 1
src.q: Indeed, the impure dissonances that provide no definite interval can be compared to the monstrous births resulting from the crossing of two animal species
src.qo: ja die unreinen Mißtöne, die kein bestimmtes Intervall geben, las- sen sich den monstrosen Mißgeburten zwischen zwei Thierspecies, oder zwischen Mensch und Thier, vergleichen.

s: For Schopenhauer melody is a constant wandering from the tonic, through every tone 'including the dissonant seventh', and a final return to it: the wandering expresses the Will's striving, the return its satisfaction; slow melodies that fall into painful dissonances are sad, as delayed satisfaction, and the sustained tonic alone, the expression of languor, would 'soon be unbearable'.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (2nd ed.), vol. 1
src.q: On all these paths, the melody expresses the multifaceted striving of the Will; but through the final rediscovery of a harmonic interval, and even more so the tonic, it also always expresses satisfaction.
src.qo: auf allen jenen Wegen drückt die Melodie das vielgestaltete Streben des Willens aus, aber immer auch, durch das endliche Wiederfinden einer harmonischen Stufe und noch mehr des Grundtons, die Befriedigung.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (2nd ed.), vol. 1

s: Critique: Archytas's evidence for 'swift motion makes a high sound' runs pitch together with force and loudness: a voice driven by strong breath is 'loud and high-pitched', a weak one 'small and low', and a stick moved strongly sounds high. Pitch depends on the rate of vibration, not on the speed or force of the blow; loud and high are separable, so his correct conclusion rests partly on a confusion of loudness with pitch.

s: Interpretive synthesis: by modern psychoacoustics each ancient school was right about a different thing. The ratio school was right about the *criterion* of consonance (fusion of simple-ratio tones, now explained by harmonicity) and about *exactness* (pure intervals are sharply tuned points where beats vanish, and the comma is audible). Aristoxenus was right about the *space* (interval size is perceived additively, on a log-frequency scale), about *tolerance* (tempered intervals within a few cents are accepted, so 12-TET works) and about *function* (a note's role depends on its place in the system). Ptolemy's division of labour (sense for the near, reason for the exact) is close to the modern picture, with one correction: the exactness the ratio school claimed is itself heard, as beating.

s: Critique (computed): the 'new' method Salinas gives (III.31) for dividing a viol string into equal semitones is repeated division in extreme and mean ratio (the golden section). That cannot yield equal semitones: each step cuts the remaining length by a factor of φ² ≈ 2.618 (about 1,666 cents), and the 'twelfth fret' at e would leave 0.382 of the string sounding instead of 0.5 for the octave. Equal semitones need the twelfth root of 2 (mean proportionals), which his first-named tool, the mesolabium, can supply.

s: Wolff (Ontologia §514) holds that an exception to a rule produces no imperfection but is made while perfection remains intact, because the exception conforms to another rule and so preserves the agreement as far as possible.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1736, Philosophia prima sive Ontologia
src.q: An exception does not produce imperfection, but is made while perfection remains intact.
src.qo: Exceptio non parit imperfectionem, sed salva perfectione fit.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1736, Philosophia prima sive Ontologia
src.q: Exceptio non parit imperfectionem, sed salva perfectione fit.

s: Wolff (German Metaphysics §701) says the perfection of the world consists in everything that exists together and in succession agreeing with everything else, and the greater the agreement the greater the perfection; §702 adds that humans cannot comprehend it.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1720, Vernünfftige Gedancken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des Menschen
src.q: the perfection of the world consists in this: that everything existing at the same time, and following one after another, agrees with one another. The greater this agreement is, the greater is also the perfection of the world.
src.qo: so bestehet die Vollkommenheit der Welt darinnen/ daß alles/ was zugleich ist/ und auf einander folget/ mit einander übereinstimmet

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1720, Vernünfftige Gedancken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des Menschen
src.q: so bestehet die Vollkommenheit der Welt darinnen/ daß alles/ was zugleich ist/ und auf einander folget/ mit einander übereinstimmet

s: Wolff (German Metaphysics §171) says that when the number of the manifold meant to agree is very large it is hard to judge the perfection of the whole, and when it exceeds what we can survey it is not in our power to judge it.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1720, Vernünfftige Gedancken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des Menschen
src.q: it becomes difficult to judge the perfection of the whole. But if the number is greater than we are capable of contemplating, then it is not at all within our power to judge the perfection of the whole.
src.qo: fället es schwer von der Vollkommenheit des ganzen zu urtheilen

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1720, Vernünfftige Gedancken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des Menschen
src.q: fället es schwer von der Vollkommenheit des ganzen zu urtheilen

src.loc: Psychologia empirica, Part II, Sect. I, Cap. I, §511, p. 389 [scan 411]
src.q: Pleasure is the intuition, or intuitive cognition, of any perfection whatsoever, whether true or apparent.
src.qo: Voluptas est intuitus, seu cognitio intuitiva perfectionis cujuscunque, sive veræ, sive apparentis.

src.q: Voluptas est intuitus, seu cognitio intuitiva perfectionis cujuscunque, sive veræ, sive apparentis.

src.q: perceptionem perfectionis, in qua voluptas confiftit, effe confufam

s: In the Psychologia rationalis (§624) Wolff defines the pre-establishment of harmony as the act of God by which the harmony of soul and body subsists without real influence of either substance on the other, through the nature of both.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1737, Psychologia rationalis
src.loc: Psychologia rationalis, Sect. III, Cap. IV, §624, p. 558 [scan 570]
src.q: It is the act of God by which He causes the harmony of soul and body to subsist without the real influence of one substance into the other, through the very essence and nature of both.
src.qo: Est nempe actus Dei, quo efficit ut harmonia animæ & corporis subfistat citra influxum realem unius substantiæ in alteram per ipsam utriusque essentiam atque naturam.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1737, Psychologia rationalis
src.q: Est nempe actus Dei, quo efficit ut harmonia animæ & corporis subfistat citra influxum realem unius substantiæ in alteram per ipsam utriusque essentiam atque naturam.

s: In the preface to the Psychologia rationalis Wolff says it is far from the truth to hold that his whole philosophy rests on pre-established harmony as its sole foundation.

src.loc: Aesthetica, Pars I, Cap. I, Sect. I, §14, p. 6 [scan 23]

s: Baumgarten (Aesthetica §24-25) allows many exceptions in beauty, not to be counted as vices, provided they do not destroy the maximum consensus of appearances; a weaker rule of beauty yields to a stronger one.

src.l: Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten, 1750, Aesthetica
src.q: Hence they admit very many exceptions, which should not be considered vices

s: Mendelssohn (Phaedon, 1768, Socrates speaking) holds that order, proportion, harmony and regularity, and all relations that require taking the manifold together and holding it against itself, are effects of the faculty of thought; without a thinking being there is no harmony in nature.

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.q: Order, proportion, harmony, regularity, and in general all relationships that require a taking together and holding against one another of the manifold, are effects of the faculty of thought.

src.l: Moses Mendelssohn, 1768, Phaedon oder über die Unsterblichkeit der Seele
src.q: sind Wirkungen des Denkungsvermögens

s: Croce reports that Mendelssohn, a follower of Baumgarten, took beauty to be an indistinct image of a perfection and concluded that God cannot have a feeling of beauty.

src.l: Benedetto Croce, 1908, Estetica come scienza dell'espressione e linguistica generale (3rd ed.)
src.loc: Estetica, ch. IV, p. 310 [scan 310], search snippet (English translation of Croce)
src.q: Mendelssohn, another follower of Baumgarten, considering beauty as an "indistinct image of a perfection," deduced from it, rightly, that God cannot have a feeling of beauty

s: Kant (KU §15) holds that the judgment of taste is entirely independent of the concept of perfection, and calls it of the greatest importance in a Critique of Taste to decide whether beauty can be dissolved into perfection.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: The judgment of taste is entirely independent of the concept of perfection.
src.qo: Das Geschmacksurteil ist von dem Begriffe der Vollkommenheit gänzlich unabhängig.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: Das Geschmacksurteil ist von dem Begriffe der Vollkommenheit gänzlich unabhängig.

s: Kant (KU §15) says perfection, as internal objective purposiveness, has been held identical with beauty by famous philosophers, with the qualification that it be thought confusedly; this describes the Wolff-Baumgarten school's definition.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: comes closer to the predicate of beauty and has therefore been held to be identical with beauty by famous philosophers
src.qo: kommt dem Prädikate der Schönheit schon näher

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: kommt dem Prädikate der Schönheit schon näher

s: Kant (KU §15) defines the qualitative perfection of a thing as the agreement of the manifold within it with the concept that gives the rule of its connection, so perfection presupposes a concept of what the thing is meant to be.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: within the thing with this concept (which provides the rule for how its parts are connected) is the qualitative perfection of a thing.
src.qo: ist die qualitative Vollkommenheit eines Dinges

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: ist die qualitative Vollkommenheit eines Dinges

s: Kant (KU §15) holds that the formal element in a representation, the harmony of the manifold into one with no determination of what the one should be, discloses no objective purposiveness; what remains is the subjective purposiveness of the representation in the viewer's mind, which gives ease but no perfection of any object.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: The formal element in the representation of a thing—that is, the harmony of the manifold into a single unity (without determining what that unity is supposed to be)—does not, by itself, allow us to recognize any objective purposiveness.
src.qo: die Zusammenstimmung des Mannigfaltigen zu Einem (unbestimmt, was es sein solle)

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: die Zusammenstimmung des Mannigfaltigen zu Einem (unbestimmt, was es sein solle)

s: Kant (KU §16) distinguishes free beauty, which presupposes no concept of what the object is meant to be, from adherent beauty, which presupposes such a concept and the object's perfection according to it.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)
src.q: The former presupposes no concept of what the object is meant to be; the second presupposes such a concept and the perfection of the object according to it.
src.qo: Die erstere setzt keinen Begriff von dem voraus, was der Gegenstand sein soll

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (Meiner ed., 1922; work first published 1790)

src.q: into that proportioned attunement that we require for all cognition
