s: Wallace (1864) defines health, strength and long life as the result of a harmony between the individual and the universe around it, and treats a change in the surroundings as the loss of that harmony.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: health, strength, and long life are the results of a harmony between the individual and the universe that surrounds it

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: no longer in harmony with its universe

s: Wallace says natural selection, acting on variation over generations, brings an animal 'again ... thoroughly in harmony with the new conditions', and that every animal in a country must at each period be brought into harmony with its surroundings.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: our animal will have again become thoroughly in harmony with the new conditions in which he is placed

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: must at each successive period be brought into harmony with the surrounding conditions

s: Wallace argues that once mind matters more than body, man is 'kept in harmony with the slowly changing universe around him, by an advance in mind, rather than by a change in body'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: he would be kept in harmony with the slowly changing universe around him, by an advance in mind, rather than by a change in body

s: Wallace says every form of life is moulded 'into such new shapes as would preserve their harmony with the ever changing universe', a single law of change that nothing escapes.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: continually, but imperceptibly moulded into such new shapes as would preserve their harmony with the ever changing universe

s: Wallace lists 'moral, social and sympathetic feelings' (with division of labour and restraint of the appetites) among the faculties on which natural selection would act most powerfully once speech and mind arose.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: moral, social and sympathetic feelings, would now have a preponderating influence on his well being, and would therefore be that part of his nature on which "natural selection" would most powerfully act

s: Darwin closes the summary of ch. V by saying that new modifications from reversion and analogous variation 'will add to the beautiful and harmonious diversity of nature'.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1859, On the Origin of Species
src.q: such modifications will add to the beautiful and harmonious diversity of nature

s: Darwin argues that the more widely and perfectly the animals and plants of a land are diversified for different habits of life, the more individuals can support themselves there, and that descendants succeed by so much the better as they diverge.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1859, On the Origin of Species
src.q: the more widely and perfectly the animals and plants are diversified for different habits of life, so will a greater number of individuals be capable of there supporting themselves

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1859, On the Origin of Species
src.q: more living beings can be supported on the same area the more they diverge in structure, habits, and constitution

s: In the 1864 paper Wallace's 'harmony' means fit between an organism and its changing surroundings. In Contributions (1870) he also uses it for the organic world as an unbroken, self-adjusting system, in harmony 'with itself' and with its parts adjusted 'to each other', but always as the outcome of selection and equilibrium, never as a value placed on diversity. 'Survival of the harmonised' is still not his phrase.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1864, The Origin of Human Races and the Antiquity of Man Deduced from Natural Selection
src.q: a harmony between the individual and the universe that surrounds it

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays

s: Darwin's divergence of character and his one phrase 'harmonious diversity' describe diversity of kinds that lets more life be supported in one place, a niche-based diversity of a whole, but he does not say the diversity is harmony or that the parts fit one another; competition is the mechanism.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1859, On the Origin of Species
src.loc: ch. V p. 169 [scan 194]; ch. IV pp. 116, 128
src.q: beautiful and harmonious diversity of nature

s: Wallace's Ternate essay (1858) says the action of selection is 'exactly like that of the centrifugal governor of the steam engine, which checks and corrects any irregularities almost before they become evident', so that no unbalanced deficiency can reach a conspicuous magnitude: a feedback picture of stability.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: exactly like that of the centrifugal governor of the steam engine

s: Darwin distinguishes sympathy from love and holds that if sympathy is strictly an instinct, its exercise gives direct pleasure; it is the base of his account of the moral sense.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1892, The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (new edition)

s: Darwin says that as man advanced his sympathies 'became more tender and widely diffused, extending to men of all races ... and finally to the lower animals', and the standard of his morality rose with them.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1892, The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (new edition)

s: Following Helmholtz, Darwin says a noise differs from a musical note only in the want of continuity of its vibrations and their 'want of harmony inter se', so an ear able to discriminate noises must be sensitive to musical notes.

src.l: Charles Darwin, 1892, The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (new edition)

s: In the Sarawak law essay (1855) Wallace says that with all extinct forms in view, the gaps between classes would be softened and 'the whole organic world would be seen to be an unbroken and harmonious system'; gradation and harmony are the rule 'in everything else in Nature'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: the whole organic world would be seen to be an unbroken and harmonious system

s: Wallace names rapid multiplication, incessant slight variation and survival of the fittest as 'the laws which ever keep the organic world in harmony with the inorganic, and with itself'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: these are the laws which ever keep the organic world in harmony with the inorganic, and with itself

s: Wallace says varieties show nature at work producing 'that endless variety of colour, and that complicated harmony of relations' which gratify the lover of nature, and that the action and reaction of all living things on each other brings every species into harmony with the surrounding universe.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: that endless variety of colour, and that complicated harmony of relations

s: Wallace believes no phenomenon stands alone: 'not the wing of a butterfly can change in form or vary in colour, except in harmony with, and as a part of the grand march of nature'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: not the wing of a butterfly can change in form or vary in colour, except in harmony with, and as a part of the grand march of nature

s: In 'Creation by Law' Wallace lists 'The Equilibrium or Harmony of Nature' as the sixth law of life, and against the Duke of Argyll holds that the universe is 'so constituted as to be self-regulating', its life-forms having 'an inherent power of adjustment to each other and to surrounding nature'; Argyll's universe without a Creator would be 'without variety, without harmony, without design, without beauty'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: the universe is so constituted as to be self-regulating

s: Wallace argues that 'purely abstract notions of form, number, and harmony', like eternity and infinity, have no use to the savage and so could not have been developed by natural selection.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1870, Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection: A Series of Essays
src.q: all those purely abstract notions of form, number, and harmony

s: In the spiritualist account Wallace reports, spirit communes with spirit 'by thought-reading and sympathy', perfectly 'between those whose beings are in harmony with each other'; those who differ widely cannot communicate and form separate 'spheres'. He sets this 'progression of the fittest' beside the survival of the fittest that keeps the organic world in harmony with external nature.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1875, On Miracles and Modern Spiritualism: Three Essays
src.q: perfect between those whose beings are in harmony with each other

s: Wallace says spiritualism alone 'is able to harmonise conflicting creeds' and must lead to 'concord among mankind in the matter of religion'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1875, On Miracles and Modern Spiritualism: Three Essays
src.q: It and it alone, is able to harmonise conflicting creeds

s: In Patrick's 1889 rendering, Heraclitus (fr. LVI, via Plutarch) says the harmony of the world is a harmony of oppositions, like that of the bow and the lyre.

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.q: The harmony of the world is a harmony of oppositions, as in the case of the bow and of the lyre.

s: In Patrick's rendering, Heraclitus (fr. XLVII, via Hippolytus and Plutarch) says 'The hidden harmony is better than the visible.'

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.q: The hidden harmony is better than the visible.

s: Aristotle (Eth. Nic. VIII.2), as translated by Patrick, reports Heraclitus saying that the unlike is joined together and that the most beautiful harmony results from differences, all things happening through strife.

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.q: The unlike is joined together, and from differences results the most beautiful harmony, and all things take place by strife.

s: Plutarch, in the context Patrick prints for fr. XLIII, argues that if strife were removed there could be no harmony without sharps and flats, nor living beings without male and female; this is Plutarch's gloss on the Homer-curse fragment, and the same page prints 'War is the father and king of all' as fr. XLIV.

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.loc: Patrick fr. XLIII context and XLIV, p. 95 [scan 111]
src.q: For there could be no harmony without sharps and flats, nor living beings without male and female, which are contraries.

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.q: War is the father and king of all, and has produced some as gods and some as men, and has made some slaves and some free.

s: Patrick reports Schuster's reading of the hidden-harmony fragment as a rhetorical question: why should an invisible harmony be better than a visible one? It is not better; Heraclitus honours whatever is seen, heard or investigated; so the fragment is evidence for a sense-based theory of knowledge, not for a hidden order.

src.l: Heraclitus, G. T. W. Patrick (trans.), 1889, The Fragments of the Work of Heraclitus of Ephesus on Nature
src.loc: Patrick, Historical and Critical (reporting Schuster), p. 13 [scan 29]
src.q: Why, asks Heraclitus (Hippolytus, Ref. haer. ix. 9; cp. frag. 47), should an invisible harmony be better than a visible? It is not better, but, on the contrary, whatever is the object of seeing, hearing, or investigation, that I particularly honor

s: Vitruvius defines eurythmy as a graceful appearance and a convenient aspect in the composition of members, achieved when height answers to width and width to length and everything answers to its own symmetry; symmetry is the convenient agreement of the work's members, each separate part answering to the look of the whole figure, as in the human body.

src.l: Vitruvius, 1523, De architectura libri decem (Aldine Press)
src.q: Eurythmy is a graceful appearance and a convenient aspect in the composition of members.
src.qo: Eurythmia est venusta species, cōmodusq; in cōpositionibus membrorum aspectus.

src.l: Vitruvius, 1523, De architectura libri decem (Aldine Press)
src.q: symmetry is the convenient agreement from the members of the work itself, and from the separate parts, the correspondence of a given part to the appearance of the whole figure, as in the human body there is a symmetry from the cubit, foot, palm, finger, and the other parts
src.qo: ex partibusq; separatis, ad vniuersæ figuræ speciē, ratæ partis respōsus, vt in hominis corpore è cubito, pede, palmo, digito, cæterisq; partibus, symmetros est,

s: Vitruvius (III.1) says a temple's composition consists in symmetry, sought from proportion (analogia); no temple can have a ratio of composition without it unless it follows the exact ratio of the members of a well-formed human body, and he lists the body's measures (face one tenth, foot one sixth, cubit one quarter).

src.l: Vitruvius, 1523, De architectura libri decem (Aldine Press)
src.q: The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the method of which architects must hold most diligently.
src.qo: Ædium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationē diligentissime architecti tenere debēt.

src.l: Vitruvius, 1523, De architectura libri decem (Aldine Press)
src.q: For nature has so composed the human body that the face of the head from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair is the tenth part.
src.qo: Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, vti os capitis à mento ad frontē summam et radices imas capilli esset decimæ partis.

src.l: Vitruvius, 1523, De architectura libri decem (Aldine Press)
src.q: The foot, indeed, is the sixth of the body's height, the cubit the fourth, the chest likewise the fourth
src.qo: Pes vero altitudinis corporis sextæ, Cubitus quartæ, pectus itē quartæ,

s: Ethics IV P31 cor.: nothing can be good except insofar as it agrees with our nature, and the more a thing agrees with our nature the more useful it is; a thing that is merely different from our nature is neither good nor bad.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.loc: Part IV, P31 dem. and cor., p. 128 [scan 143]
src.q: Nothing, therefore, can be good except insofar as it agrees with our nature; and thus, the more a thing agrees with our nature, the more useful it is, and vice versa.
src.qo: Nihil igitur, nisi quatenus cum nostra natura convenit, potest esse bonum, atque adeo, quo res aliqua magis cum nostra natura convenit, eo est utilior, et contra.

s: For Smith we approve another's passion when it matches ours and disapprove when it does not; he names the test concord or dissonance, and speaks of sympathy that 'keeps time' with another's grief.

s: Smith holds that approval of a sorrow rests on 'conditional sympathy': what we would feel if we took time to consider the situation fully; general rules from past experience correct our present emotions.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1759, The Theory of Moral Sentiments

s: Smith says the sufferer must make a great effort to bring his emotions to 'compleat harmony and concord' with the spectator's, and that the spectator must find it harder to 'keep perfect time' with sorrow than with joy.

s: The Suda's entry ἁρμονία (largely compiled from Philoponus on the De anima) says harmony is the union (ἕνωσις) of many-mixed things and of those of different mind (δίχα φρονεόντων), so that sound cannot come from one thing; it is a ratio (λόγος) of what is mixed, and the lack of it (ἀναρμοστία) in a living body is disease, weakness and deformity, each a failure of proportion (ἀσυμμετρία).

src.qo: ཤེས་ རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་དང་མཐུན་པར་སྤྱོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར།

s: A biographical passage in the Derge Tengyur catalogue volume (SL translation) lists cymbals 'played in harmony with vocal melodies', where the Tibetan is sil snyan glu dbyangs dang bstun pa.

src.l: Unknown, 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 213 (catalogue, dkar chag)
src.q: cymbals played in harmony with vocal melodies

s: In the Four Medical Tantras (SL translation) health is the humours kept 'in balance without excess or deficiency' (lhag chad med par mnyam), and the twenty-five categories 'cause growth if they remain in balance' (mnyam par gnas pa).

src.l: Yuthok Yonten Gonpo, 1888, bDud rtsi snying po (rGyud bzhi / Four Medical Tantras)
src.q: Therefore, maintain the humors in balance without excess or deficiency.
src.qo: དེས་ན་འདུ་བ་ལྷག་ཆད་མེད་པར་མཉམ།།

src.l: Yuthok Yonten Gonpo, 1888, bDud rtsi snying po (rGyud bzhi / Four Medical Tantras)
src.q: will cause growth if they remain in balance
src.qo: ཐམས་ཅད་མཉམ་པར་གནས་པས་འཕེལ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་།

s: The Four Medical Tantras (SL translation) call a balance of cool and warm behaviour 'compatible' for combined heats: Tibetan bsil drod snyoms pa mthun, where mthun is the 'compatible' of mthun/mi mthun (compatible/incompatible).

src.l: Yuthok Yonten Gonpo, 1888, bDud rtsi snying po (rGyud bzhi / Four Medical Tantras)
src.q: For combined heats, a balance of cool and warm behavior is compatible.
src.qo: ལྡན་ཚད་རྣམས་ལ་བསིལ་དྲོད་སྙམས་པ་མཐུན།

s: A Tengyur tantra commentary (SL translation) defines yoga as the 'balanced entry' (snyoms par 'jug pa) of method and wisdom, two unlike things: wisdom is lack of inherent nature, method is the characteristic of phenomena.

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 32 (tantra commentary, ki)
src.q: The balanced entry into those two is Yoga.
src.qo: དེ་དག་སྙོམས་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་རོ། །

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 32 (tantra commentary, ki)
src.q:
Wisdom is the lack of inherent nature;
Method is the characteristic of phenomena.

s: A Tengyur commentary on a tantra (SL translation) says the union of method and wisdom through great passion is taught 'to generate the diversity within the nature of the mandala circle' (sna tshogs pa bskyed pa), and that when great bliss enters the bodhicitta drops 'they are made into a single flavor' (ro gcig pa).

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 9 (tantra commentary, nya)
src.q: Now, in order to generate the diversity within the nature of the mandala circle, the union of method and wisdom through great passion is taught.

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 9 (tantra commentary, nya)
src.q: if the ultimate great bliss enters into them, they are made into a single flavor
src.qo: དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེ་བ་ཆེན་པོ་རྗེས་སུ་ཞུགས་པ་ཡོད་ན་རོ་གཅིག་པའི་གཟུགས་སུ་བྱེད་དོ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །

s: A Tengyur commentary on a Dohakosha-type text (SL translation) uses water poured into water as 'one taste' (ro gcig) and 'equal taste of non-duality' (gnyis med ro mnyam), and then rejects the inference that all empty things are the same: 'look at the pig and the elephant; though they are like that, they are not the same'.

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 51 (tantra commentary, wi)
src.q: As water poured into water becomes of one taste, so too does it dissolve into the fundamental mind.
src.qo: ཆུ་ལ་ཆུ་བཞག་པ། །དེ་སྲིད་ཆུ་རུ་རོ་མཉམ་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་པས་སྟོན་ཏེ།

src.l: Unknown (Indian tantra commentary in Tibetan), 1982, Derge Tengyur vol. 51 (tantra commentary, wi)
src.q: "Friends, look at the pig and the elephant; though they are like that, they are not the same."
src.qo: སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་པས་མི་འཆིང་བའི་ཕྱིར། སྟོང་ན་གང་ཡང་འདྲ་འམ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། གྲོགས་དག་ཕག་དང་གླང་པོ་ལྟོས། །དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཏེ་དེ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་སྟེ།

s: Khamtrul's Mahamudra manual (SL translation, 1710) describes one taste (ro gcig) as realising the many as one and the one arising as many, and says that if this does not turn into compassion 'the seed of the Form Body has not been planted'.

src.l: Khamtrul Ngawang Kunga Tenzin (1680-1728), 1710, Introduction to the Preliminary Practice of Mahamudra (Innate Union)
src.q: Even if one realizes the many as one taste and the one taste arises as many
src.qo: དུ་མ་རོ་གཅིག་ཏུ་རྟོགས་ཤིང་རོ་གཅིག་དུ་མར་ཤར་བ་ཙམ་འདུག་ཀྱང་རྟོགས་པའི་རྩལ་སྣང་སྙིང་རྗེར་མ་ཐོན།

s: Drukpa Kunley (SL translation) says a realised person is 'in harmony with all' (kun dang mthun pa) with whomever they associate, 'yet they do not hand over their personal power to others' (gzhan la dbang mi gtod).

src.l: Drukpa Kunley (1455-1529), 1500, Miscellaneous Writings of Drukpa Kunley
src.q: Whomever they associate with, they are in harmony with all, yet they do not hand over their personal power to others.

s: Lipps (1885) holds that the ratios of the tone-rhythms make harmony and disharmony, and that ratios differing from simple ones by few elements act nearly like the simple ones.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1885, Psychologische Studien (essay 'Das Wesen der musikalischen Harmonie und Disharmonie', leaves 103-155)
src.q: Die Verhältnisse der Rhythmen, so müssen wir sagen, machen die Harmonie und Disharmonie, nur dass solche Verhältnisse, die sich von einfachen nur durch relativ wenige Elemente unterscheiden, annähernd wie die einfachen wirken.

s: Lipps (1885): rhythms that cross each other sufficiently make disharmony, provided the crossing is decided enough.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1885, Psychologische Studien (essay 'Das Wesen der musikalischen Harmonie und Disharmonie', leaves 103-155)
src.q: Insbesondere machen die Rhythmen, die sich genügend durchkreuzen, die Disharmonie; es muss aber diese Durchkreuzung zugleich eine genügend entschiedene sein.

s: Lipps (1905) says he defends the oldest theory: simple and less simple vibration ratios between simple tones are responsible for all consonance and dissonance.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1905, Psychologische Studien, 2nd ed. ('Konsonanz und Dissonanz')
src.q: Die älteste unter ihnen allen macht die einfacheren und weniger einfachen Schwingungsverhältnisse zwischen einfachen Tönen für alle Konsonanz und Dissonanz verantwortlich.

s: Lipps (1905) argues against the beats theory (Helmholtz's) that dissonance cannot consist in beats, because then dissonance-awareness would be awareness of beats, which anyone striking dissonant tones can see it is not.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1905, Psychologische Studien, 2nd ed. ('Konsonanz und Dissonanz')
src.q: Besteht die Dissonanz in Schwebungen oder sind die Schwebungen die Dissonanz, dann ist das Dissonanzbewußtsein das Bewußtsein der Schwebungen.

s: Lipps (1905) describes a single sound as a rhythmic system built on one ground-rhythm, differentiated more or less richly in the rhythms of the single tones.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1905, Psychologische Studien, 2nd ed. ('Konsonanz und Dissonanz')
src.q: Der Klang ist ein rhythmisches System, aufgebaut auf einem Grundrhythmus. Dieser Grundrhythmus wird in den Rhythmen der einzelnen Töne mehr oder weniger reich differenziert.

s: Lipps (1905) says different people find in the pleasant a different 'Resonanz', according to their own nature, which explains why tastes in consonance differ.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1905, Psychologische Studien, 2nd ed. ('Konsonanz und Dissonanz')
src.q: den Unterschied der besonderen „Resonanz“, die das in dieser oder jener Art Angenehme in Menschen je nach ihrem besonderen Wesen finden kann und finden muß

s: Lipps (1903) introduces Einfühlung as inwardly joining in a heard cry of joy (Mitfreuen), and makes it the basic concept of what follows.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, vol. 1
src.q: Dieser Sachverhalt, dies sich Mitfreuen in dem gehörten Freudenlaut, fassen wir gleich in den Begriff

s: Lipps (1903) ties a rhythmic movement to the mood of the same kind by a bond of likeness (Gleichartigkeit), under a heading 'Gesetz der Resonanz des Gleichartigen'.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, vol. 1
src.q: ein Aneinandergebundensein durch das Band der Gleichartigkeit ... Zu jeder rhythmischen Bewegung gehört die gleichartige Stimmung

s: Lipps (1903): an experience creates its corresponding psychic resonance, bringing to strength in us those ways of inner living that are of the same kind as its own character of excitement.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, vol. 1
src.q: Das Erlebnis schafft sich seine entsprechende psychische Resonanz. Es läfst diejenigen Weisen des inneren Erlebens überhaupt in uns Kraft gewinnen oder anklingen, die seinem eigenen Erregungscharakter gleichartig sind.

s: Lipps (1903): when several melodies are to combine into a unity, one must appear as the ruling one (the melody); the serving voices form with it the single system resting on one basis.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, vol. 1
src.q: so mufs eine unter ihnen als die herrschende oder als die Melodie erscheinen

s: Lipps (1903) says we know the resolution of dissonance in many forms in life: sun breaking through clouds, a quarrel settled, doubt lifted, an inner conflict resolved.

src.l: Theodor Lipps, 1903, Ästhetik: Psychologie des Schönen und der Kunst, vol. 1
src.q: wenn die Sonne durch Wolken bricht, wenn Streit sich schlichtet, wenn wir aus materieller Not befreit werden, wenn Zweifel sich heben, wenn ein innerer Konflikt sich löst

s: Spencer (1858) holds that music intensifies and combines the vocal modifications of excited feeling (loudness, resonance, pitch, intervals, variability) and so produces an idealized language of emotion.

src.l: Herbert Spencer, 1858, Essays: Moral, Political, and Aesthetic (incl. 'The Origin and Function of Music', leaves 379-403)
src.loc: leaf 396 (essay 'The Origin and Function of Music')
src.q: it produces an idealized language of emotion

s: Spencer (1858) says the modifications of voice produced by feeling are the means of exciting like feelings in others, and calls them the chief media of sympathy.

src.l: Herbert Spencer, 1858, Essays: Moral, Political, and Aesthetic (incl. 'The Origin and Function of Music', leaves 379-403)
src.q: the means of exciting like feelings in others ... In short, they are the chief media of sympathy.

s: Wallace (Light, 30 May 1885) ends on Pope's lines 'All Discord, Harmony not understood; All partial Evil universal Good', calling the poet's vision the best expression of the truth.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, Frederick F. Cook, 1885, Light: A Journal of Psychical, Occult, and Mystical Research, vol. 5 (30 May, 18 July, 25 July 1885)
src.q: All Discord, Harmony not understood

s: Wallace (30 May 1885) argues that in a perfect and harmonious world perfect beings might have been created but could hardly have been evolved, so evolution (labour, struggle, antagonism) needs imperfection.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, Frederick F. Cook, 1885, Light: A Journal of Psychical, Occult, and Mystical Research, vol. 5 (30 May, 18 July, 25 July 1885)
src.q: In a perfect and harmonious world perfect beings might possibly have been created but could hardly have been evolved, and it may well be that evolution is the great fundamental law of the universe of mind as well as of matter.

s: In his reply of 25 July 1885 Wallace quotes his own sentence ('evolution is a fundamental law of the universe of mind as well as that of matter') and restricts it to the development of individualised human minds, not mind in the abstract.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, Frederick F. Cook, 1885, Light: A Journal of Psychical, Occult, and Mystical Research, vol. 5 (30 May, 18 July, 25 July 1885)
src.q: it may well be that evolution is a fundamental law of the universe of mind as well as that of matter. ... I am referring solely to the development of individualised human minds

s: In the 9th-century copy of Boethius, Arithmetic II.32, harmony is defined as the unification of many and the consensus of dissenters (Est enim armonia plurimorum adunatio et dissentientium consensio).

src.l: Boethius, 850, De institutione arithmetica (9th-century copy)
src.q: harmony is the unification of many and the consensus of dissenters

s: Remigius on Martianus (12th-century manuscript) defines music, or harmony, as the concord of many dissimilar things brought into one.

src.l: Remigius of Auxerre, 1170, Commentary on Martianus Capella (12th-century manuscript)
src.q: sica sive armonia est plurium dissimilium in unum redactorum concordia

s: Theon of Smyrna defines harmonia as a system of genus and order (σύστημα γένους καὶ τάξεως): the order family of definitions.

src.l: Theon of Smyrna, 1350, Expositio rerum mathematicarum ad legendum Platonem utilium (Greek manuscript)
src.q: Ἁρμονία δέ ἐστι, σύστημα γένους καὶ τάξεως

s: Chen Yang's Yueshu quotes the Zhongyong: emotions not yet aroused are called the mean (zhong); aroused and all hitting due measure, they are called he (harmony).

src.l: Chen Yang 陳暘, 1101, Yueshu 樂書 (Siku quanshu copy), vol. 1
src.q: 中庸曰喜怒哀樂未發謂之中發而皆中節謂之和

s: Xiao Ji's Wuxing dayi quotes the Guoyu on bells: sounds answering and protecting one another is called he; small and large not overstepping each other is called ping.

src.l: Xiao Ji 蕭吉, 594, Wuxing dayi 五行大義
src.q: 相保曰和細大不踰曰平

s: A Byzantine excerpt list on the wolf in Bodleian MS. Barocci 50 says the wolf is so hostile to sheep that a wolf-gut string on a kithara silences the sheep-gut strings struck with it, and that the same happens with drums: the oldest witness of the wolf-drum topos in our holdings, with both forms together.

src.l: Anonymous (Byzantine excerpts), 950, Bodleian Library MS. Barocci 50 (grammatical and poetical texts, Physiologus)
src.q: That it is so hostile toward the sheep that if a string made from it is found in a lyre, the strings struck alongside it do not sound. This would also happen with drums.

s: Bartholomaeus Anglicus (De proprietatibus rerum) cites Aristotle for the enmity of wolf and sheep and reports from "a book" that a wolf-gut string on a lute ruins a sheep-gut string.

src.l: Bartholomaeus Anglicus, 1275, De proprietatibus rerum (manuscript)
src.q: I have read that if a string made from wolf guts is put on a lute along with a string made from sheep guts, the wolf string will consume or ruin the sheep string.

s: Pseudo-Albertus (De mirabilibus mundi, 1478 edition) says a drum of wolf skin makes a drum of sheep skin fall silent.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1478, De mirabilibus mundi (with the Liber aggregationis)
src.q: a drum made from the skin of a wolf causes one made from the skin of a sheep to fall silent

s: In 1665 Huygens reports that two pendulum clocks hung a foot or two apart keep beating together "by a kind of sympathy" and, when disturbed, return within half an hour "to the consonance"; in this letter he blames an imperceptible agitation of the air.

src.l: Christiaan Huygens, 1893, Oeuvres complètes, tome V: Correspondance 1664-1665
src.q: cela arrivoit par une espece de sympathie: en sorte que faisant battre les Pendules par des coups entremeslez; j’ay trouvè que dans une demieheure de temps, elles se remettoient tousjours à la consonance

s: In a later 1665 letter Huygens corrects himself: the cause of the clocks' sympathy is not the motion of the air but the slight, imperceptible motion of their common support.

src.l: Christiaan Huygens, 1893, Oeuvres complètes, tome V: Correspondance 1664-1665
src.q: la cause de la sympathie dont je vous ay escrit par ma derniere ⁴) ne provient pas du mouuement de l’air mais du dit petit branflement

s: The Royal Society, hearing of Huygens's clocks in 1665, asked Moray to find out "upon what account this pretended sympathy should happen; whether from a magnetical cause, or from the agitation of the air".

src.l: Thomas Birch, 1756, The History of the Royal Society of London
src.q: to find out upon what account this pretended sympathy should happen ; whether from a magnetical cause, or from the agitation of the air

s: Dong Zhongshu (Chunqiu fanlu, quoted in the Peiwen yunfu) says that when the gong string is struck the other gong strings answer, and that the five notes sounding of themselves is not spirits: the numbers make it so.

src.l: Zhang Yushu 張玉書 et al. (comp.), 1711, Peiwen yunfu 佩文韻府, vol. 402
src.q: 鼓其宮則 他宮應之

src.l: Zhang Yushu 張玉書 et al. (comp.), 1711, Peiwen yunfu 佩文韻府, vol. 402
src.q: 五音比 而自鳴非有 神其數然也

s: Shen Kuo (Bu bitan, quoted in the Zishi jinghua) finds the answering string by tuning the strings, setting paper figures on them and striking: the paper figure on the answering string jumps and the others do not move.

src.l: Kangxi court (comp.), 1727, Zishi jinghua 子史精華
src.q: 則紙人躍他絃即不動

s: Kong Yingda's subcommentary (quoted in the Peiwen yunfu) glosses the Yijing's "like sounds answer each other" as string resonance: striking the gong makes the gong answer.

src.l: Zhang Yushu 張玉書 et al. (comp.), 1711, Peiwen yunfu 佩文韻府, vol. 656
src.q: 同聲相應者若彈宫而宫應

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ match the four ʿūd strings to the four elements and say the tone of the mathlath strengthens the phlegm humour and opposes bile.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Bombay edition), part 1
src.q: The tone of the *mathlath* strengthens the phlegm humor, increases its power and effect, and opposes the bile humor, breaking its sharpness.
src.qo: ونغمة المثلث تقوي خلط البلغم وتزيد في قوته وتاثيره وتضاد خلط الصفراء وتكسر حدتها

s: Before Huygens, "sympathetic clock" was a term of occult horology: Kircher writes that a water lily was the Egyptians' sympathetic clock.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1653, Oedipus Aegyptiacus (Class VII, Hieroglyphic mathematics)
src.q: The water lily constituted a sympathetic clock among the Egyptians.

s: In the Heike monogatari, when Tsunemasa plays the biwa at Chikubushima the deity cannot withhold its response (kannō) and a white dragon appears on his sleeve.

src.l: Anonymous, 1371, Heike monogatari 平家物語, vol. 2
src.q: 明神感應に堪ずして、經正の袖の上に、白龍現じて見え給へり。

s: Fracastoro (De sympathia, 1546) explains that one unison sets another in motion because strings stretched alike are suited to make and receive similar waves of air.

src.l: Girolamo Fracastoro, 1546, De sympathia et antipathia rerum
src.q: one unison note sets another unison in motion, because strings that are stretched similarly are naturally suited both to create and to receive similar waves

s: Bermudo (1555) gives the straw test: a straw on the strings of one vihuela does not move until a second vihuela is brought into unison, and then it trembles.

src.l: Juan Bermudo, 1555, Declaración de instrumentos musicales
src.q: as long as the second vihuela is not in unison with the first, the straw on the strings of the first vihuela will not move; but upon reaching unison, the straw trembles because the string moves

s: Shen Kuo (Mengxi bitan, 1088) records a pipa in an empty room whose strings sounded whenever a wind instrument played in the Shuangdiao mode, and not for other modes.

src.l: Shen Kuo 沈括, 1088, Mengxi bitan 夢溪筆談 (Dream Pool Essays)
src.q: the lute strings would immediately sound in sympathetic response

s: In a census of 3,933 sentences that define harmony, concord, consonance or he in 2,088 Source Library books (original languages plus English translations), the diversity/opposites-in-a-whole family appears in 15% of definitions and ratio/consonance in 32%; the diversity share stays between 12% and 27% in every century from the 9th to the 20th.

src.l: Source Library (job harmony-census-7117), 2026, Harmony definition census and five resonance topoi (experiment entry, #7117)

s: Outside Chinese, 203 of the 428 diversity-in-a-whole definitions in the census are also ratio/consonance definitions (e.g. consonance as the concord of dissimilar voices reduced to one): in the Western texts the two are usually one sentence, not rival definitions.

src.l: Source Library (job harmony-census-7117), 2026, Harmony definition census and five resonance topoi (experiment entry, #7117)

s: Chinese definitions of he in the census mostly quote two loci, Analects 13.23 (harmonious but not the same, 246 rows) and Zhongyong 1 (feelings hitting due measure, 204); balance/mean is the largest Chinese family (366 of 1,266), ahead of diversity (165).

src.l: Source Library (job harmony-census-7117), 2026, Harmony definition census and five resonance topoi (experiment entry, #7117)

s: On English-translation pages that name sympathy, the share that also names the magnet rises from 3-6% before 1500 to 24% in the 17th century and falls to 6-10% in the 19th-20th, while health/temperament peaks at 38% in the 17th century: sympathy is a medical-magnetic concept in the weapon-salve century and a moral-social one after.

src.l: Source Library (job harmony-census-7117), 2026, Harmony definition census and five resonance topoi (experiment entry, #7117)

s: If harmony = diversity in wholeness and the universe is diverse and whole, 'the universe is harmonious' is true by definition and explains nothing; the programme needs degree measures taken independently of the outcomes they are meant to predict.

src.l: Susan K. Mills, John H. Beatty, 1979, The Propensity Interpretation of Fitness
src.loc: not read; cited for the way out, not the objection (see phil-propensity-fitness)

s: Aristotle (Topics VI.2) offers, as a test of definitions, that defining temperance as a 'harmony' is a metaphor and so obscure, and that harmony is not a genus containing virtue: 'harmony does not contain virtue, nor virtue harmony'. Lomas & Xue cite this as a caution that cross-domain 'harmony' may obscure.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design
src.loc: p. 20, RP.26 (citing Aristotle, Topics, Barnes ed. p. 236)

src.l: Aristotle, c. 340 BCE, Topics, Book VI

s: Zhmud's 1989 article "All is number?" challenges Aristotle's testimony that "all is number" was the fundamental definition of Pythagorean philosophy: per Cornelli's 2016 account, no testimony earlier than Aristotle attests the doctrine, and Zhmud allows that it was not actually a Pythagorean doctrine. That Philolaus' own claim is epistemic (knowable things have number) is Huffman's reading, treated at anc-philolaus-number-knowable.

s: Most of the mythical elements in the Pythagorean tradition (the smithy, hearing the spheres, music therapy, the Olympic boxing story) are late additions in the Neopythagorean and Neoplatonic sources (Iamblichus, Porphyry, 3rd-4th c. CE) in Zhmud's view, and Burkert likewise treats the Academic presentation as the start of the Neopythagorean tradition that makes Pythagoras anticipate Plato. But Zhmud, unlike Burkert, argues Pythagoras himself had both a religious and a scientific/mathematical side and seeks to rehabilitate him as a mathematician, so 'the historical Pythagoras is unrecoverable' is Burkert's pole, not a joint Burkert-Zhmud verdict. Use these stories as the tradition's ideas, not as history.

s: Goodhart's law warns that optimising a harmony or resonance score too hard may degrade the thing it measures. Karwowski et al. show empirically, for reinforcement learning, that optimising an imperfect proxy reward often leads to the behaviour Goodhart's law predicts: increasing optimisation beyond a critical point reduces performance on the true objective.

src.l: Jacek Karwowski, et al., 2023, Goodhart's Law in Reinforcement Learning

s: Schoenberg coined 'the emancipation of the dissonance' for the idea that, as the ear becomes acquainted with remoter overtone-related dissonances, their comprehensibility becomes equivalent to the consonance's, so a style may treat dissonances like consonances and renounce a tonal centre. On this view the consonance/dissonance difference is one of degree of familiarity, not a natural divide, which is a historical challenge to models that put tonal consonance at the base (Plomp-Levelt, Sethares): they cover one idiom. The last step is our inference, not Schoenberg's wording.

src.l: Arnold Schoenberg, 1941, Composition with Twelve Tones (in Style and Idea, 1950)

s: Adorno, in Philosophy of New Music, treats musical material as historically developed and takes Schoenberg's atonal path as the paradigm of musical progress; on that view tonal harmony is not a timeless model of order, and presenting it as one can serve an ideology.

src.l: Anon. (Brazilian thesis abstract), 2017, Schoenberg and progress in Adorno's Philosophy of New Music

s: Sharf argues that the category of 'experience' in modern studies of Buddhism, the assumption that meditation aims at discrete mystical experiences, is a modern construction, not a neutral report. Extending this to cross-tradition claims of a shared 'perennial harmony' (Pythagoras, the Dao, Hermes) is our extrapolation, not Sharf's argument.

src.l: Robert H. Sharf, 1995, Buddhist Modernism and the Rhetoric of Meditative Experience

s: Shadlen & Movshon (1999) critically evaluate the temporal-binding (synchrony) hypothesis and conclude that it is 'untenable' as proposed: incomplete as a solution to binding, with significant obstacles to encoding and decoding information as synchrony, and experimental evidence that is largely indirect and of no proven relevance to binding itself. A programme that cites synchrony as the neural face of harmony (lomas-rp69-sync-balance) rests on a contested hypothesis.

src.l: Michael N. Shadlen, J. Anthony Movshon, 1999, Synchrony Unbound

s: Bostrom's orthogonality thesis: intelligence and final goals vary independently, so more or less any level of intelligence can pair with more or less any goal. If true, greater intelligence does not by itself make a system more harmonizing, and prop-intelligence-is-harmonizing needs an argument that blocks it.

src.l: Nick Bostrom, 2012, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents

s: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis authors themselves list limits: convergence is shown mainly for vision and language, not all domains converge, possible sociological bias toward human-like representations, and special-purpose systems may not converge. So it cannot yet underwrite a claim that AI is converging on a harmonious or true structure of reality.

src.l: Minyoung Huh, et al., 2024, The Platonic Representation Hypothesis

s: Huh et al. note that researcher preferences to mimic human reasoning could produce convergence toward human-like representations even if other kinds of intelligence are possible. Convergence may measure a shared design culture, not a deep structure.

s: May (1972) showed that randomly connected model ecosystems are stable only up to a critical level of connectance and species number, beyond which they become abruptly unstable, which overturned the expectation that complexity brings stability.

src.l: May, R. M., 1972, Will a large complex system be stable?
Allesina, S., Tang, S., 2012, Stability criteria for complex ecosystems

s: Allesina & Tang (2012) extended May's analysis to structured networks and found that predator-prey interactions are stabilising while mutualistic and competitive interactions are destabilising, so the kind of relation matters more than the count of species.

src.l: Allesina, S., Tang, S., 2012, Stability criteria for complex ecosystems

s: In Allesina & Tang's model the probability of stability for predator-prey networks falls when realistic food-web structure is imposed or when weak interactions predominate, and nestedness lowers stability in mutualistic networks; this runs against the weak-interaction stabilisation reported by McCann et al.

src.l: Allesina, S., Tang, S., 2012, Stability criteria for complex ecosystems

s: McCann, Hastings and Huxel (1998) report that weak to intermediate strength trophic links promote community persistence and stability, and that natural food webs are characterised by many weak links.

src.l: McCann, K., Hastings, A., Huxel, G. R., 1998, Weak trophic interactions and the balance of nature

s: McCann (2000) reviews the diversity-stability debate and concludes that theory and empirical evidence both lead us to expect that declines in diversity will accelerate the simplification of ecological communities.

src.l: McCann, K. S., 2000, The diversity-stability debate

s: Tilman & Downing (1994) found that primary productivity in more diverse grassland plots was more resistant to, and recovered more fully from, a major drought.

src.l: Tilman, D., Downing, J. A., 1994, Biodiversity and stability in grasslands

s: In a decade-long grassland experiment controlling plant species number, Tilman, Reich & Knops (2006) found that ecosystem productivity was more stable over time at higher diversity, although individual species were less stable.

src.l: Tilman, D., Reich, P. B., Knops, J. M. H., 2006, Biodiversity and ecosystem stability in a decade-long grassland experiment

s: The grassland result has the shape of harmony as diversity in wholeness: the whole is steadier because the parts differ and fluctuate out of step (portfolio averaging and overyielding), not because the parts are alike.

src.l: Tilman, D., Reich, P. B., Knops, J. M. H., 2006, Biodiversity and ecosystem stability in a decade-long grassland experiment
Yachi, S., Loreau, M., 1999, Biodiversity and ecosystem productivity in a fluctuating environment: the insurance hypothesis

s: Yachi & Loreau's stochastic model shows two insurance effects of species richness on ecosystem productivity, a lower temporal variance and a higher temporal mean, whose strength depends on how asynchronous the species' responses to the environment are.

src.l: Yachi, S., Loreau, M., 1999, Biodiversity and ecosystem productivity in a fluctuating environment: the insurance hypothesis

s: Loreau & de Mazancourt (2013) argue that interspecific competition generally destabilises communities, and that diversity stabilises ecosystem properties mainly through asynchrony of species' responses, differences in response speed, and weaker competition.

src.l: Loreau, M., de Mazancourt, C., 2013, Biodiversity and ecosystem stability: a synthesis of underlying mechanisms

s: The ecological record does not support one 'diversity makes things stable' law: stability has many types, each giving a different relation to diversity, and diversity and stability are often driven together by environmental change, so the useful question is which factors, diversity among them, set stability.

src.l: Ives, A. R., Carpenter, S. R., 2007, Stability and diversity of ecosystems

s: Ecology's diversity (species richness) and stability (low variance or return to equilibrium) are measurable but are not the harmony definition: stability can be bought at the parts' expense (species less stable), and a stable monoculture or a stable predator-prey pair would count as stable, so mapping these results onto 'parts and whole strengthen each other' needs an independent measure of part flourishing.

src.l: Tilman, D., Reich, P. B., Knops, J. M. H., 2006, Biodiversity and ecosystem stability in a decade-long grassland experiment
Allesina, S., Tang, S., 2012, Stability criteria for complex ecosystems

s: Bastiat framed the dispute between the economists and the socialists as one starting-point question: are human interests, left to themselves, harmonious or antagonistic? He argued that what is harmonious of itself needs no constraint.

s: Bastiat grounded economic harmony in providence: he believed the Author of the material world arranged free agents harmoniously as well as inert molecules, and concluded that because interests are harmonic the whole solution is the word Liberty.

s: In his Compendium on the Timaeus, Ficino explains why Plato built the world-soul from harmonic ratios (1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27): the soul is tuned like a musician's mind, and the world is the sounding of that tuning. The spheres were composed, set and moved by these proportions, so the soul that moves them must be tempered by the same ones, and harmony flows from soul into cosmos as an artful mind's concord flows into a voice.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: so that just as the concert of an artificial mind flows into the voice among musicians, so the harmony of the celestial soul passes into the world
src.qo: ut quemadmodum apud musicos à concentu artificiosæ mentis profluit & concentus in uocem, sic ab harmonia cœlestis animæ in mundum transeat harmonia.

s: Ficino argues that the harmonic ratio, not the arithmetic or the geometric, is the right bond for the soul's dealings with bodies: it makes unlike things like and joins unequal things in a shared equality. That is the soul's job both toward itself and toward bodies, and so the world-soul is made by harmonic ratio.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: the harmonic ratio, consisting in the similarity of various things, both makes dissimilar things similar and connects unequal things by a common equality

s: In the Timaeus Compendium (the chapter on how consonance makes one from many) Ficino offers sympathetic resonance as proof, not decoration: sound in a lyre suddenly resonates in a similarly tuned lyre, and a vibrating string passes its vibration to an equally tensioned one. He infers that several voices fused by a ratio echo together into a new form, 'the foundation of a new and miraculous power' coming from heaven by occult ways.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: if from a sounding lyre, sound suddenly resonates in a similarly tuned lyre; and if from a vibrating string, a similar vibration passes immediately to an equally tensioned string

s: Ficino says the ancients traced medicine and music to one source, the Apollonian number, because both are medicine: one cures the soul through the body, the other the body through the soul. He supports this with reports that harmonies miraculously cure diseases of body and mind.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: For both are medicine. But the one cures the soul through the body, while the other cures the body through the soul.
src.qo: Vtraq; enim medicina est. Sed altera quidem ex corpore animam, altera uero ex anima curat corpus.

s: In the same Compendium Ficino maps the seven strings of Terpander's lyre onto the seven planets, lowest string (Hypate) to Saturn in quality or to the Moon in daily speed, and finds deep and sharp sounds mixed in heaven. This is a seven-planet gamut, which sits beside (and complicates) the De vita claim that only four planets sing.

src.l: Plato, Marsilio Ficino (tr., comm.), 1561, Omnia divini Platonis opera (Ficino's Latin, with the De amore commentary on the Symposium)
src.q: we will confer Hypate with Saturn, and the subsequent ones with the subsequent planets in order
src.qo: Præterea si in qualitate motuq; diuturno comparatio fiat, Hypaten cum Saturno, sequentesq; sequentibus planetis ordine conferemus.

s: In a letter of 19 June 1477 to Bernardo Bembo about Marco Aurelio, Ficino describes friendship as two lyres tuned alike by a god (Mercury or Phoebus), so that when one sounds the other resounds. A 'celestial spirit blowing' them together made the friends conspire as one, almost without knowing it. The letter's rubric says love kindled by a divine spirit is returned, and one thinks what the other thinks. The letter's printed rubric states the doctrine outright: 'When love is kindled by the breathing of a divine spirit, when one loves, the other always loves in return; often, when one thinks, the other thinks the same thing.'

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1561, Opera omnia (Basel: Heinrich Petri, 1561)
src.loc: Epistolae IV, to Bernardo Bembo, 19 June 1477; fol. 771 [scan 800]
src.q: tuned the twin lyres of Aurelio and Marsilio so similarly that when one sounds, the other resounds in turn

src.q: with a certain celestial spirit blowing us together, we conspired as one, almost without knowing it

s: In De lumine Ficino defines light as a spiritual, sudden and far-reaching emanation from bodies that costs the bodies nothing. Light is the visible type of how a quality is passed on without being used up, and in the same chapter he sets it as the shadow and splendor of God, the 'Father of lights'.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1561, Opera omnia (Basel: Heinrich Petri, 1561)
src.q: Light is a certain spiritual, sudden, and most wide-reaching emanation from bodies, occurring without any loss to the bodies themselves
src.qo: Lumen est spiritalis quædam & subita, & latissima à corporibus natura eorum sine detrimẽto proprio ema- natio,

s: The Ragusan Niccolò Vito di Gozze (1591) quotes Ficino by name for the claim that musical harmonies miraculously cure diseases of body and soul, and his margin names the source: Ficino's commentary on the Timaeus, chapter 30. Gozze takes it into a civic argument that music can be used to bring the soul's passions to consonance and to govern a state.

src.l: Niccolò Vito di Gozze, 1591, Dello stato delle republiche secondo la mente di Aristotele (Venice, Aldine)
src.q: Whence we can say with Marsilio Ficino:

s: Jacques Gaffarel (1650) uses Ficino to explain sympathy in music: after saying one can make several instruments sound at once without touching them if tuned in the same proportion, he adds 'Something here causes, says M. Ficino,' one lute to be affected by another unless a position or conforming shape is lacking. He turns Ficino's resonance image into an argument for hidden resemblance ('works wonders everywhere') in a book on talismans.

src.l: Jacques Gaffarel, 1650, Curiositez inouyes (Paris)
src.q: Admirable resemblance, which works wonders everywhere! Something here causes, says M. Ficino
src.qo: Admirable ressemblance, qui fait des merueilles par tout!

s: In De vita Book III Ficino argues that the world's body is alive, and that between it and the world's soul there is everywhere a spirit, the same mediating thing that stands between soul and body in us: a nearly bodiless body without which the divine soul could neither be present to the denser body nor give it life. This is the first statement in the Latin tradition we hold that the 'one cosmic spirit' is an engineering necessity: a middle term.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: such a spirit is necessarily required as a medium, so that the divine soul may both be present to the denser body

s: In De vita Book III Ficino says the world lives and breathes, and that a person can draw in its spirit: the human spirit does this because it is by nature 'conformable' to the world's spirit, more so if it is made celestial by purging filth, by orbit-like movement, by light and by Sun-treatment. Attunement is therefore a matter of likeness between two spirits, not of belief or will alone.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: This spirit is properly drawn by a human through their own spirit, which is conformable to the world’s spirit by its very nature.
src.qo: Haurit̃ aut̃ proprie ab homine per suũ spiritũ illi suapte natura conformẽ.

s: In De vita Book III Ficino says 'everywhere' remember that through the mind's affection and study, and through the very quality of the spirit, we are suddenly and easily exposed to the planets that signify that same affection, study and quality. He then assigns moods and pursuits to planets: grief and solitude to Saturn, anger to Mars, joy and music to Venus, eloquence and song to the Sun and Mercury. A state of mind is a planetary exposure; mood is the tuning.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: through the affection and study of the mind, and through the very quality of the spirit, we are most easily and suddenly exposed to the planets

s: In De vita III.21 Ficino says song is 'the most powerful imitator of all things' (of the soul's intentions and affections, of words, gestures, actions and characters) and that it imitates so vehemently that it suddenly provokes both singer and listeners to do the same. When it imitates celestial things it likewise provokes our spirit towards the celestial influx. This is emotional contagion by performance, stated as the mechanism of musical magic; it is separate from the 'aerial animal' passage already in the KB.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: It imitates and acts all these things so vehemently that it suddenly provokes both the singer and the listeners to imitate or do the same.
src.qo: Tamq; ue- hemēter omnia imitat̄ & agit: ut ad eadē imitāda/uel agenda/tū cantantē/tum audiētes ſubito puocet.

s: In De vita I.18 (the book on the health of scholars) Ficino says black bile, when it overflows, weakens the whole body but above all the spirit, which he calls the instrument of the intellect, and then intellect and judgment themselves. The same spirit that Book III will tune to the world is here the physical organ of thought, so a scholar's mood-state is a spirit-state.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De vita libri tres
src.q: it weakens not only the whole body but especially the spirit—which is the instrument of the intellect—and the intellect and judgment themselves.
src.qo: cum corpus totū tum uel maxime spiritum quasi quoddam istrūmētum ingenii ipsumq; igenium & iudiciū labefactat.

s: In Ficino's Latin of Proclus, De sacrificio et magia, the heliotrope turns with the sun and 'prays and sings hymns' to the leader of its order; if one could hear the pulsation it makes in the air, one would hear a sound composed for its king. The ancient priests built their sacred science on such kinship and sympathy, and found 'all things in all things'. Ficino's printed text is the route by which this vibration-as-prayer image reaches Renaissance magic.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino (translator), Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyry, Synesius, Psellus, 1497, Iamblichus De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, with Proclus, Porphyry, Synesius, Psellus (Ficino's translations)
src.q: if anyone could hear the vibration made by it in the air's circuit, they would surely perceive it as a kind of sound composed for its king

s: In Ficino's Latin of Synesius, De insomniis, the 'phantastic spirit' (spiritus phantasticus) is the most common of the senses and the first body of the soul; it sits hidden inside, holds the principle of the living being as from a citadel, and is what dreams act on. This is the pneuma-as-vehicle theory that Ficino folds into his own account of spiritus in De vita.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino (translator), Synesius, Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyry, Priscianus, 1450, Synesius De somniis, Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyrius, Ficino interprete (illuminated manuscript)
src.q: the phantastic spirit itself is the most common of the senses, and the first body of the soul

s: In Ficino's digest of Iamblichus De mysteriis, Porphyry says music moves passions and frenzy; Iamblichus grants it moves the body but denies it causes divine inspiration. Music, he says, is in tune with the soul and enters the spirit with motion and meaning, but the cause of possession is not the man's passion excited by music but the music's congruence with the god, to whom the god is naturally present. Ficino thus records the sharpest ancient statement that music works by correspondence, not by emotion alone.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino (translator), Synesius, Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyry, Priscianus, 1450, Synesius De somniis, Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyrius, Ficino interprete (illuminated manuscript)
src.q: The cause of this inspiration is not so much the passion of the man excited by music, as the very congruence of the music to the god

s: Pomponazzi (De incantationibus, written 1520) cites Ficino by name as 'most copious' on the power of the affections, quoting Platonic Theology XIII.1 that imagination's four effects (appetite, pleasure, fear, pain), when most intense, 'suddenly affect one's own body entirely, never another's'. He uses Ficino's physiology of passion as the base on which to build a wholly natural account of enchantment: the soul moves the body's spirits, and he then asks (pp. 90 ff.) whether such spirits can carry effects outside the body. Ficino's spirit-psychology becomes the engine of a deflationary theory of magic.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, 1556, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.loc: De incant., on Ficino Plat. Theol. XIII.1; p. 57
src.q: All of these, when they are at their most intense, suddenly affect one’s own body entirely—never another's.
src.qo: Hi omnes, quādo uehementissimi sunt, subitò corpus proprium omnino, nūquam alienum, afficiunt.

s: In the chapter on whether a desiring, imagining soul can act at a distance (fascination, cures), Pomponazzi sets out a series of objections ('doubts') to transmitted spirits and vapours as the medium. The fourth: 'spirits and vapors are very weak bodies', so they seem to be 'suddenly destroyed or lose their power when they are sent outside the body'. The same page argues that in fascination the vapours infect with a physical quality, not only a spiritual one. The early-sixteenth-century Italian question was therefore not whether spirit is the medium, but whether it can survive the air between two bodies.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, 1556, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.loc: De incant., fourth doubt on vapours; p. 90
src.q: The fourth doubt is that since spirits and vapors are very weak bodies, they seem to be suddenly destroyed or lose their power when they are sent outside the body.

s: Pomponazzi cites Ficino by name ('in the place cited', Platonic Theology XIV) as the source of a rational cause for love-binding and ligature: if herbs and stones can induce madness or wisdom, 'it is not inconsistent that things might also be found which compel one into love or drive one away from love'. On p. 224 he says that Ficino 'expanded greatly' in Platonic Theology XIV on the view of poets and philosophers that a person can be compelled to love or hate. Ficino's doctrine of attraction by natural kinship becomes, in Pomponazzi, an explanation of why the love-spell appears to work, with no demon needed.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, 1556, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.loc: De incant., on Ficino Plat. Theol. XIV; p. 226
src.q: it is not inconsistent that things might also be found which compel one into love or drive one away from love.

s: Pomponazzi cites Ficino (Platonic Theology IV.1) as a catalogue of the 'almost infinite' occult virtues of things (magnet, diamond, sapphire), and builds on it a thesis that people who know such virtues produce effects that the common folk, 'seeing and not knowing how to trace back to a cause', attribute to God, angels or demons. Ficino's occult properties are kept; the demonic reading of them is removed.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, 1556, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.loc: De incant., second and third suppositions; p. 48
