s: Campanella (De sensu rerum et magia IV.17, 1620) teaches that sounds 'contain a magical power' because they move the mobile spirit of nature to different affects: sharp sounds to anger, soft sounds to love, temple organs to piety. He cites the tarantula cure and Pythagoras calming the insane 'by composing the motions of the spirit with sweet and gentle music'. The mechanism is Ficino's (music acts on spirit, spirit on affect), but spirit is now a corporeal sensing air in the body of every thing, and music cures by regulating its motion. Ficino is not named on the pages read.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia
src.q: Sharp sounds, like trumpets and drums, agitate it to anger; soft and smooth sounds, like lutes and lyres, to love
src.qo: asperi vt tubæ & Tympani, agitant ad iram, molles planique vt fidis & cytharæ ad amorem,

s: Burton (Anatomy of Melancholy, 1621) cites Ficino by name and by place (Platonic Theology XIII.18, margin: 'Imaginatio est tanquam Proteus vel Chamelion corpus proprium & alienum nonnunquam afficiens') to say the imagination, like a Proteus or chameleon, takes all shapes and 'can worke upon others as well as our selves'. He goes on at once to yawning, contagious eye-disease, and witches who fascinate children, explained by one imagination moving 'the spirits of the other'. The chain imagination, spirit, contagion, fascination is stated in English with Ficino as its authority.

src.l: Robert Burton, 1621, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621 first edition)
src.q: is of such force, as Ficinus addes, that it can worke upon others as well as our selves.

s: Daniel Sennert (1619) names Marsilius Ficinus as the author of the 'foundations' of a magic of imagination: in De vita coelitus comparanda, he says, Ficino teaches that by applying our spirit to the spirit of the world, heavenly goods pass into our soul and body. Sennert hedges whether Ficino approved it or only narrated it (citing the preface), tolerates the astral part, and rejects the demonic part (ch. 4). He traces the line through Avicenna and the Platonists to Paracelsus and Crollius.

src.l: Daniel Sennert, 1619, De chymicorum cum Aristotelicis et Galenicis consensu
src.q: through a certain application of our spirit to the spirit of the world, heavenly goods are transferred to our soul and body through physical art and affection
src.qo: in quo docet, ex applicatione quadam spiritus nostri ad spiritū mundi per artem physicam affectumque facta traijci ad animam corpusq; nostrum bona cælestia.

s: Sennert (1619, ch. XIV 'De viribus imaginationis') reports as 'dreams' two claims he refutes: Paracelsus that imaginations rise to the heavens and compel the stars, and Crollius (preface to the Admonitions) that 'the imagination is a magnet attracting, beyond a thousand miles, whatever it wishes'. Sennert's own answer: seeing and hearing do not act on another, so neither does imagination. This is the magnet metaphor for imagination fixed in print by 1619, before van Helmont's weapon-salve tract and a century before Mesmer.

src.l: Daniel Sennert, 1619, De chymicorum cum Aristotelicis et Galenicis consensu
src.q: the imagination is a magnet attracting, beyond a thousand miles, whatever it wishes; and that it works miracles.
src.qo: Imaginationem esse magnetem at- trahentem ultra mille milliaria, quicquid vult; miracula operari.

s: Guazzo's Compendium maleficarum (1608) opens Book I, 'On the power and nature of the imagination', by listing who has written on it: Pico, Marsilius Ficinus 'in book 13 of his Platonic Theology', Tostatus, Medina, Vairus on fascination. Ficino is the standard Platonic authority in the Counter-Reformation witch-treatise genre for imagination changing a body.

src.l: Francesco Maria Guazzo, 1608, Compendium maleficarum
src.q: Marsilius Ficinus in book 13 of his Platonic Theology
src.qo: Marsilius Ficinus lib. 13. de Theolog. Platonica.

s: Marci of Kronland (Philosophia vetus restituta, 1662; section 'On the attraction of celestial powers') says wombs on earth become fertile so that by imagination or celestial irradiation they are impregnated with the powers of a planet, and refers the reader to Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda for the full account. The section heading also lists 'magnetism' (its immediate subject is the spirit) and the archeus conceiving ideas through imagination: Ficino's celestial attraction is merged with Helmontian archeus and magnetic language.

src.l: Jan Marek Marci z Kronlandu, 1662, Philosophia vetus restituta
src.q: by imagination or celestial irradiation, they are impregnated with the powers of this or that planet. About which Marsilius Ficinus speaks at length in his book

s: Jacques Gohory (De usu et mysteriis notarum, Paris 1550), on the Ars Notoria's planetary prayers for instant learning, cites Ficino by name: in his letters Ficino 'finally interprets' what he wrote in De vita on drawing life from heaven through sacrifices, images and rings as 'not so much the precepts of one who believes or hopes, but rather the prayers of one who wishes'. Gohory is thus a witness that by 1550 readers took Ficino's own letters to disown a literal image-magic.

src.l: Jacques Gohory, 1550, De usu et mysteriis notarum liber
src.q: these are not so much the precepts of one who believes or hopes, but rather the prayers of one who wishes.
src.qo: non tam sunt hæc præcepta credentis vel sperantis, quàm optantis vota.

s: A scholium on Hermes in the Theatrum chemicum (1613, vol. 1, 'De lapidis physici decreto') makes spirit the lawful mediator that joins heaven (like soul) to earth (like body), and quotes Ficino, De vita coelitus comparanda III.3, on that spirit: 'a most thin body, and not a body, and as if already a soul' and 'as if not a soul, and as if already a body'. Ficino's medical spiritus becomes the alchemists' middle term between celestial and terrestrial.

src.l: various, 1613, Theatrum chemicum, vol. 1
src.q: is a most thin body, and not a body, and as if already a soul; likewise, as if not a soul, and as if already a body
src.qo: Spiritus iste, inquit, est corpus tenuissimum, & non corpus, & quasi jam anima: item quasi non anima, & quasi jam corpus.

s: In the 1567 Paris Paracelsus compendium, the editor's preface (Leo Suavius, i.e. Jacques Gohory) quotes Ficino by name: 'There exists also in metals and stones a spirit, but it lies hidden, oppressed by the mass of matter', which when rightly separated can generate its like (the Arabs' elixir). Paracelsian editors thus read Ficino's spiritus into mineral alchemy. The same book's scholia also argue against Ficino (p. 294 [scan 310], margin 'Contra Ficinum de lapidibus et metallis': he ranks metal above stone), so Ficino is both source and sparring partner.

src.l: Paracelsus, Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory), 1567, Theophrasti Paracelsi philosophiae et medicinae compendium, with Suavius' scholia
src.q: There exists also in metals and stones a spirit, but it lies hidden, oppressed by the mass of matter
src.qo: Inest etiam metallis spiritus & lapidibus sed latet materiæ mole oppressus:

s: Thomas Taylor (1818) says Proclus's dissertation on the magic of the ancients survives only in Latin, because Ficino published it after his excerpts from Proclus on the First Alcibiades. Taylor then reprints it in English. Its core is Ficino's route for sympathy: the ancient priests saw an 'alliance and sympathy in natural things', and built a sacred science from it; 'similitude itself' binds things in union and consent. The English reception of Proclus on sympathetic magic therefore runs through Ficino's Latin, and Taylor says so.

src.l: Thomas Taylor (tr.), Iamblichus, 1818, Iamblichus' Life of Pythagoras
src.q: this Dissertation on Magic, which is only extant in Latin, was published by Ficinus the translator

src.l: Thomas Taylor (tr.), Iamblichus, 1818, Iamblichus' Life of Pythagoras
src.q: similitude itself is a sufficient cause of binding things together in union and consent.

s: In his dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic mysteries, Thomas Taylor ends his argument on the soul after death by adopting Ficino's summary of the ancient theologians. He calls Ficino's words 'as express to our purpose as possible' and quotes a long passage. Taylor takes Ficino as a witness to the ancient theology, not only as translator.

src.l: Thomas Taylor, 1891, The Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries
src.q: we may safely conclude with Ficinus, whose words are as express to our purpose as possible.

s: In the preface to his 1793 Plato, Thomas Taylor writes that while translating he 'frequently found a necessity of differing from Ficinus'. Ficino's Latin Plato is thus the baseline text that Taylor corrects, using the manuscript Proclus commentary. English Platonism before Jowett starts from Ficino's Latin and departs from it.

src.l: Plato, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1793, The Cratylus, Phaedo, Parmenides, and Timaeus of Plato
src.q: though in the courſe of the tranſlations I frequently found a neceſſity of differing from Ficinus

s: Ralph Cudworth (1678) cites Ficino's commentary on Plotinus (Enn. I.2) by name as the authority for the Platonic Trinity's joint creation: 'Hi Tres uno quodam consensu omnia producunt'. He renders it 'These Three with one common consent produce all things'. Cudworth takes his Plotinus through Ficino and reads Ficino's word consensus as a harmony of the divine principles.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The True Intellectual System of the Universe
src.q: Ficinus more than once declares the Tenour thereof, Hi Tres uno quodam consensu omnia producunt, These Three with one common consent produce all things
src.qo: Hi Tres uno quodam consensu omnia producunt

s: Cudworth (1678) names Ficinus and Scutellius as the Latin translators of Iamblichus (De mysteriis) and says Casaubon was 'abused by those Translators': a word Ficino's Latin printed as 'Salaminiaca' is not in the Greek. Seventeenth-century English Platonists used Ficino's Iamblichus as the standard text and already checked it against the Greek.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The True Intellectual System of the Universe
src.q: the Latin Translations of Iamblichus made by Ficinus and Scutellius.

s: In 1600 William Gilbert, founding the science of magnetism, lists Marsilio Ficino among the philosophers who sought the cause of the magnet's motion in the heavens, and dismisses his view as 'a most vain dream'. By Gilbert's report Ficino had the magnet follow the Arctic pole, iron the magnet, and amber the chaff: a celestial chain of sympathetic attractions (De vita III). Gilbert's own move is to put the magnetic power in the Earth itself, so that Ficino's cosmic spirit-and-star sympathy is where 'magnetism' is first separated out as a terrestrial, measurable force.

src.l: William Gilbert, 1600, De Magnete, Magneticisque Corporibus, et de Magno Magnete Tellure
src.q: Marsilio Ficino wants the magnet to follow its Arctic pole, and iron the magnet, and amber the chaff
src.qo: Marsilius Ficinus polum suum Arcticum sequi vult magnetem, ferrum verò magnetem, succinum paleas; hoc verò polùs-fortassis Antarcticum, vanissimo infomnio.

s: Mersenne accused Ficino of raising the power of music to the stars, so that songs could draw down higher influences, and denied he was a Catholic for it. Fludd's defender (the Summum Bonum, c. 1629, in German) reports the charge and Ficino's answer in the Apologia: he reports Plotinus's views, rejects demon-cult magic, and defends 'natural magic' that unites the earthly with the heavenly. This is the seventeenth-century fault line on which Ficino's musical spirit-theory was argued: harmony as a natural channel versus harmony as magic.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1629, Das hoechste Gut (Summum Bonum), German edition
src.q: He accuses Marsilio Ficino, a Catholic and very learned man, of elevating the power of music to the stars, such that higher influences might be attracted through songs.
src.qo: Er wirft dem Marsilius Fiscinus, einem katholischen und sehr gebildeten Mann, vor, dass er die Macht der Musik zu den Sternen erhebe, so dass durch Lieder höhere Einflüsse angezogen würden.

s: Kircher (Magnes, 1641, III.viii 'Magnetismus musicae') holds that music's power over the passions does not act on the immortal soul directly but on the spirit, 'a most subtle and highly mobile vapor of the blood', which harmonically excited air sets 'rippling' (crispatur); faster harmonic motions rarefy and dilate it, and joy follows. He proves it with a wet finger round a water-glass: the tone ripples the water. Mesmer's 1779 Mémoire, founding text of animal magnetism, reprints Kircher's sentence verbatim in a footnote and concludes that these faculties of music 'were conflated with magnetism'.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1641, Magnes sive de arte magnetica
src.q: is easily stirred by air that has been harmonically excited

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, 1779, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
src.q: ces deux facultés se confondoient avec le magnétisme

s: Robert Fludd's Macrocosm and Microcosm (1617-18), in the chapter 'Of the operation of Music in soul and body', sets Ficino beside Plato in a classification diagram titled as the effects of musical harmony 'according to Plato and Marsilio Ficino'. Plato's branch (Republic III) is education and civic mildness. Ficino's branch is physical: music penetrates the motion of subtle air, its aerial nature moves the body, it stirs 'the spirits of purified air, the aerial knot of the soul and body', affects feeling, drives meaning into the mind, and imbues spirit and matter alike with a conformable quality of wonder and pleasure, seizing the whole person at once. A 17th-century Rosicrucian physician thus files Ficino's music-and-spirit doctrine as a standard medical-physical theory, summarized from De vita III in a diagram.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi majoris scilicet et minoris metaphysica, physica atque technica historia (BnF copy, English translation)
src.loc: Tract. II, Part II, Book I, ch. 3; p. 166 [scan 160]
src.q: It stirs the spirits of purified air, the aerial knot of the soul and body.
src.qo: Purificatum aërem concitat spiritus, aëreumq; animi & corporis nodum.

s: Johann Virdung's astrological-medical textbook (Venice 1584) reprints Ficino's De vita III music chapter as a numbered section under the running head 'De vita coeli. Comp.' ('On obtaining life from the heavens. Compendium'). The paragraph argues that a song full of spirit and meaning, tuned to a star, passes that star's power into the singer and from him into the nearest listener, and that a song so conceived is 'another spirit' made solar and acting on you and your neighbour; it then reasons that if a vapor and spirit sent out through the eyes can fascinate, how much more can a spirit flowing from imagination and heart together. So the spirit-music-fascination doctrine reached late-16th-century physicians verbatim, bound into a clinical manual, with no attribution on this page.

src.l: Johann Virdung von Hasfurt, 1584, De cognoscendis et medendis morbis ex corporum coelestium positione libri IIII
src.loc: On obtaining life from the heavens, Compendium; p. 460
src.q: For if a vapor and a certain spirit emitted through the rays of the eyes (or otherwise) can sometimes fascinate, infect, or otherwise affect a neighbor
src.qo: Si enim vapor, & ſpiritus quidam aliquando per radios ocu- lorum, vel aliter foras emiſſus faſcinare, inficere, aliterque afficere pro- ximū poteſt, multo magis id valet ſpiritus ab imaginatione, cordeque ſimul vberior profluens, & feruentior, motuq; valentior, vt nō omni

s: Gioseffo Zarlino (Le Istitutioni harmoniche, 1558) cites 'the Platonic Philosopher Marsilio Ficino' in the Compendium of the Timaeus as his authority that Pythagoras forbade passing beyond the quadruple (4:1) because beyond it he heard no harmony. Then Zarlino checks the arithmetic and corrects Ficino: taken literally his words give the quintuple between 5 and 4, which is false, so the text must be corrupt (unity for 4) or must mean the added 5:4 produces 5:1 and 5:3. Practising musicians in Venice thus treated Ficino's Timaeus Compendium as a live number authority for musica mundana, and audited it rather than reverenced it.

src.l: Gioseffo Zarlino, 1558, Le Istitutioni harmoniche
src.q: if Ficino's words were taken literally, they would be misunderstood; for the Quintuple is not found between 5 and 4, but rather between 5 and 1

s: Francesco Patrizi (Nova de universis philosophia, 1593) opens his discussion of whether the stars act by laying out Plotinus's view: things in the universe serve one another and act and suffer on one another from the common 'symphonia' (concordant resonance) and sympathy of the world's parts, and not just anything from just anything. He says Ficino expounded Plotinus's thoughts more broadly and more eloquently, and that Pico imitated both but tried to overturn astrology from its roots. Patrizi then complains that these three confined the question to men and widens it to whether stars act on all bodies (metals, stones, plants, animals), arguing from light as the vehicle that carried the seeds of things through space. For him Ficino is the conduit of Plotinian sympathy, whose question he enlarges into a physics of light.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia
src.q: Ficinus, in truth, expounded the thoughts of Plotinus more broadly and pursued them more eloquently.
src.qo: Ficinus vero, Plotini sensa latius exposuit, & facundius est persecutus.

s: Burton closes the cure of melancholy by passing on Ficino's letter to Canisianus and friends: 'live merrily' (vivite laeti), repeated and sworn to, for 'this I enjoin you not as a Divine alone but as a Physician', since without mirth, 'the life and Quintessence of all Physicke', all medicines are 'dull, dead and of no force'. Burton's marginal note says Ficino 'was both Sacerdos & Medicus'. Ficino's cheerfulness, which in De vita was a matter of spirit and planets, reaches the English reader of 1621 as a priest-physician's plain prescription of good company and merriment.

src.l: Robert Burton, 1621, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621 first edition)
src.q: Againe and againe, I request you to be merry;
src.qo: Iterum precor & obtestor vivite læti

s: Burton (1621) lists 'Marsilius Ficinus de vit. caelit. compar. cap. 13. 15. 18. 21.' among the authorities who say that cures by spells, characters, images, amulets, ligatures and philtres are real, placing him with Paracelsus, Agrippa, Bodin and Goclenius, against the camp (Hippocrates, Avicenna, Pomponazzi of Padua) that 'referre all to naturall causes and humors'. So the 17th-century medical reader met the De vita as a license for image-magic cures, even though Ficino's own letters (and Pomponazzi, who took his spirit-physiology) pull the other way. Burton cites chapters, not sentences, which marks the work as a known reference rather than a text under discussion.

src.l: Robert Burton, 1621, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621 first edition)
src.q: Marsilius Ficinus de vit. cælit. compar. cap. 13. 15. 18. 21.

s: In De vinculis / De magia (Latin Works III), Bruno's 'second bond' is the one from voice and song: it 'arises from the correspondence of numbers to numbers, measure to measure, and beat to beat', which gives rhythms and songs 'said to possess the greatest power'. People differ in what binds them (tragic harmony for some, comic for others, a king who preferred a horse's neigh). This is Ficino's matching principle turned into an operator's technique: Ficino's song works because it is an air-animal tuned to the listener's spirit, Bruno's because one can be bound by finding the measure that answers theirs. Bruno does not name Ficino on this page, and a search of the book for Ficino found nothing.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, F. Tocco & H. Vitelli (eds.), 1879, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.loc: De magia, 'Secundum vinculum ex voce et cantu'; p. 443 [scan 511]
src.q: arises from the correspondence of numbers to numbers, measure to measure, and beat to beat; from this come those rhythms and songs which are said to possess the greatest power
src.qo: mensurae ad mensuram, momenti ad momentum ; unde illi rhythmi atque cantus qui maximam habere efficaciam perhibentur.

s: Bruno (De vinculis in genere, Art. XVI) says the more skilful snarer (irretitor) opens a path to the other bonds through what the person to be bound loves and hates, 'for indeed, Love is the bond of bonds'. Ficino's De amore had made love the knot of the world and magic the attraction of kin by kin; Bruno keeps the cosmic sentence and uses it as a rule of practice, so that love becomes the lever by which one mind captures another. The page does not name Ficino.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, F. Tocco & H. Vitelli (eds.), 1879, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.q: Love is the bond of bonds.
src.qo: vinculum quippe vinculorum amor est.

s: The Theosophical Path (1913) strings together passages on the soul's pre-existence from Emerson and, in a footnote, credits one of them to Emerson's 1830 journal: 'The soul is an emanation of the Divinity, a part of the soul of the world, a ray from the source of light.' That is Neoplatonic emanation language, with the world-soul named, in the young Emerson's own register; the paragraph itself prints no author, so the attribution rests on the article's footnote 24 (E. W. Emerson, Journals, 1901, II, p. 341).

src.l: Katherine Tingley (ed.), 1913, The Theosophical Path, Vol. 4 (January-June 1913)
src.q: The soul is an emanation of the Divinity, a part of the soul of the world, a ray from the source of light.

s: The same Theosophical Path article quotes Emerson (Representative Men) rendering Plato's Meno: 'all things in nature being linked and related, and the soul having heretofore known all'. Its footnote 23 says the passage is based on Sydenham's translation as printed in Thomas Taylor's Works of Plato (1804), vol. V. So the doctrine that nature is bound by kinship (the ground of sympathy) reached Emerson through Taylor's English Plato, which is the same Taylor who published Proclus on sympathetic magic from Ficino's Latin.

src.l: Katherine Tingley (ed.), 1913, The Theosophical Path, Vol. 4 (January-June 1913)
src.q: all things in nature being linked and related, and the soul having heretofore known all

s: In The Secret Doctrine of the Rosicrucians, Atkinson (the New Thought author of Thought Vibration) says Emerson's essay 'The Over-Soul' shows he knew 'Cosmic Consciousness', and prints Emerson's list of the great enthusiasts: 'The trances of Socrates; the Union of Plotinus; the vision of Porphyry; the conversion of Paul'. A New Thought writer therefore passes the Over-Soul on to his readers with Plotinus named in the very passage.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson (as Magus Incognito), 1918, The Secret Doctrine of the Rosicrucians
src.q: The trances of Socrates; the 'Union' of Plotinus; the vision of Porphyry; the conversion of Paul

s: On the next page Atkinson's Rosicrucian book continues the Emerson quotation: 'within man is the soul of the whole; the wise silence; the universal beauty to which every part and particle is equally related; the eternal One'. Here the Platonist world-soul and its relation of every part to the whole (the ground of sympathy) are handed to a New Thought readership. The passage is not framed as vibration; vibration is Atkinson's own addition in his other books.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson (as Magus Incognito), 1918, The Secret Doctrine of the Rosicrucians
src.q: within man is the soul of the whole; the wise silence; the universal beauty to which every part and particle is equally related; the eternal One

s: Colquhoun's History of Magic, Witchcraft, and Animal Magnetism (1851) states the handover from the old world-soul to the magnetists' ether outright: the ancients' 'universal aether, or anima mundi' (cited from Cicero and Apuleius, never Ficino) was 'entertained, in modern times, by Descartes, Newton, Mesmer', and 'a similar principle has been adopted by several of the most eminent Magnetists'. He adds that modern investigation does not reject the idea.

src.l: John Campbell Colquhoun, 1851, An History of Magic, Witchcraft, and Animal Magnetism, Vol. 1
src.q: This same hypothesis of an universal æther pervading all space, was, under certain modifications, entertained, in modern times, by DESCARTES, NEWTON, MESMER, and other philosophers

s: Dresser (The Power of Silence, 1895) explains thought-transfer by analogy with sound: thought is a wave in 'the finest form of ether', 'setting up vibrations in the recipient corresponding to those in the sender', and those 'open to it through sympathy' receive it. This is vibration plus sympathy in a mind sense in the 1890s New Thought, and it rests on the ether of the mesmerists, not on the world-soul. The page names no Platonist, Ficino or Mesmer.

src.l: Horatio W. Dresser, 1895, The Power of Silence
src.q: setting up vibrations in the recipient corresponding to those in the sender

s: Bloomfield-Moore's Keely and His Discoveries (1893) sets 'sympathetical' against 'mechanical' force, and says Keely deals 'entirely with VIBRATORY SYMPATHETIC and POLAR flows'. His engine runs while 'the transmitter is in sympathy with the sympathetic current', started by a twanged string or tuning-fork. This is sympathy turned into engineering: Ficino's struck lyre answering another, now a motor. No Ficino, Plotinus, Paracelsus or Mesmer appears on the page, though the next lines invoke Pythagoras.

src.l: Clara Sophia Jessup Bloomfield-Moore, 1893, Keely and His Discoveries
src.q: Something like this is the difference between sympathetical and mechanical force.

s: The Kybalion (1908) tells its readers that science's vibrations 'are manifestations of some form of vibratory energy, a fact which the Hermetists have held and taught for ages past', and that the ether is 'Matter at a higher degree of vibration'. This is the reverse handover: New Thought projects its own vibration vocabulary back onto Hermes, and names no Ficino, Plotinus or Renaissance source for it.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion
src.q: these too are manifestations of some form of vibratory energy, a fact which the Hermetists have held and taught for ages past

s: Lomas & Xue define harmony as the process of integrating diverse parts into a whole such that both the parts and the whole are mutually strengthened — a theory of fitness of parts with each other and within a whole.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Lomas & Xue's central conclusion: harmony involves the integration of diversity into a greater whole and is not pure agreement or sameness (citing Confucius' he vs tong and Shi Bo).

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: RP.7: resonance, based on shared similarities, is the counterpart to harmony; harmony can emerge from natural resonances (via the Huainanzi's sympathetic lute strings and kan-ying).

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: RP.20: dissonance can be resolved into harmony and strengthen the whole, whereas disharmony is a mis-fitting that detracts from the whole.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: RP.69: harmony in the brain lies in a dynamic balance of synchronization and desynchronization; too much of either is unhealthy.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: RP.72–73: deep networks optimise harmony under the name 'goodness-of-fit', so harmony measures could serve as AI objective functions.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: RP.75: there is a danger in mistaking measures of harmony for the concept of harmony, particularly in computational optimisation.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Following Chenyang Li's reading of the Great Learning, Lomas & Xue frame harmony at nested levels — individual, interpersonal, societal, natural world — with harmony possible within and between levels.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Lomas & Xue propose that the harmonization of humankind and nature is a concise definition of sustainable design (RP.98).

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Lomas et al. define sympathetic resonance as external forced oscillations aligned to a system's natural oscillations, producing amplification and synchronization; synchronization and entrainment are treated as subsets of resonance.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Albert Lin, Suzanne Dikker, Deborah Forster, Maria Luce Lupetti, Gijs Huisman, Julika Habekost, Caiseal Beardow, Pankaj Pandey, Nashra Ahmad, Krishna Miyapuram, Tim Mullen, Patrick Cooper, Willem van der Maden, Emily S. Cross, 2022, Resonance as a Design Strategy for AI and Social Robots
src.loc: Box 2 and 'Resonance as a Physical Mechanism'

s: Lomas et al. conclude that measuring resonance in interactions could give AI–human interaction a meaningful 'objective function' for optimisation.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Albert Lin, Suzanne Dikker, Deborah Forster, Maria Luce Lupetti, Gijs Huisman, Julika Habekost, Caiseal Beardow, Pankaj Pandey, Nashra Ahmad, Krishna Miyapuram, Tim Mullen, Patrick Cooper, Willem van der Maden, Emily S. Cross, 2022, Resonance as a Design Strategy for AI and Social Robots

s: Lomas et al. flag that robots able to build resonant rapport could more effectively persuade or manipulate people.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Albert Lin, Suzanne Dikker, Deborah Forster, Maria Luce Lupetti, Gijs Huisman, Julika Habekost, Caiseal Beardow, Pankaj Pandey, Nashra Ahmad, Krishna Miyapuram, Tim Mullen, Patrick Cooper, Willem van der Maden, Emily S. Cross, 2022, Resonance as a Design Strategy for AI and Social Robots

s: Lomas & Xue (2025): the harmony of opposites is found not by choosing the middle ground between extremes but by supporting the strength of both parts.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2025, The Harmony of Opposites in Design and Philosophy

s: Lomas & Xue (2025) compile a cross-cultural table of opposites by domain (metaphysical, physical, biological, perceptual, emotional, cognitive, conceptual, social, economic, designerly), drawing on the Pythagorean table, Heraclitus, the Dao De Jing and Hekkert's UMA.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2025, The Harmony of Opposites in Design and Philosophy

s: Plomp & Levelt's listeners judged simple-tone intervals consonant once the frequency difference exceeded the critical bandwidth, and judged the most dissonant intervals to be those with a difference of about a quarter of the critical bandwidth; they used this to explain some properties of consonant intervals of complex tones.

src.l: R. Plomp, W. J. M. Levelt, 1965, Tonal Consonance and Critical Bandwidth

s: Helmholtz (in the English edition on Source Library) explained dissonance as the roughness into which rapid beats merge, and consonance as a continuous, undisturbed sensation of tone.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.q: Consonance is a continuous sensation of tone; dissonance is an intermittent one.

s: Across more than 250 listeners, only the preference for harmonic spectra was consistently correlated with preference for consonant over dissonant chords; the preference for beat-free sounds was not. Harmonicity preference, not consonance preference itself, was correlated with years of playing an instrument.

src.l: Josh H. McDermott, Andriana J. Lehr, Andrew J. Oxenham, 2010, Individual Differences Reveal the Basis of Consonance

s: The Tsimane' of Bolivia, with minimal exposure to Western music, rated consonant and dissonant chords and vocal harmonies as equally pleasant, yet showed an aversion to acoustic roughness like that of Western listeners; Bolivian city- and town-dwellers preferred consonance, but less than US residents. The authors presume that variation in consonance preference is determined by exposure to musical harmony.

src.l: Josh H. McDermott, Alan F. Schultz, Eduardo A. Undurraga, Ricardo A. Godoy, 2016, Indifference to dissonance in native Amazonians reveals cultural variation in music perception
J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Both Tsimane' and US listeners were more likely to mistake note combinations related by simple integer ratios for a single sound (fusion), with the octave, fifth and fourth fusing most. Fusion did not predict aesthetic judgments in Westerners, and the Tsimane' were indifferent to consonance, so fusion is widespread while liking is culture-dependent.

src.l: Malinda J. McPherson, et al., 2020, Perceptual fusion of musical notes by native Amazonians suggests universal representations of musical intervals
J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Sethares shows that tuning and timbre interact: for a given spectrum one computes a dissonance curve whose minima define a matched scale. For harmonic timbres the minima fall near simple ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, 5:3); he also derives scales for stretched, compressed and FM timbres and timbres for equal-tempered scales.

src.l: William A. Sethares, 1993, Relating Tuning and Timbre

s: Bowling & Purves argue that the mathematical-ratio and physical-interference accounts of consonance are at odds with accumulated evidence, and that consonance preference plausibly derives from the similarity of a tone combination's spectrum to human vocalization.

src.l: Daniel L. Bowling, Dale Purves, 2015, A biological rationale for musical consonance

s: In an online experiment (N = 410) rating 15 piano chords, the mildly dissonant minor ninth, major ninth and minor seventh were rated highest for preference, regardless of musical sophistication; perceived dissonance correlated strongly with tension.

src.l: Imre Lahdelma, Tuomas Eerola, 2016, Mild Dissonance Preferred Over Consonance in Single Chord Perception
J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Weinreich's theory and measurements show that piano strings of one note are coupled through the bridge into a single dynamical system, so the rate of energy transmission to the bridge (beats and 'aftersound') depends on bridge admittance and on how finely the unisons are tuned; a good tuner can use fine unison tuning to make the aftersound more uniform.

src.l: Gabriel Weinreich, 1977, Coupled piano strings

s: Large and colleagues present a dynamical-systems analysis of mode-locked neural oscillation that predicts cross-cultural invariances in music perception, and show that with short- and long-term learning it explains perception of Hindustani ragas by Indian and by Western listeners.

src.l: Edward W. Large, Ji Chul Kim, Nicole K. Flaig, Jamshed J. Bharucha, Carol Lynne Krumhansl, 2016, A Neurodynamic Account of Musical Tonality

s: In tonal music theory, harmony is a temporal grammar: dissonance creates tension that implies a direction, and resolution is defined relative to a tonal center; a chord is harmonious for where the piece is going.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Harrison & Pearce question the consensus that simultaneous consonance is primarily driven by harmonicity, and conclude from a review, reanalysis of four behavioural datasets (over 500 participants) and corpus modelling (over 100,000 compositions) that it is a composite of interference, periodicity/harmonicity and cultural familiarity.

src.l: Peter M. C. Harrison, Marcus T. Pearce, 2020, Simultaneous consonance in music perception and composition

s: Terhardt argued that psychoacoustic consonance merely corresponds to the absence of roughness and is only slightly and indirectly correlated with musical intervals; he proposed that virtual pitch, not roughness, provides the basis of the sense of musical intervals.

src.l: Ernst Terhardt, 1974, Pitch, consonance, and harmony

s: Euler's Tentamen (1739) rates the pleasantness of a consonance by a 'degree of sweetness' computed from the prime factors of its ratio: s - n + 1, where s is the sum of the simple factors and n their number; the smaller the number, the sweeter or easier to perceive the consonance.

src.l: Leonhard Euler, 1739, Tentamen novae theoriae musicae
src.q: the smaller this number is found to be, the sweeter or easier to perceive the consonance will be.
src.qo: eo erit consonantia suavior seu perceptu facilior.

s: Joseph Sauveur is credited with the 1701 discovery of vibration nodes in strings (Chladni, as cited in Tyndall's Sound); that he also introduced the terms for nodes and harmonics and the word 'acoustique' is the standard account but is not checked here.

src.l: John Tyndall, 1867 (SL copy cited as 1969 reprint), Sound
src.q: with the 1701 discovery of vibration nodes corresponding to

src.l: Joseph Sauveur, 1701, Systeme general des intervalles des sons / Mem. Acad. Roy. Sci.

s: In his Traité (1722), Rameau treats the 'fundamental bass' as the part that regulates the progression of harmony, which he says must move by consonant intervals (third, fourth, fifth, sixth), preferring the smallest.

src.l: Jean-Philippe Rameau, 1722, Traite de l'harmonie reduite a ses principes naturels
src.loc: Book III, Chap. II, printed p. 185 (scan p. 223)
src.q: the bass, which we call fundamental, and which must proceed in this case by consonant intervals. These are those of the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth.
src.qo: & qui doit proceder en ce cas, par des Intervales consonans, qui sont ceux de la Tierce, de la Quarte, de la Quinte, & de la Sixte ;

s: Krumhansl & Kessler's probe-tone method, where listeners rate how well each of the 12 tones follows a key context, gives stable tonal-hierarchy profiles for major and minor keys, and their intercorrelation maps keys onto a four-dimensional space located on a torus that encodes the circle of fifths and parallel and relative relations.

src.l: Carol L. Krumhansl, Edward J. Kessler, 1982, Tracing the dynamic changes in perceived tonal organization in a spatial representation of musical keys

s: Huron's theory of expectation proposes that emotions evoked by expectation involve five response systems: reaction, tension, prediction, imagination and appraisal (ITPRA).

src.l: David Huron, 2006, Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation

s: Lerdahl & Krumhansl test a four-component model of tonal tension (prolongational structure, pitch space, surface tension, attraction) against listeners' continuous tension ratings, for Classical and chromatic tonal music.

src.l: Fred Lerdahl, Carol L. Krumhansl, 2007, Modeling Tonal Tension

s: Evidence against a universal, innate preference for consonance: the Tsimane' rated consonant and dissonant chords as equally pleasant, while still disliking roughness; and in Westerners, fusion (the main harmonic-series prediction) did not predict interval preference.

src.l: Josh H. McDermott, Alan F. Schultz, Eduardo A. Undurraga, Ricardo A. Godoy, 2016, Indifference to dissonance in native Amazonians reveals cultural variation in music perception
Malinda J. McPherson, et al., 2020, Perceptual fusion of musical notes by native Amazonians suggests universal representations of musical intervals

s: Roughness theory is insufficient: Terhardt argued consonance as roughness-absence is only slightly correlated with musical intervals, and Harrison & Pearce found consonance depends on harmonicity and cultural familiarity as well as interference. Plomp-Levelt curves describe roughness, not the whole of consonance.

src.l: Ernst Terhardt, 1974, Pitch, consonance, and harmony
Peter M. C. Harrison, Marcus T. Pearce, 2020, Simultaneous consonance in music perception and composition

s: The assumption that consonant means more pleasant is not safe: in a 410-listener online study the mildly dissonant minor ninth, major ninth and minor seventh were preferred over consonant chords, regardless of musical sophistication.

src.l: Imre Lahdelma, Tuomas Eerola, 2016, Mild Dissonance Preferred Over Consonance in Single Chord Perception

s: Single-cause stories of consonance (harmonicity, roughness, vocal similarity) are each contested by the others: Bowling-Purves dismiss ratio and interference accounts, McDermott 2010 favours harmonicity over beating, Harrison-Pearce call it a composite of interference, harmonicity and familiarity. A writer should not present any single mechanism as established.

src.l: Peter M. C. Harrison, Marcus T. Pearce, 2020, Simultaneous consonance in music perception and composition
Daniel L. Bowling, Dale Purves, 2015, A biological rationale for musical consonance

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ music epistle builds the oud from proportions: four strings of 64, 48, 36 and 27 silk strands, each 4/3 the thickness of the next, frets at a quarter and at ninths of the string, and tuning by ear until two notes sound as one; it concludes that every string and fret stands in a ratio to the others.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.loc: music epistle (Fourth Epistle in this edition), chapter on instruments; scan 101, printed p. 98
src.q: the bamm is sixty-four strands of silk, the mathlath is forty-eight strands, the mathna is thirty-six strands, and the zir is twenty-seven strands.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.q: In sum, there is no string or fret among these strings and frets that does not have a proportional relationship to the others. However, some of these proportions are excellent and noble, while others are less so.
src.qo: وبالجملة ما من وتر ولا دستان من هذه الاوتار والدساتين الا ولنغمتها نسبة بعضها الى بعض ولكن منهما ماهى فاضلة شريفة ومنها دون ذلك

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ argue that the celestial spheres, though a fifth essence, touch, rub and resonate like iron and copper, with proportional and harmonious tones, and that the musician's melodies remind souls in the world of generation and corruption of the joy of the spheres, as the spheres' tones remind their souls of the world of spirits above.

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.q: They touch one another, collide, rub against each other, and resonate just as iron and copper resonate. Their tones are proportional and harmonious, and their melodies are balanced, as we have shown in the example of the tones of lute strings and their proportions.
src.qo: وانها يماس بعضها بعضا وتصطك وتحتك وتطن كما يطن الحديد والنحاس وتكون نغماتها متناسبات مؤتلفات والحانها موزونات كما بينا مثالها فى نغمات اوتار العيدان ومناسباتها

src.l: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, 1887, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), part 1
src.q: the tones of the movements of the musician remind the partial souls in the world of generation and corruption of the joy of the world of the spheres
src.qo: بان نغمات حركات الموسيقار تذكر النفوس الجزئية التى فى عالم الكون والفساد سرور عالم الافلاك

s: Helmholtz (Sensations of Tone, Part III) argues that because a melodic step of a fifth is marked by a shared partial tone, the diatonic scale lets sensation measure intervals directly, giving 'a definiteness and certainty in the measurement of intervals for our sensation, such as might be looked for in vain in the system of colours, otherwise so similar'.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1863, On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music
src.q: such as might be looked for in vain in the system of colours, otherwise so similar

s: Helmholtz (Sensations of Tone, ch. XIV), citing Aristotle's Problems XIX.29 that melodies resemble feelings because they are motions, argues that the motion of tone can imitate expression better than any corporeal motion, and that music represents not feelings or situations 'but only frames of mind'.

src.l: Hermann von Helmholtz, Alexander J. Ellis (tr.), 1885, On the Sensations of Tone (Ellis 2nd English ed.)
src.q: music does not represent feelings and situations, but only frames of mind

s: Tononi, Sporns & Edelman define neural complexity as high only when a system is both functionally segregated (differentiated parts) and integrated; it is low for fully independent and for fully synchronized systems.

src.l: Giulio Tononi, Olaf Sporns, Gerald M. Edelman, 1994, A measure for brain complexity: relating functional segregation and integration in the nervous system

s: Friston's free-energy principle proposes that self-organising systems minimise variational free energy, an upper bound on surprise, often decomposed as complexity minus accuracy.

src.l: Karl Friston, 2010, The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?

s: Dayan, Hinton, Neal & Zemel's 'Helmholtz machine' is introduced as a statistical inference engine for perception ('Following Helmholtz'), trained by maximising a lower bound on the data probability, expressed in terms of Helmholtz free energy (a statistical-mechanics quantity).

src.l: Peter Dayan, Geoffrey E. Hinton, Radford M. Neal, Richard S. Zemel, 1995, The Helmholtz Machine

s: Klimesch proposes a 'binary hierarchy' of EEG frequencies in which neighbouring band centre frequencies stand in 1:2 (doubling) relations, and argues the golden mean, as the 'most irrational' ratio, gives the best frequency separation between coupled oscillators.

s: Fechner (Elemente der Psychophysik II, 1860) models psychophysical activity as oscillation: a 'main wave' (Hauptwelle) whose crest lies above the threshold (Schwelle) in waking and below it in sleep, with smaller 'upper waves' (Oberwellen) above threshold carrying dream images; he suggests the temporal oscillation is causally linked to a spatial oscillation 'as in periodic phenomena in external nature'.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1860, Elemente der Psychophysik, vol. II
src.q: the peak of the main wave of our psychophysical activity, when pushed down below the threshold during sleep, normally occupies a different location than the peak above it during waking

s: Working definition (hard core): harmony is diversity in wholeness, where the parts and the whole strengthen each other. Ratios, consonance, mode-locking, health, justice and sustainability are manifestations, not the definition; dissonance belongs inside harmony, and its opposites are homogenization (whole without diversity) and fragmentation (diversity without whole).

s: Harmony should be treated as a Lakatosian research programme, like natural selection or spectroscopy: an untested hard core plus level-specific auxiliary hypotheses that must predict novel facts; 'survival of the harmonized' is circular unless harmony is measured independently of the outcome.

s: Harmony as free energy: −F = H + T·S, where H is constraint satisfaction among parts (Smolensky harmony = negative energy), S is entropy of open states (diversity), T the exchange rate. At T=0 the system freezes into lock; at high T, noise; 'diversity in wholeness' is the moderate-T optimum. RLHF's optimum π_ref·exp(r/β) is a special case.

s: Harmony ≈ Differentiation × Integration (product or geometric mean, zero if either is zero). The primary text for a compound measure is Hutcheson (1725): beauty is 'in a compound Ratio of Uniformity and Variety'. Leibniz's own line (Monadology §58) is only 'as great variety as possible, along with the greatest possible order' giving perfection; the 'unity in variety' formula long attributed to him is Latta's editorial note. Fechner (1876) adds an optimum. TSE neural complexity is an information-theoretic instance.

s: Harmony window: between fragmentation (coupling too weak) and unison (coupling too strong, 1:1 has the widest locking region) lies a band of coupling strength where diverse oscillators cohere; chimera states are a dynamical instance. Prediction for human–AI systems: diversity and joint productivity peak at intermediate mutual adaptation.

s: Lomas thesis: intelligence is harmonizing — integrating diverse motivations into coherent action that supports the whole; read substantively, harmonizing systems outperform narrow optimizers over long horizons, so alignment is the problem of the short horizon. Directly opposes Bostrom's orthogonality thesis; restates Plato's Republic wager.

Harmony is fit that keeps its tension; lock is fit with the tension gone. Exact lock (tidal 1:1, unison, seizure, monoculture) is not 'too much harmony' but its collapse into sameness; near-resonance keeps systems alive (cycles, sustain, character).

Mathematics has two harmonies: commensurability (rational ratios that lock coupled dissipative oscillators — consonance, fusion, entrainment) and maximal incommensurability (irrational ratios that let conservative systems avoid destructive resonance — KAM tori, with the golden mean conjectured the most robust, and golden-mean multiplexing). Both belong to the whole; cf. Philolaus' limit and unlimited.

src.l: Philolaus, F. W. A. Mullach (ed.), 5th c. BCE (ed. 1881), Fragmenta philosophorum graecorum, vol. 2 (Philolai fragmenta)

s: Bridge between feeling and number: because single sources (voices) are harmonic, brains evolved to treat harmonicity as a cue for 'one source', so the felt sense of harmony may be mathematics internalised by evolution. This explains why harmony feels good, not what it is like (the hard problem remains).

src.l: Daniel L. Bowling, Dale Purves, 2015, A biological rationale for musical consonance

s: Wellbeing is harmonizing within, peace harmonizing between, sustainability harmonizing with the whole AND across time — like tonal harmony, held together by a centre that lasts the length of the piece; a civilization consonant this quarter and ruinous next century is an unresolved chord.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Pairwise tuning drifts (the comma), so two parties tuned only to each other accumulate error; harmony across unlike parties needs a reference neither owns (in the tradition: cosmos, nature, the Good). For alignment: human and AI tuned to a third string, with nature as reference rather than as a third party to please; and the distribution of the comma is a justice question.

s: Design heuristics from oscillator physics for human–AI coupling: (1) unison is the strongest attractor, so homogenization is the default; (2) damp, don't detune — add friction/delay/disagreement rather than cut coupling (Millennium Bridge dampers); (3) tune the scale to both instruments — human–AI harmony needs its own 'scale', not imported human–human norms (Sethares); (4) beware a high-Q companion — sharply tuned to one person, rings long (echo chamber).

A harmony test for a human–AI–nature system: is it more differentiated (people, cultures, species keep distinct voices)? more integrated (parts inform and support each other)? are the parts strengthened, not only the whole? Yes/yes/yes = harmony; integration without differentiation = homogenization; differentiation without integration = fragmentation; strong whole with weakened parts = the totalitarian failure.

src.l: J. Derek Lomas, Haian Xue, 2022, Harmony in Design: A Synthesis of Literature from Classical Philosophy, the Sciences, Economics, and Design

s: Harmony is hierarchical — levels of wholeness (note, chord, song, album, culture; self, family, state, nature) — and persists when coupling is strong within a level and weak between levels (near-decomposability), with levels separated in timescale. Collapse modes: one fast level dictating the slow ones; one level absorbing the others.

s: Dikker et al. recorded portable EEG from a class of 12 high school students over 11 classes and report that brain-to-brain synchrony across students predicted class engagement and social dynamics, which they attribute likely to shared attention.

src.l: Suzanne Dikker, Lu Wan, Ido Davidesco, et al., 2017, Brain-to-brain synchrony tracks real-world dynamic group interactions in the classroom

s: In EEG from thousands of museum and festival visitors, pairs' empathy, social closeness, engagement and joint action/eye contact predicted inter-brain coupling, mainly in low alpha and beta bands, using metrics designed to resist noise-driven correlations.

src.l: Suzanne Dikker, et al., 2021, Crowdsourcing neuroscience: Inter-brain coupling during face-to-face interactions outside the laboratory

s: Across three experiments Wiltermuth and Heath found that people acting in synchrony cooperated more in later group economic exercises, including where it required personal sacrifice, and that positive emotion was not needed.

src.l: Scott S. Wiltermuth, Chip Heath, 2009, Synchrony and cooperation

s: Mogan et al. (2017) and Rennung & Goeritz (2016) meta-analyses found weak-to-moderate effects of interpersonal synchrony on prosociality, as characterised by Atwood et al. 2022.

src.l: Stephanie Atwood, Adena Schachner, Samuel A. Mehr, 2022, Expectancy Effects Threaten the Inferential Validity of Synchrony-Prosociality Research

s: A 2023 review of 215 hyperscanning studies found 27 different methods for computing inter-brain coupling (fNIRS dominant: 119 studies, 89 using wavelet coherence), raising comparability and reproducibility concerns.

src.l: (author list not retrieved), 2023, Quantification of inter-brain coupling: A review of current methods used in haemodynamic and electrophysiological hyperscanning studies

s: Synchrony-prosociality effects may be inflated by experimenter and participant expectancy: most published studies lack naive experimenters, and participants asked without doing synchrony predicted the published effects.

s: Two replications of Wiltermuth and Heath's Experiment 3 with experimenters naive to condition (Schachner & Garvin 2010) found no effect of synchrony on cooperation, conformity, trust, similarity or team feeling.

src.l: Stephanie Atwood, Adena Schachner, Samuel A. Mehr, 2022, Expectancy Effects Threaten the Inferential Validity of Synchrony-Prosociality Research

s: Inter-brain synchrony is hard to interpret: correlated EEG can arise from shared stimuli, shared attention or noise rather than interaction, so group-scale synchrony such as the classroom result does not show that people are 'in sync' through each other. Remedies proposed: behavioural data, mutual-prediction models, explanatory rather than correlational designs.

s: Mulford ('Thought Currents', 1890) holds that thought runs in currents 'as real as those of air and water', that we attract a like current by what we think and say, and that a person in low spirits ('blue') is joined to the current of all others in that mood, each strengthening it.

src.l: Prentice Mulford, 1888, Your Forces, and How to Use Them: Fifth Series
src.q: When you are in low spirits or "blue" you have acting on you the thought current coming from all others in low spirits. You are in oneness with the despondent order of thought.

s: Atkinson's Thought Vibration (1906; SL 1908 printing) states the New Thought 'Law of Attraction': thoughts are real things that go out as vibrations and combine with thoughts of like kind; a mind attracts only thoughts 'in harmony with its own', and one's prevailing thought or mood sets a 'keynote' that draws people and things that fit 'the mental tune'.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: But it attracts only those thoughts which are in harmony with its own. Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: I cite the above authorities merely to give you food for thought, not to attempt to demonstrate to you the fact that thought vibrations exist.

s: Besant (The Ancient Wisdom, 1897) describes mental training as refining the brain so that it 'can vibrate in unison with the thought-vibrations sent to it', its nervous matter becoming 'adapted to respond to thought-vibrations'.

src.l: Annie Besant, 1897, The Ancient Wisdom: An Outline of Theosophical Teachings
src.q: the coarser materials are gradually expelled to make room for the finer, which can vibrate in unison with the thought-vibrations sent to them

s: Townshend (Facts in Mesmerism, 1840/41) proposes that every thought moves the brain and, through a pervading ethereal medium, imparts motion that a mesmerised person can sense, so that mesmeriser and patient are brought 'into sympathetic vibration' and the patient 'takes ... the tone of his mind' from the mesmeriser's.

src.l: Chauncy Hare Townshend, 1841, Facts in Mesmerism, or Animal Magnetism
src.q: so as (if I may so express myself) to bring into sympathetic vibration the very brain and nervous fibres of mesmeriser and patient

s: Andrew Jackson Davis (The Principles of Nature, 1847) describes an impression as a vibration that 'undulates the portion of the mind with which it comes in contact', and states: 'This vibration is the idea.'

src.l: Andrew Jackson Davis, 1847, The Principles of Nature, Her Divine Revelations, and a Voice to Mankind
src.q: This vibration is the idea. The vibration and idea are simultaneous, yet perfect.

s: Henry Wood (1893) explains New Thought mental healing as treatment 'through thought-vibrations received' from a concentrated healer, and likens the patient to 'a discordant musical instrument' waiting 'to respond in unison to active harmony'.

src.l: Henry Wood, 1893, Ideal Suggestion Through Mental Photography
src.q: Treatments from another, through thought-vibrations received, bring the truth into the deeps of mind more directly than it comes by filtration from consciousness.

s: Hill (Think and Grow Rich, 1937, ch. 13 'The Brain') calls every human brain 'both a broadcasting and receiving station for the vibration of thought'; thought is 'energy travelling at an exceedingly high rate of vibration', emotion 'steps it up', and only such raised vibrations pass from one brain to another through the ether, on the model of radio.

src.l: Napoleon Hill, 1937, Think and Grow Rich

s: Hill (1937, ch. 3 'Faith') restates the law of attraction: thoughts mixed with feeling or emotion form a 'magnetic' force that attracts from the vibrations of the ether 'other similar, or related thoughts'; the ether carries both destructive and constructive vibrations, and the mind attracts those 'which harmonize with that which DOMINATES the human mind'.

src.l: Napoleon Hill, 1937, Think and Grow Rich

s: Hill (1937, ch. 15 'The Six Ghosts of Fear') says a fearful person 'transmits these destructive vibrations' to everyone nearby, that a dog or a horse 'will pick up the vibrations of fear thrown off by its master', and that fear passes mind to mind 'BY THE SELF-SAME MEDIUM' as radio.

s: Schott (1674) reports that Kircher tested the antipathy topos: he had one polychord strung with wolf-gut and one with sheep-gut strings, played the wolf one inside the sheepfold and both together outside, and observed neither the sheep's terror nor the strings rupturing; Schott concludes one should not assert such things, even from approved authors, without performing the experiment oneself.

src.l: Kaspar Schott, 1674, Magiae universalis naturae et artis, pars II, acustica
src.q: In order to make an experiment of some of these, Kircher had two polychords prepared, one strung with wolf-gut strings, the other with sheep-gut strings; and he had the wolf polychord played inside the sheepfold, then had both played together outside; but he could not in any way note the terror of the sheep, nor that celebrated rupturing of the strings born from antipathy, as was believed.
